Germany is getting rid of paper checks at the end of 2027. Australia is bidding them farewell by 2030. U.S. President Donald Trump followed up his order killing off the penny with an executive order stopping check writing by the federal government.

Should the U.S. follow these other countries and broadly eliminate the ability to write checks?

Years ago, experts predicted that checks would have disappeared by now. However, they are still around, and billions are written each year in the United States.

Why? The quick answer is that businesses love them. And plenty of Americans still use checks for good reasons. But there is more to the story.

open image in gallery Plenty of Americans still use checks for good reasons ( Getty Images/iStockphoto )

I am a business school professor and one of the few academics who advocates for the use of cash. While I have long told everyone about the benefits of paper money, I didn’t give paper checks much thought or use them until my mother’s recent death. Then I found myself writing checks to the cemetery, funeral home, gravestone engraver and a host of other places. Plus, I started getting refund checks back from her landlord and insurance companies.

These experiences made me look more deeply into this form of payment to understand what was happening.

Fewer checks for bigger bucks

Every three years the U.S. government runs the Federal Reserve Payments Study by asking banks and credit unions for internal information. This survey tracks everything from how often credit cards are used to the number of checks written.

While check usage has sharply declined in the U.S., a significant number – about 9.2 billion in 2024 – are still written, the data shows. The face value of those checks is probably bigger than you’d expect: more than US$24 trillion, not adjusted for inflation. That is almost as large as U.S. gross domestic product of $29 trillion that year.

Not everyone can imagine numbers in billions or trillions, so let’s put those figures in more manageable terms.

A little over 150 checks were written per person in 2000. By 2024, the average had plummeted to 27 checks – slightly more than two per month. However, over that time, the amounts typically scribbled or printed on the face of those checks rose.

In 2000, the typical check was worth less than $1,000. By 2024, the average amount had more than doubled to $2,600.

Trends elsewhere are similar. The Bank for International Settlements, which serves as a bank for central banks like the Federal Reserve, has tracked check usage in 25 countries since 2012. Its data shows that in only two other countries is payment by check still commonplace.

And in both of those countries, check usage has fallen more sharply than in the United States.

Who uses checks today?

While check payments have declined, there are still two big groups of check writers in the United States.

The Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta runs the Survey and Diary of Consumer Payment Choice. This survey asks people, rather than banks, for information on their payment habits. Roughly one-third of all respondents stated they used a paper check in the past 30 days.

Not surprisingly, the answers vary by age. About 60% of people 65 and over say they wrote a check. Among those 18 to 24, under 6% said they did.

It also turns out that a lot of people who think they never write checks actually unknowingly do it all the time. If you pay your bills online, your bank tries to pay them electronically. If it cannot electronically make the payment, the bank cuts a paper check on your behalf. Any online bill payment taking more than a couple of business days to post is being sent by check.

Another important factor is that small businesses love checks. Over 80% of businesses with sales between $1 and $10 million make payments using checks. Why? Small businesses often require two signatures on a check. The need for signatures means owners have to sign their name before any money goes out the door. This gives them control over money and a clear idea who is getting paid and how much.

Small businesses also like receiving checks. I wrote a lot of checks after my mother’s death because many of those small businesses I dealt with wanted an extra 3% and sometimes more to cover the cost to them of a credit card payment. Writing paper checks saved me and the businesses a lot of money.

The future

While many Americans still write checks, their declining usage clearly underscores that they are not ideal for making payments in all situations.

One of the biggest problems with checks is that you never know if the check writer has sufficient funds to cover the amount. When an account doesn’t have enough money, the check bounces. The Federal Reserve, which clears about one-third of all U.S. checks, returned about 22 million checks, with a total face value of around $80 billion. While these numbers are large, over 99% of all checks written don’t bounce.

Another problem with checks is forgery. Thieves steal checks from mailboxes, alter information and then cash them. The most recent figures show about 500,000 annual cases of check fraud in the U.S. Again, while a half-million is large, it is a tiny fraction of the 9.2 billion checks written annually.

About the author Jay L. Zagorsky is an Associate Professor of Business, Boston University. This article was first published by The Conversation and is republished under a Creative Commons licence. Read the original article.

Because of these problems, the Federal Reserve is contemplating leaving the check processing business. In early 2026, it accepted public comments on whether it should wind down, improve or leave alone its check processing unit.

The unit, which costs about $100 million a year to run, turned a $6.6 million profit in 2024. But its machines need replacing, and the Federal Reserve is wavering on spending the money.

Should checks be killed off like the penny, which the federal government stopped minting in 2025, and the haypenny, which was worth half a cent and hasn’t been produced since 1857?

For me, the answer is a clear no. While checks are clearly less important today than in the past, the numbers show that the American people and businesses still use and need checks.

News.title: One may lose an eye, another will live with it forever: Delhi protesters describe life-altering injuries after pellet-gun firing
News.content:

It happened within seconds. Scores of pellets shredded Shaikh Irshad Mansoori’s face, neck, and shoulder as Gen Z protesters took to the streets of Delhi demanding reform of India‘s education system, only to face police batons, teargas and, in some cases, pellet guns.

One of the pellets is still inside Mansoori’s body. It’s lodged too close to a critical blood vessel near his neck to be safely removed, doctors have told him, and he may have to live with it for the rest of his life.

Mansoori, 25, was marching alongside thousands of protesters to India’s parliament on 20 July when he says he was fired at from close range with a pellet gun, a controversial weapon capable of discharging hundreds of tiny balls of lead in a single shot.

He’s one of four people believed to have suffered pellet injuries during a brutal police crackdown that has drawn international criticism and failed to deter a youth-led movement that represents a major challenge to the authority of the prime minister, Narendra Modi.

The Delhi police have denied using pellet guns during the crackdown and issued a “fake news alert” on the claim, while another branch of the security forces has said it is investigating the reports.

open image in gallery Shaikh Irshad Mansoori in a Delhi hospital ( Supplied )

Mansoori, who works at a multinational company in Gurugram near Delhi, said he had travelled about 30 miles to the national capital that day for visa-related work and decided to briefly join the march on his way.

The march was called by the Cockroach Janata Party, a youth-led movement that has been protesting for more than a month to demand the resignation of education minister Dharmendra Pradhan over an exam paper leak that affected over two million students and reportedly caused at least 21 of them to take their lives.

As the protesters defied restrictions and marched towards the parliament, police and paramilitary forces used teargas and batons. The clashes left more than 60 protesters and 118 police personnel injured, according to local media.

open image in gallery Shaikh Irshad Mansoori in hospital ahead of his surgery ( Supplied )

Mansoori’s friend, who asked not to be named, described how the incident unfolded as Mansoori was still finding it difficult to speak at length following surgery to remove pellets from his body.

The friend told The Independent that Mansoori was with a group of marchers near Jantar Mantar, the main protest site, when police fired teargas and charged them with batons.

“Everyone was walking peacefully when police began firing teargas. People started feeling the smoke in their throats and eyes,” he said. “Irshad went ahead to plead with the security personnel not to hit them, saying they were only students, when a force member in blue pointed a gun at him.”

He said a member of the Rapid Action Force, a federal paramilitary, fired at Mansoori within seconds.

“Multiple pellets struck me and I felt a stinging sensation near my eyes,” Mansoori said. “Pellets pierced through my right eye and down onto my cheek and nose. I could taste blood, and I began bleeding from everywhere.”

open image in gallery Irshad Mansoori after pellets were removed from his face and near the eye ( Supplied )

Mansoori, who is from the central state of Madhya Pradesh and lives alone in Gurugram, was taken to hospital by fellow protesters.

He asked his family not to travel to Delhi, saying he was being looked after by friends. “He had three or four pellets that penetrated deep into his body. One was close to his eye, another deep in his neck, and one near his nose. Another hit his scalp, but that one didn’t cause much damage,” his friend said.

“Initially, the doctors said he would need three or four separate surgeries but the teams worked together and removed almost all the pellets in a single operation. Only one pellet, near his neck, remains, because it’s next to a critical blood vessel. They said they won’t touch it.”

Mansoori fears living with the pellet lodged in his body forever. “We asked what would happen to that pellet. The doctors said it would stay there for the rest of his life. We asked if they could guarantee nothing would happen because of it, but they said they could not make any guarantees, only that it would remain there permanently,” his friend said.

Pellet-firing shotguns were first used in the restive Himalayan region of Kashmir in 2010 to suppress anti-India protests, with authorities describing it as a “non-lethal” crowd-control weapon. In 2018, the government acknowledged in the parliament that 17 people had been killed by pellet guns in Kashmir during the previous two years.

More recently, Indian forces were accused of using pellet guns during the 2024 protests by farmers, though the police denied the allegations.

Not far from where Mansoori was shot at, Sahil Lohchab was leading a group of protesters with the Indian flag in his hand when he was similarly injured. The 20-year-old Delhi University student is most likely to turn “completely blind in his right eye” from pellet injuries, his friend Shivam Reddy tells The Independent.

Lohchab wanted to join police himself and sat for an entrance exam earlier this year. It’s an irony not lost on his family friends and given a permanent visual or hearing impairment can disqualify a person from ever joining the service.

Reddy said that Lohchab was leading a group of about 500 protesters when he was injured at around 3.30pm.

“He ran towards police and RAF to tell them to not attack them as they were protesting peacefully, but police likely perceived him as a threat and directly targeted him,” he said. “He was shot with a pellet gun. The pellets dispersed and hit him multiple times across his body and face.”

“There is only one per cent chance his eye could be saved, the doctors have told us,” Reddy said, adding that a doctor also confirmed his injuries were from a pellet gun.

open image in gallery Sahil Lohchab’s friends and family says he only has a slim chance of regaining vision in his eye ( Supplied )

Lohchab was moved from the Lady Hardinge Medical College hospital to the Safdarjung Hospital and even a private hospital but he couldn’t be treated due to his condition, Reddy said. “We then took him to AIIMS where he was admitted and he underwent surgery to have the pellets removed, including from his eye,” he said.

Lohchab’s friends expressed dissatisfaction with the Cockroach Janta Party – the group leading the protests – for not helping them or even reaching out to them.

"We went out for our country, but the Cockroach Janta Party should have at least tried to ask about the wellbeing of Sahil, who is going through so much pain and could have life-altering injuries," Reddy said.

They have launched a fundraiser to pay for Lohchab’s treatment and rehabilitation. “We seek support from the people, the government and campaigners for Sahil,” he said.

The Independent has reached out to the Rapid Action Force for comment by email. Attempts to reach its office by phone were unsuccessful.

The Rapid Action Force is the riot-control wing of the Central Reserve Police Force, the country’s largest paramilitary.

open image in gallery Sahil Lohchab after surgery to remove pellets from his face and chest ( Supplied )

The Central Reserve Police Force said they had initiated an inquiry to ascertain the exact sequence of events following reports of pellet injuries to students.

“We are comprehensively enquiring into the whole gamut of events. It will be premature to comment now,” a spokesperson told the Indian Express on Friday.

The Delhi police denied that its personnel forces had used pellet guns against the protesters, saying such claims were “completely false and misleading”.

“Delhi police neither possess pellet guns nor do they use them in the ongoing protest. The public is requested not to share or circulate any unverified or misleading information,” they said in an X post.

The two other people who reportedly suffered pellet injuries during the march have chosen to remain anonymous. One was said to be a reporter from Outlook magazine who was hit in the back and an arm.

He said he saw a security personnel raise a gun towards the crowd and turned his back. "I saw it aimed at me and immediately ran," he told his magazine.

"Something struck my backpack and my arm. If I hadn't turned, it could have hit my chest or my face."

“The people were pelting stones and the police were lobbing teargas cans,” he later told Scroll. “Then I saw them deploying pellet guns. I saw one personnel pointing a pellet gun at me. I turned around and started running and was hit in my back and hand.”

His prescription from a government hospital mentions "26 small round wounds” that are “consistent with pellets striking” the right side of his body “at an oblique angle”, according to Scroll.

“The defects cover an area of 32cm x 12cm with inverted margins and circumferential abrasion collars surrounding the individual perforations with patchy bluish coloured contusions surrounding the perforations suggestive of pellet entrance wounds,” it notes.

The fourth victim, who is seen in videos showing his injuries, was yet to be publicly identified. According to Alt News and The Wire, he sustained minor injuries.

The alleged use of pellets against student protesters has sparked widespread condemnation.

“The use of pellet guns against protesters began in Kashmir, and now those guns are being deployed in the nation's capital,” Amitav Ghosh, an award winning writer, said.

“One clear lesson of recent US and Indian history is that tactics that originate in the 'periphery' will eventually be used in the centre as well.”

Harsh Mander, author and activist, questioned who put pellet guns in the hands of the Rapid Action Force. “Does no one in the security establishment have a conscience?” he asked.

Romania shot down a foreign drone in its airspace on Friday in the first interception of its kind, amid growing concern over stray weapons straying into Nato territory.

An F-16 fighter jet shot down the drone near the town of Padina, in the east, at around 11am after it entered the country’s airspace, officials said, adding that an investigation was underway.

The Romanian army said the drone’s origin and purpose is yet to be identified, but chief of staff General Gheorghita Vlad said it appeared to be a Shahed - the Iran-designed attack drones used by Russia against Ukraine.

"Visually, the pilots reported the drone looked to be a Shahed type," he ⁠said, adding it was too soon to draw conclusions.

Earlier in the day an army source ​told ⁠Reuters: “There is an ongoing investigation to determine the ‌origin of the drone. But in this part of the world it is Russia that is the attacker.”

open image in gallery A Romanian air force F-16 jet shot down a drone in Romanian airspace on Friday (file image, 2024) ( AFP/Getty )

Western officials have accused Russia for months of testing Nato’s reactions with limited incursions across the border. Russia has denied deliberately provoking Nato allies. Ukrainian drones have also been identified crossing into neighbouring countries.

The incident intensifies concerns over the security of Nato's eastern flank, as the conflict between Russia and Ukraine continues.

The Romanian defence ministry said that the drone was picked up by radars at around 9.30am local time, around 12 miles east of Sulina on the Black Sea coast.

President Nicusor Dan said on social media that a Romanian pilot shot down the drone, adding: “The area was uninhabited, so the pilot was able to shoot without any risk.”

open image in gallery Romanian officials said the drone appeared to be an Iranian-designed Shahed (Shahed pictured over Iran in 2024, file) ( Middle East Images/AFP/Getty )

Fragments of the drone fell on a wheat field but caused no damage or injuries, the Buzau county ‌prefect told reporters.

Romania, which shares a 650-km (400-mile) land border with Ukraine, has reported more than a dozen ​breaches of its airspace by Russian drones since Moscow began attacking Ukrainian ports across the Danube ‌River following its full-scale invasion in 2022.

General Vlad ⁠said Russian attacks against Ukraine's Odessa region had increased ahead of the harvest season, ⁠further pressuring key energy and trade routes in the Black Sea.

At the end of June, the defence ministry detonated drone fragments found in the southeastern village of Rachelu, near the border with Ukraine. They said the fragments were from a Russian attack on Kyiv's port infrastructure in April.

The ministry at the time reported that Russian drones had breached its national airspace at least 15 times this year.

In late May, a drone crashed into an apartment building in the town ‌of Galati, near the ​Ukrainian border, injuring two people, the first time a ‌strike had hit a densely populated area in ​a Nato country and caused injuries during the Ukraine war.

Nato accused Moscow of “reckless behaviour” following the incident and reiterated its commitment to defend “every inch of Allied territory”.

More follows on this breaking news story....

Farmers have warned the industry "can't carry on like this" as they struggle following back-to-back heatwaves and prolonged periods of dry weather across the UK.

With drought declared in parts of Wales, regions across the east and south of England continue to suffer exceptionally low or no rainfall, leaving agricultural workers under severe pressure.

Ben Andrews, who runs Broadward Hall Farm in Herefordshire, told The Independent: “Our veg is seriously struggling this year. At this point, we’re really having to sit down and consider whether we’re even going to plant vegetables next year.

“For many farmers, this is the worst harvest yet, and for the second year in a row. We can’t carry on like this.”

open image in gallery Ben Andrews runs Broadward Hall Farm in Herefordshire ( Supplied )

Mr Andrews is a fourth-generation farmer who keeps up to 600 acres of land with permanent grazing cattle, and grows vegetables including potatoes, broccoli, kale and lettuce for a national veg box scheme.

“I'd say a lot of farmers have taken big hits because of this weather,” he warned.

The National Drought Group earlier this week identified eight areas as being in "prolonged dry weather", which is the final stage before an official drought is declared.

Simon Wright, who runs Lamb Farm in Romney Marsh, on the Kent-East Sussex border, told The Independent: “I farm livestock and it’s probably one of the driest times we’ve ever had, I think.

“All of our fields are divided by ditches which obviously keep our sheep and cows in the right place, but all the ditches are now dry so basically the sheep and cows just wander where they like. Water is a problem too. Luckily we have got mains water, but it’s obviously going to cost us a fortune."

open image in gallery Simon Wright keeps thousands of animals at Lamb Farm in Romney Marsh ( Supplied )

The farmer, who keeps several thousand sheep and cattle across 1,200 acres of property, added: "We’ve run out of food. We’re starting to use our winter food. We’ve just started feeding the sheep hay now, and then hopefully the weather’s going to break. It’s very expensive. Normally they rely on eating grass at this time of year.

“There’ll be no profit in the job if it carries on like this for much longer – we’ll be digging into the reserves.”

National Farmers’ Union deputy president, Paul Tompkins, said growers are working "around the clock" to water crops and care for livestock, coming off the back of consecutive years of volatile weather.

"For many arable farmers, this could be another difficult and expensive harvest after extreme weather impacts in both 2024 and 2025, which saw both drought and flood,” he said.

Mr Tompkins urged the government to strengthen long-term resilience against climate change by overhauling licensing and easing planning rules to make building on-farm water reservoirs easier.

open image in gallery Mr Wright said the animals at his farm are already having to be given their winter food because there isn’t enough grass for them to eat ( Supplied )

Mr Andrews added: “It’s only getting hotter. The weather is getting more extreme – six months ago, our crops were basically underwater.

“Farms in the North, who haven’t been too badly affected yet, will be. This is a warning not to wait; farmers need to be prepared.

“We need to have better weather-proofing so we can be more resilient, because nobody is escaping this.”

Retailers say they are also monitoring the situation closely as reduced crop yields threaten to push up grocery prices.

Andrew Opie, director of food and sustainability at the British Retail Consortium (BRC), said: "Extreme weather, including drought, can affect crop yields and place upward pressure on prices.”

He added retailers are looking into alternative suppliers where appropriate to minimise the impact on shoppers.

open image in gallery Large parts of England are on the verge of drought, according to the National Drought Group ( PA Archive )

Forecasters offer little prospect of immediate relief. Will Lang, chief meteorologist at the Met Office, warned rainfall over the coming weeks is “unlikely to be widespread or substantial”, particularly in the driest southern regions.

Helen Wakeham, chair of the National Drought Group and director of water at the Environment Agency, said hot conditions were rapidly depleting resources while pushing demand higher.

“This is a difficult combination, and we are seeing the effects on our farmers, our wildlife, and the amount available for public and business use,” she said, urging the public to conserve water where possible.

A spokesperson for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said the government recognises the toll extreme weather takes on the sector.

"We are helping the sector build greater resilience to climate shocks through our farming schemes and through our work with the National Drought Group," they added.

News.content:

President Donald Trump touted a non-binding pledge Thursday, calling on U.S. power producers and data centers to fund or construct energy infrastructure.

The initiative aims to meet the escalating power demands of artificial intelligence while simultaneously protecting consumers from soaring electricity costs.

However, consumer advocacy groups and other critics of the administration swiftly dismissed the pledge as an empty promise. They argue it fails to address public anger over rising utility bills, even as Trump champions an aggressive build-out of AI-related infrastructure as part of his economic agenda to win the AI race against China.

The burgeoning demands of data centers are straining already overloaded transmission lines, a problem compounded by labor shortages in the power sector and plant retirements. This has made rising energy costs a volatile issue for voters ahead of November's elections.

open image in gallery Trump first introduced the pledge with prominent AI and technology firms in March ( Getty Images )

"Under this groundbreaking plan, America's largest tech companies have formally committed to fund or build all energy infrastructure required to meet the demand they are placing on the grid," Trump said at an Environmental Protection Agency event attended by Republican governors, power sector CEOs, and data center developers.

He added, "So they're going to be funding all of those electric needs, and we're giving them the right to build their own power plants."

The Energy Information Administration predicts average annual residential electricity prices will climb by 5.1% in 2026 and 2.4% in 2027, before accounting for inflation. Meanwhile, community meetings across many states have seen residents vehemently oppose data center developments, citing concerns over noise, environmental impact, and their contribution to higher electric bills.

Trump, however, offered a more positive outlook, remarking, "You have communities that really want the data centers, and frankly those are the smart communities."

Trump’s data center pledge blasted by critics

Critics question whether the voluntary pledge will genuinely prevent higher bills as AI power demand accelerates. Jesse Lee, a senior adviser at advocacy group Climate Power, criticized the pledge's lack of enforcement mechanisms, labeling it a "pinky promise."

Lee further asserted, "Instead of allowing affordable, scalable clean energy onto the grid, Trump has actively pressured tech companies to power their data centers with fossil fuels that will increase utility costs and expose Americans to toxic pollutants."

Josh Levi, president of the Data Center Coalition, defended the industry, highlighting its role in powering essential services such as telehealth appointments, digital classrooms, secure banking systems, and air traffic control networks.

open image in gallery Protesters hold up signs on a pedestrian bridge during a nationwide demonstration against AI data center expansion in Berkeley, California on July 18, 2026 ( AFP via Getty Images )

The event saw attendance from Republican governors of Georgia, Idaho, Louisiana, and Nebraska, alongside chief executives Drew Marsh of Entergy Corp and Chris Womack of Southern Co. A Reuters analysis indicates Marsh and Womack are among a group of CEOs at the 15 largest U.S. power companies holding nearly $1 billion in stock-based pay, a value expected to rise as firms invest in grid improvements.

At the heart of the political debate over data centers is PJM Interconnection, the largest U.S. grid operator.

Analysts at Siebert Williams Shank describe PJM as "the face of a national problem," citing its struggle with unprecedented power consumption, power plant retirements, transmission line congestion, and construction bottlenecks. They noted, "AI data centers did not create every challenge facing electric systems, but they have amplified nearly all of them."

PJM is grappling with escalating costs as it manages electricity flow for 67 million people from Washington, D.C., to Chicago. In PJM's latest capacity-market auction, which secures power for peak demand, data centers accounted for $6.3 billion in capacity-market charges, nearly 40% of the total. These charges are ultimately passed on to customers through their monthly bills.

News.title: Africa improves health defences, but it remains vulnerable to pandemics
News.content:
Africa is significantly better prepared for a pandemic than it was five years ago, a major review of the continent’s health security has found.

The review, which tracked dozens of health metrics across the continent, found that local and international investments in Africa’s health sector since the pandemic have “paid off.”

Published by the Brown University Pandemic Centre and the Nuclear Threat Initiative, a US non-profit, the report is the third of its kind and provides an update on two previous reviews from 2019 and 2021.

Investment in health by African governments grew rapidly during the pandemic. Post-pandemic, the average spend now sits at around 7.4 per cent of GDP, roughly $135 billion per year across the continent.

That figure still falls significantly below those of high-income countries, where the average spend on health sits at around 11.2 per cent of GDP.

The new African Health Security Index report found that almost every African country – 53 out of 54, excluding only the Republic of the Congo – has improved its ability to prevent, detect, and respond to disease outbreaks since 2021, the last time the index was updated.

Overall, the continent scores 41.2 out of 100 on its health security – up from 32.9 five years ago.

The score is built from hundreds of specific indicators covering things like how far people live from a hospital, how well infectious patients can be isolated, the size and training level of the health workforce, laboratory capacity, and the availability of vaccines and other critical medicines during an outbreak.

News.title: Ebola death toll passes 1,000 as outbreak shows no signs of slowing
News.content:
More than 1,000 people have now died in the outbreak of Ebola in the Congo, as medics struggle to curb the fastest-growing epidemic of the virus.

Dozens of deaths are being recorded each day and modelling has forecast that, in a worst case scenario, it could become the worst Ebola outbreak in history.

The outbreak, centred on the north east of Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), passed the four-figure death milestone little more than two months after it was first declared.

By contrast, the worst outbreak of the haemorrhagic fever on record, which struck West Africa from 2014 to 2016, took eight months from the first case to reach 1,000 deaths. It went on to kill 11,000 people.

The latest figures from the DRC’s national public health institute show 2,536 confirmed Ebola cases and 1,033 deaths, with at least 738 patients in isolation or hospitalised.

News.title: Inflation fall a ‘false dawn’, Burnham warned
News.content:
Falling inflation is a “false dawn” for Andy Burnham, economists warned after the pace of price rises slowed in June.

The consumer prices index (CPI) fell from 2.8pc in May to 2.6pc last month, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS), beating economists’ expectations of a drop to 2.7pc to mark the lowest rate in 15 months.

Lower petrol and diesel prices drove the slowdown amid a short-lived peace deal between the US and Iran, while price pressures from chocolate, oils and fats, dairy and meat also weakened.

However, economists warned a rise in household energy bills in July may already have pushed inflation back up above 3pc.

Suren Thiru, chief economist at the Institute of Chartered Accountants, said: “June’s slowdown is a false dawn as it may have already been reversed this month with higher energy bills, following Ofgem’s energy price cap rise, likely to have lifted inflation above 3pc.”

July’s 13pc increase in the energy price cap has pushed typical annual bills to around £1,862, while renewed fighting between the US and Iran has reignited concerns over oil and gas supplies.

Mr Thiru said elevated inflation would create a fresh headache for John Healey, the newly appointed Chancellor, by squeezing household budgets, raising government borrowing costs and limiting his room for tax cuts or spending increases.

Charlotte O’Leary, at the National Institute of Economic and Social Research, said: “June’s peace deal and the subsequent reduction in oil and gas prices helped cool consumer price inflation. This will be a welcome figure to start the new Prime Minister’s premiership, but the honeymoon period will be short-lived.”

The Bank of England will also be watching closely as it weighs further interest rate cuts, though economists warned renewed instability in the Middle East and higher energy bills could keep inflation close to 3pc for the rest of the year.

Mr Healey said: “Falling inflation is news families want to hear, but there is much more to do to give people the breathing space they need.”

News.title: Russia destroys Ukraine HIV warehouse
News.content:
A Russian missile strike has destroyed $2.6m (£1.9m) worth of HIV prevention supplies in Ukraine, according to an international aid group.

The Alliance for Public Health said the attack on Sunday night near Kyiv hit a warehouse holding 62 million prevention items earmarked for Ukraine’s harm reduction programmes next year. It includes syringes, needles, alcohol wipes, and condoms intended to support more than 300,000 people.

“This is not just another strike. It is an attack on 300,000 Ukrainians who depend on HIV prevention services and on their fundamental right to health,” said Andriy Klepikov, executive director of the Alliance for Public Health.

Efforts to prevent the spread of HIV rely heavily on harm reduction programmes that supply sterile syringes and needles to people who inject drugs, alongside condoms and other supplies that help curb sexual transmission.

Mr Klepikov said the destruction of the warehouse would not immediately disrupt services, because his organisation had moved its supplies for the rest of the year out of central storage and into regional distribution centres several weeks ago as part of contingency planning.

“Russia failed,” he said, adding that the Alliance had notified international partners and appealed for urgent support to rebuild next year’s inventory.

News.title: Private sector pay suffers worst growth since Covid
News.content:
Private sector wages are growing at their slowest pace since the pandemic, piling pressure on Andy Burnham as he enters Downing Street facing a fragile economy and strained public finances.

Salaries rose by 2.9pc in the three months to May, the first time growth has dipped below 3pc since October 2020 and only narrowly ahead of inflation at 2.8pc.

The slowdown was most acute in key industries, with wages in finance and business services up just 2.3pc, manufacturing at 2.5pc and construction earnings falling by 0.2pc over the year.

In contrast, public sector pay accelerated to 5.5pc after striking workers secured higher settlements, widening the gap between state and private sectors.

The cooling labour market came as borrowing overshot official forecasts, leaving John Healey, the new Chancellor, with a £2.7bn gap against expectations.

The Government borrowed £57.6bn between April and June – less than a year earlier but still ahead of projections – pushing public debt to nearly £3tn, or 94.9pc of GDP.

Mr Healey said: “The Prime Minister and I have talked about how we will work in lockstep to meet the fiscal rules with a buffer against uncertainty and how we’ll make life more affordable for working people right across the UK.”

However, Sir Mel Stride, the shadow business secretary, said: “If Andy Burnham and John Healey are really serious about the future of our economy then they must get borrowing under control.”

News.title: Scammers stole $114 billion as Southeast Asia’s crime gangs go corporate
News.content:
Scam gangs stole up to $114 billion from people in Asia-Pacific alone in 2025, the UN has warned, as crime syndicates rapidly professionalise their tactics to evade law enforcement in Southeast Asia.

By way of comparison, the sum dwarfs the $85 billion the UK spends each year on defence.

The Asia-Pacific region has emerged as an epicentre for massive cyber fraud operations since the Covid pandemic. Scammers – some willingly, others under duress – are now stealing billions from internet users across the world via fake romance and cryptocurrency investment schemes.

In 2025, these fraud operations stole between $88.3 and $114.1bn from just people across East Asia, Southeast Asia, Australia and New Zealand, according to a report on Tuesday from the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC).

Those figures are triple the estimated losses in 2023, between $18 and $37bn, and don’t account for victims in Europe or the US.

The scam centres – which began in fortified compounds but are now increasingly housed in innocuous office blocks and villas – are found across the region, but have especially exploited power vacuums caused by war, corruption and weak governance in Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos.

Although the scammers initially targeted people in China, they have dramatically expanded their ambitions. The UNODC said people from at least 80 countries and territories had been identified in compounds, with recruiters seeking people from outside Asia as they look to expand new markets.

News.title: UK borrowing costs rise at fastest pace in G7
News.content:
Britain’s borrowing costs rose at the fastest pace in the G7 after Andy Burnham said he would take a “flexible” approach to the UK’s fiscal rules.

In his maiden speech as prime minister, Mr Burnham on Monday signalled he could bend the rules underpinning Britain’s finances, spooking financial markets fearful of higher government spending.

UK gilts – a benchmark for how much the Government pays on its debt – saw yields rise 0.08 percentage points to an eight-week high of 5.03pc for the 10-year bond. Thirty-year gilts also pushed higher.

The rise was the fastest in the G7, excluding Japan, whose markets are closed for a national holiday.

After markets closed on Monday, Mr Burnham surprised the City by picking John Healey as his next Chancellor.

Mr Healey, who quit over defence funding rising too slowly, will now be tasked with finding billions of pounds in Britain’s stretched public finances.

Shabana Mahmood, the Home Secretary, had widely been expected for the role. Ed Miliband, the former Energy Secretary, was also in contention.

Mr Healey will replace Rachel Reeves, who resigned on Monday.

The appointment of Mr Healey, a veteran of the Blair-Brown government, may calm fears in the City after Mr Burnham pledged to stretch the fiscal rules by using “flexibility” within them.

Speaking in Downing Street, Mr Burnham said: “I’ve said we’ll stick to the fiscal rules, and by that I mean the existing fiscal rules, and use obviously any flexibility within them.”

James Athey, a fund manager at Marlborough, said: “It’s not a good start because bandying around the words fiscal rules seems to be believed within government circles to be a sufficient condition to get financial markets on side, and that just misunderstands an element of the problem.”

He added that investors were watching closely for any signs that the Government will increase borrowing.

Matt Amis, investment director at Aberdeen, said Mr Burnham’s comments had “got the markets’ attention.”

He said “It just shows this week in particular the language from the Burnham administration, the new chancellor, is going to be key here. The gilt market is on edge.”

Mr Burnham, who has become the UK’s seventh prime minister in just a decade, has inherited a troubled economy as businesses grapple with low confidence and strained public finances.

Monday’s comment suggests the new prime minister will use measures to raise borrowing while keeping the additional sums off the Government’s book.

The Resolution Foundation, a think tank, said he could do this by expanding the remit of institutions like the National Wealth Fund, an arms-length government investment vehicle.

His plan to use “flexibility” in the fiscal rules comes after Ms Reeves altered the main indicator of government debt in 2024.

She tweaked the primary measure of the UK’s debt to Public Sector Net Financial Liabilities, meaning that when public financial institutions borrow to invest in a private business it does not count towards the government’s fiscal rules.

However, the think tank warned that boosting the financial capacity of public financial institutions like the National Wealth Fund by £16bn would cost around £400 million a year in debt interest.

Helen Miller, director at the Institute for Fiscal Studies, warned that challenging public finances will mean Mr Burnham will be forced to make tough choices on spending.

She said: “While chancellors come and go, the underlying fiscal constraints remain the same. Public debt, borrowing and debt-interest costs are all high. One in every £12 the government spends currently goes on debt interest.”

Higher borrowing costs threaten to increase the Government’s debt interest bill, which is already forecast to hit £111.2bn for the financial year - equivalent to 8.3pc of public spending.

Mr Burnham said he would announce a set of measures on Tuesday to give households “breathing space” to help with the cost of living.

“I will set out some of those measures starting tomorrow, including how we pay for them,” he said.

“We will help more young people into education... and we will build more council homes. That is the fair and sustainable way to bring the welfare bill down, to meet our fiscal rules and to honour our commitments on defence to our international partners.”

Mr Amis said: “Tomorrow we’re getting some cost of living news. [Burnham] said he was going to state where that funding’s come from. I think that’s key, any unfunded spending from here would get the market’s attention.”

Bradley Barcola, Manu Kone and Aurelien Tchouameni could be on the move this summer

Liverpool, Manchester United and Arsenal are looking to get busy in the transfer market, while Chelsea completed the biggest deal of the summer in landing Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa

Welcome to Mirror Football's live transfer blog for Friday, July 24.

The World Cup is over and now the focus is on the Premier League with clubs all over the world continuing their preparations. Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes is set to put rumours of an Old Trafford exit to bed as he has agreed to extend his Red Devils stay.

After missing out on Victor Munoz and Johan Manzambi, Newcastle United are closing in on a fourth signing of the summer. The Magpies are on the verge of signing Aladji Bamba from Monaco with the 20-year-old flying to the North East to complete his move.

Liverpool are facing a crucial summer under new head coach Andoni Iraola and amid the backdrop of takeover talks, the former Cherries boss wants transfers.

The Reds made an approach for PSG target Maghnes Akliouche with the Parisiens unable to meet the demands of Ligue 1 rivals AS Monaco. Meanwhile, Liverpool are said to be leading the race to sign Bradley Barcola, a move which would be another blow for Arsenal, who are also rumoured to hold an interest.

There's a month to go until the Premier League returns, and with pre-season getting underway across the division, the transfer action is picking up. Chelsea completed a deal to sign England star Morgan Rogers after footing up a £117million fee to set the pace for the summer while Alejandro Garnacho has joined Aston Villa on loan.

Arsenal have welcomed Christos Tzolis from Club Brugge, but their bid to sign Newcastle star Bruno Guimaraes is stealing the headlines. The Magpies remain adamant that their captain is not for sale but could they see an Alexander Isak repeat?

Follow all of the transfer news, rumours and updates below:

Sports.title: Leandro Paredes breaks silence on World Cup final conspiracy theories and Spain victory
Sports.content:
Leandro Paredes breaks silence on World Cup final conspiracy theories and Spain victory

Spain's World Cup win over Argentina in extra time, thanks to Ferran Torres goal, is the subject of conspiracy theories, and their opponents are now addressing them

View 2 Images Leandro Paredes has spoken out about the World Cup final back in Argentina (Image: Diego Alberto Haliasz, Getty Images)

Leandro Paredes believes Spain were worthy World Cup winners and is not entertaining talk of conspiracy theories after the final. Argentina's midfielder was central to the controversial scenes after Sunday's match, pushing and shoving multiple opposition players.

‌



Paredes, 32, is now back in his homeland, where he plays for Boca Juniors. Instead of taking a break like most of his international team-mates, he is already playing in South America, as the season has resumed after pausing for this summer's tournament.

‌



He played the full 90 minutes of their first game back. Paredes even assisted the game's only goal against O'Higgins.

‌



World Cup star allegedly tests positive for cocaine after double police stop READ MORE :

Jude Bellingham's parting shot to Argentina referee in unseen World Cup footage READ MORE :

Afterwards, he was inevitably asked about the World Cup. Conspiracy theories were among the topics of conversation.

Footage of Lionel Messi addressing his players before the match, urging them to "forget what happened", has sparked speculation that something suspicious took place. A clip of the incident doing the rounds on social media appears to show Enzo Fernandez and Lisandro Martinez visibly distressed as they emerge from the dressing room.

Martinez was substituted just before the break, apparently through injury, having already been booked. Fernandez departed early, too, after receiving his marching orders in the third minute of second-half stoppage time.

‌



View 2 Images Leandro Paredes lost his head after Argentina lost the World Cup final to Spain (Image: Al Bello, Getty Images)

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Paredes, however, has refused to entertain the rumours. In quotes reported by AS and translated into English from Spanish, he said: "Spain was superior to us in the final; they are a fair winner of the World Cup.

‌



"We don't give a damn about these theories. If it's what I hear, I have to go crazy.

"Everything that was said before, during and after the World Cup. We had a great tournament. We have to enjoy what we achieved in these eight years; it was a spectacular process. Surely we will fall when time passes because it is something incredible."

He told ESPN: "For many, it will be a decision whether to continue or not. It was a spectacular process. It will be very difficult to maintain this level and keep the group functioning in this way. You have to think, take stock, and talk to the coach. Decisions must be made calmly. I don't know if I'm going to go on.

"I think it's going to be a long process to overcome what we experienced. Although we achieved a lot, the pain of losing the final is going to hurt for a long time, because we were very close again.

"But we have to enjoy it because it's not easy to maintain the level we had for so long to achieve what we did. Although we lost the final, I think we had a World Cup where the people saw themselves reflected, and for us that is very gratifying."

Sports.title: Two West Ham transfers sum up mad market - but the spending is not going to stop
Sports.content:
Two West Ham transfers sum up mad market - but the spending is not going to stop

Al-Hilal are forking out big money for Crysencio Summerville but Premier League clubs are still the main spenders and are already heading for a record-breaking window

View 3 Images Crysencio Summerville is joining Al Hilal after two seasons at West Ham United (Image: Getty Images)

If anything symbolises the madness of the transfer market, it is the selling business done by West Ham United since they were relegated to the Championship. They have sold Mateus Fernandes to Spurs for £85million and just when you thought the silly money was confined to Premier League purchasers, along come Al-Hilal with £55million for Crysencio Summerville, it seems.

‌



Some reports suggest the fee could go up to £60million, some suggest £65million. And there are some who thought the Saudis had curbed their daft spending.

‌



Seriously, Summerville is a nice player to watch - and, at 24, at a nice age - but in the two seasons he had after joining West Ham from Leeds for £25million, he made 50 Premier League appearances and scored the grand total of six Premier League goals. He produced four assists in those 50 appearances.

‌



He had a decent World Cup, scoring for the Netherlands against Japan and Sweden, but has been prone to long periods of low productivity. He started last season by going 16 Premier League matches without a goal and finished it by going seven Premier League matches without a goal.

He was part of the reason West Ham went down - as, of course, was Fernandes, who was making it two relegations on the spin after helping Southampton into the Championship. Yet somehow, West Ham have got a minimum of £140million for this pair.

We know the market inflates at a serious rate but it is getting to the stage where it simply does not make sense. Summerville cost West Ham £25million two years ago. Has he really improved that much?

‌



View 3 Images Chelsea had to pay £117million to prise Morgan Rogers away from Aston Villa (Image: Darren Walsh, Chelsea FC via Getty Images)

Of course, the same could apply to so many of the signings made this summer. This is shaping up to be another record-breaking transfer window.

It does not close until September 1 - more than five weeks away - and by my rough calculations, well over £1.6billion has been spent by Premier League clubs alone. On the global list of spenders this summer, Premier League clubs occupy the top six places.

‌



Spurs head the table, followed by Chelsea and Manchester City, with Newcastle United in fourth spot. Newcastle, though, are showing a £50million profit as it stands.

With big transfer fees come big wages and there is no doubt a lot of clubs will be treading carefully when it comes to complying with the Premier League’s financial regulations. But there does not seem to be much restraint right now.

View 3 Images West Ham United pocketed £85million from the sale of Mateus Fernandes to Spurs (Image: Spurs)

‌



The money, of course, has to come from somewhere and it is the fans who will eventually pay. But as attendances continue to be exceptional and commercial interest remains high, Premier League clubs feel empowered to take the transfer market to new levels.

A lot of people say the bubble has to burst. And the sort of money that is being spent on some players - a combined £233million on Morgan Rogers and Elliot Anderson - feels like madness.

But there is no sign of it stopping. And it is hard to deny the market madness is a big part of what makes the Premier League so compelling.

Sports.title: Bruno Guimaraes agent takes to social media as Arsenal prepare £70m bid for Newcastle star
Sports.content:
Bruno Guimaraes agent takes to social media as Arsenal prepare £70m bid for Newcastle star

Bruno Guimaraes' agent has posted a cryptic message on social media amid reports that Arsenal are preparing a £70million bid for the Newcastle United midfielder

View 2 Images Arsenal are believed to be preparing a bid for Newcastle's Bruno Guimaraes (Image: Richard Lee/Shutterstock)

The representative of Bruno Guimaraes, Alexis Malavolta, has shared a social media update just as Arsenal intensify their pursuit of the Newcastle United midfielder. It comes amid suggestions from London that the Gunners are preparing a £70million offer for Guimaraes.

‌



However, sources on Tyneside insist Arsenal's chances of landing Guimaraes for anything close to £70m are a 'non‑starter.' Speculation has grown following Newcastle's capture of Aladji Bamba from Monaco, but it is not believed that the youngster has been signed as a direct successor to Guimaraes.

‌



Our colleagues at ChronicleLive previously reported that neither the player nor his representatives have submitted a formal transfer request, and Guimaraes remains under contract at St James’ Park for at least another two years.

‌



Arsenal readying player-plus-cash offer in mega Julian Alvarez transfer bid READ MORE :

Arsenal can give Bruno Guimaraes perfect sweetener if £70million transfer goes through READ MORE :

On Thursday, Guimaraes' representative, Malavolta, shared a mysterious message on social media. The photograph, uploaded via his Instagram story, depicted him positioned at the bow of a vessel, gazing across a vivid blue ocean in an unidentified location.

With his right arm lifted to his head, potentially engaged in a telephone conversation, the sole caption accompanying the image stated: "Always working."

View 2 Images Alexis Malavolta posted a cryptic message on Instagram

‌



The message appeared just a few hours before claims of a £70m bid for Guimaraes started to surface. It's difficult to determine whether the post was connected to the midfielder, but the timing is undoubtedly significant.

Guimaraes continues to be a priority target for Premier League champions Arsenal, though as reported by ChronicleLive, Newcastle have not yet received any formal approach from the Gunners.

While the Magpies' position remains firm, the circumstances would shift dramatically should he lodge a transfer request, with Newcastle prepared to take a hardline approach and demand a figure nearer £100million. This sits considerably above the sums being discussed from Arsenal's camp, which have ranged from as little as £45m to £60m.

‌



FOLLOW OUR ARSENAL FB PAGE! Latest Gunners news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Newcastle will be determined to prevent a repeat of last summer's impasse, when Alexander Isak refused to return to pre-season following the opening week in Austria. The Swede declined to travel to Singapore and South Korea for the club's Far East tour and subsequently trained alone in Spain.

He never re-joined the main squad after that point and eventually secured his £125m transfer to Liverpool.

Article continues below

Regarding Guimaraes, the internal belief is that the 28 year old will report back during the first week of August, with Eddie Howe eager to ensure he's completely concentrated on the 2026/27 season.

Sports.title: Jurgen Klopp issues spiky ultimatum after taking Germany job - 'I will be gone'
Sports.content:
Jurgen Klopp issues spiky ultimatum after taking Germany job - 'I will be gone'

Jurgen Klopp has become Germany manager on a four-year contract and the former Liverpool boss did not hold back in his first press conference while addressing the media

View 2 Images Jurgen Klopp speaking at his first press conference as Germany manager (Image: Markus Ulmer - GES Sportfoto/Getty Images)

Jurgen Klopp has threatened to walk away from his role as Germany manager on the first day in the job. The former Liverpool boss was announced as Julian Nagelsmann's successor on a four-year deal on Friday - and immediately went on the offensive.

‌



The 59-year-old has left his role as Red Bull's global head of soccer to try and turn around the team which was knocked out of the World Cup in the last 32 by Paraguay. Klopp will work alongside his former Liverpool assistants Pep Lijnders and Peter Krawietz.

‌



He left Liverpool in 2024, having grown tired of the intense job and has enjoyed stepping away from the spotlight. And it seems that while the national team job is a dream one, Klopp is not looking forward to the increased scrutiny.

‌



Klopp succeeding Nagelsmann has been an open secret for some time and that appears to have frustrated him - and prompted an ultimatum for the press. "Now is the time where I'm really in the middle of the media focus," he said at a press conference in Frankfurt.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Jurgen Klopp officially named as Germany boss as worst-kept secret in football confirmed READ MORE :

Argentina president goes on rant as calls for country to be banned from World Cup grow READ MORE :

"I was surprised, not negatively or positively surprised, at how fast news spread. And it's sometimes hard for people to just think 'let's turn a blind eye to things' and not to divulge any information. Sometimes that is the right thing to do, not to publish things that happened.

‌



“I know full well this is job number one for me. It is my mission to make the national squad better and to hope the pool for me to choose from is bigger.

“But it is not something I will do against you, but I’m doing it for you. It is an honour. I will be remunerated very graciously and if tomorrow it's 'Jurgen Klopp is s***', then I will be gone.

View 2 Images Jurgen Klopp gave the media an ultimatum (Image: Markus Ulmer - GES Sportfoto/Getty Images)

‌



“But if the DFB (German FA) says ‘Come on let us not continue the job’ then that’s it. And if you (the media) behave badly and don’t let my family live in peace. I’ll be gone and I'll just turn away.

“I know there are other countries where the national team head coaches are treated even worse. But I love this job, but I’m always ready to call just call it quits if need be.

“Jurgen Klopp is not going to have any ‘career’ after the national team, this is the absolute pinnacle of my footballing career as a coach. I will give everything I’ve got."

Article continues below

Klopp won the Premier League, Champions League, FA Cup and two League Cups during a hugely successful nine-year spell at Liverpool. He departed two years ago due to burn-out but is now recharged for the Germany job.

Sports.title: Jude Bellingham's parting shot to Argentina referee in unseen World Cup footage
Sports.content:
Jude Bellingham's parting shot to Argentina referee in unseen World Cup footage

Jude Bellingham has been spotted clashing with the referee from England's defeat to Argentina in the World Cup semi-final in new footage

View Image Jude Bellingham was emotional following England's defeat to Argentina (Image: Justin Setterfield, Getty Images)

Fresh ref cam footage has surfaced showing Jude Bellingham lambasting the official's 'shocking decisions' following England's defeat to Argentina.

‌



The Three Lions' World Cup dreams were ended as La Albiceleste came from behind to earn a place in the final. There was no shortage of frustration on display from England as Argentina racked up fouls throughout the game.

‌



Moroccan-USA referee Ismail Elfath came in for considerable scrutiny before kick-off after being labelled Lionel Messi's favourite official.

‌



Argentina racked up 12 fouls in the opening half against England but received just one yellow card. Bellingham was dragged down on four separate occasions as he attempted to launch counterattacks.

The Stourbridge-born midfielder's frustration with Argentina's aggressive tactics was plain to see as they sought to halt him by any means necessary. Bellingham told the referee exactly what he thought after the full-time whistle.

Argentina FA intervene as World Cup final conspiracy theories emerge after Spain win READ MORE :

The Real Madrid star was visibly furious at how the match was handled. In the ref-cam footage, Bellingham can be seen shaking Elfath's hand before remarking, "Some shocking ones but all the best."

‌



During the game, Bellingham was also spotted in animated conversation with Argentina captain Messi. However, he played down their interaction following the match,

"The chat with Messi? Actually, we were arguing about a foul. It wasn't anything serious. I'm sure everyone will make a big deal out of it, but it was nothing," Bellingham said.

"I thought there was a foul earlier, and he said, ‘What about the one I was fouled on?’

‌

"And I said, ‘You're tough enough to take it,’ you know what I mean."

‌



Bellingham did manage to net his seventh goal of the tournament in superb style, grabbing England's sixth in a thrilling 6-4 victory over France in the third-place play-off. In doing so, he etched his name in the history books as the first Englishman ever to score seven goals at a single World Cup.

Argentina, meanwhile, suffered a 1-0 defeat to Spain in the World Cup final. Ugly scenes erupted after the final whistle, as several Argentine players sparked a brawl, throwing punches and clashing violently with their Spanish opponents.

Sports.title: Arsenal readying player-plus-cash offer in mega Julian Alvarez transfer bid
Sports.content:
Arsenal readying player-plus-cash offer in mega Julian Alvarez transfer bid

Arsenal are still keen on signing Julian Alvarez from Atletico Madrid and are reportedly willing to offer up one of their key stars

View 3 Images Julian Alvarez is being pursued by Arsenal (Image: NurPhoto, NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Viktor Gyokeres could be offered up to Atletico Madrid by Arsenal as a makeweight in any deal to sign Julian Alvarez.

‌



Mikel Arteta's side recently announced the £34million arrival of Christian Tzolis from Club Brugge, having already brought in Illan Meslier as a free agent from Leeds United, while also making Piero Hincapie's loan move from Bayer Leverkusen a £34m permanent transfer.

‌



However, Alvarez has been a transfer target for the reigning Premier League champions all summer. Arsenal had the rug pulled from under them in their pursuit for Morgan Rogers, who was signed for £117m by Chelsea, while the Gunners were negotiating with Aston Villa.

‌



With the England international out of the picture, Alvarez appears to be back at the top of Arteta's transfer list. It's even been claimed that Arsenal are so interested in the Argentina international that they could offer up Gyokeres as part of any transfer deal.

FOLLOW OUR ARSENAL FB PAGE! Latest Gunners news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

As per the Times, Arsenal are keen to present the Swedish player to Diego Simeone's team as part of a player-plus-cash deal for the Argentinian World Cup victor. Last summer, Gyokeres made the switch to the Gunners from Sporting and experienced a varied debut season.

‌



He contributed 21 goals and three assists in 55 outings across all competitions, a commendable performance, but not one that sparked the same enthusiasm as the 54 goals and 13 assists he netted during his final campaign with Sporting.

That campaign convinced the Gunners to splash out approximately £64m on the Swedish international, who netted one goal and provided two more at the World Cup. Following the Champions League final defeat, Arteta made it evident his team must recruit more world-class talent if they are to continue claiming major silverware.

View 3 Images Gyokeres had a mixed debut campaign at Arsenal (Image: OLI SCARFF, AFP via Getty Images)

‌



He said: "We'll [have to] start to make some very important decisions if we want to reach another level. We're going to have to show that ambition.

"We are more than capable of doing it, but it's going to demand being very, very ambitious, very fast and very smart."

Thus far, the transfer window has proved challenging for Arteta's outfit. They were caught off-guard by Chelsea abruptly submitting a £117m offer to secure Aston Villa midfielder Morgan Rogers following several weeks of talks with the Midlands club.

‌



View 3 Images Rogers was heavily linked to Arsenal before Chelsea trumped the Gunners with a huge bid (Image: Darren Walsh, Chelsea FC via Getty Images)

Bradley Barcola of Paris Saint-Germain is also believed to feature on Arteta's wishlist. Additionally, Arteta may seek fresh defensive reinforcements with William Saliba scheduled to have back surgery this summer.

A potential swoop for free agent and England World Cup star John Stones has been discussed, while Ezri Konsa from Villa has similarly been earmarked as a possible acquisition. Bruno Guimaraes of Newcastle United also sits atop their priorities, especially with Declan Rice battling his neural hamstring problem at the World Cup.

Arsenal's Premier League title defence commences on August 21st, when they welcome newly promoted Coventry City.

Sports.title: Pep Guardiola's telling reasons for rejecting Italy job as England learn stance
Sports.content:
Pep Guardiola's telling reasons for rejecting Italy job as England learn stance

Italy were looking to appoint Pep Guardiola as their new manager following their disastrous failure to qualify for the World Cup this summer

View 2 Images Pep Guardiola has turned down the Italy job (Image: Adam Davy/PA Wire)

Pep Guardiola has reportedly rejected the Italy job after telling bosses "I don't feel it". It is also claimed that he still needs a break and is not sure about international management - dealing a blow to England's prospects of appointing him.

‌



The Catalan left Manchester City this summer after a decade in charge. The 55-year-old had another year left to run on his contract with City, but decided to call time after a decade in the role.

‌



He won six Premier League titles, the Champions League, three FA Cups and five Carabao Cups. While he missed out on the league title for the second successive year, he bowed out with the FA Cup and Carabao Cup.

‌



And the Italian national team were hoping to persuade Guardiola for a swift return to management this summer. The Azzurri failed to qualify for a third successive World Cup after losing to Bosnia & Herzegovina in the playoffs.

But Italian publication La Gazzetta dello Sport claim that he has turned them down, having said: “Thank you, I’m honoured, but at this moment, I don’t feel it.”

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

‌



The report claims that Guardiola's decision was not easy and he had given it considerable thought. However, it is said that reason prevailed over emotion.

Guardiola is also reportedly keen for a break after intense spells at Bayern Munich and City since his sabbatical 13 years ago. The ex-Barcelona boss is also said to have doubts over whether international football would suit him.

View 2 Images Pep Guardiola has been out of work since leaving Man City at the end of last season (Image: Nick Potts/PA Wire)

‌



Italian football president Giovanni Malago also hinted at a financial disparity in talks with Guardiola earlier this week . In an interview with the Italian media, he said: "There are certain financial aspects to be considered, and it's an understatement to say we'd have to grit our teeth for this.

"Some exceptions have been made, for example, exceptions that regard the name making such waves at the moment: Pep Guardiola. I don't need to sit here and explain the obvious reasons why he'd be an exception, but that is also no guarantee that this will go through."

The English FA could be watching the situation closely, with a long-term interest in Guardiola. Current Three Lions manager Thomas Tuchel is still in post, and despite calls for his dismissal following the World Cup semi-final loss to Argentina, the FA is expected to stand by him.

‌

Sports.title: Scott: The 'scrawny-looking kid' turned complete midfielder wanted by the elite
Sports.content:
Across the seven games in which Bournemouth took points off Arsenal, Manchester City, Manchester United, Liverpool and Chelsea last season, it is telling that Alex Scott was nearly ever-present, playing 625 of a possible 630 minutes.

Scott was one of Andoni Iraola's most valued and trusted players in an historic season for the club. Clearly, he made a mark on their opponents too. Coveted by the elite, he could become the latest Premier League midfielder to make a high-profile move.

His future at Bournemouth is uncertain but it seems increasingly clear that the 22-year-old, nicknamed the 'Guernsey Grealish' as a teenager and described by Pep Guardiola as an "unbelievable player" as far back as 2023, has a bright future ahead of him.

'Scrawny-looking kid' turned duel-winner

Scott stands out for his technical ability. He boasts excellent close control and is comfortable in tight spaces. With his socks slung low around his ankles, and a capacity to glide away from defenders, the Jack Grealish comparisons are easy to understand.

Scott counts Grealish among his admirers. Like Guardiola, Grealish was left impressed by his performance in an FA Cup meeting between Manchester City and Bristol City when he was 19. "Top, top talent," wrote Grealish on social media after the game.

The technical qualities that stood out to Guardiola and Grealish that day had convinced Bristol City to pluck him from non-league Guernsey in the Channel Islands only a few years earlier in a move overseen by then director of youth recruitment Brian Tinnion.

Nigel Pearson, the manager who subsequently gave Scott his Championship debut, remembers him arriving as a "scrawny-looking youngster" with "incredible" talent. Before long, he was predicting Scott would one day represent England.

Scott is still waiting on his first cap. But he is a European Championship winner with England's U19s and U21s and a first senior call-up in November was followed by an invitation from Thomas Tuchel to join their pre-World Cup training camp in June.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Alex Scott's best passes, tricks, tackles and goals for Bournemouth last season

Back at Bristol City, Scott handled the jump to the Championship impressively, making 35 starts in the competition in the 2021/22 campaign, then bettering his total with 40 in 2022/23. A £25m move to Bournemouth demanded another step up physically.

Scott was hindered by injuries in his first two seasons. He arrived at the Vitality Stadium in 2023 with a knee problem, then sustained another early in his second campaign at the club.

But his physical improvement has been evident across his time in the Premier League. Last season, he was finally deemed ready to become a regular starter and only missed one game for Bournemouth over the course of the campaign.

His ground duel success rate of 56 per cent was up from 47 per cent in his first season at Bournemouth and put him above Elliot Anderson, Bruno Guimaraes and Martin Zubimendi.

Scott's aerial success rate followed a similar trajectory, up from 44 per cent in his first campaign in the Premier League to 54 per cent last season. "He has really filled out and matured as a player," noted his former boss Pearson to Sky Sports.

Scott can now be viewed as one of the best ball-winners in the division in his position. Last season, only Anderson and Wolves' Andre won possession more times among midfielders. Scott also ranked in the top 10 for interceptions and duels won.

Ball-carrying and off-the-ball runs

Scott brought the same dynamism to Bournemouth's attack, with Iraola's team set up to allow as many opportunities as possible for him to utilise another of his strengths: his ball-carrying ability.

As well as being comfortable under pressure, Scott excels at attacking space, meaning the emphasis placed on maximising transitions and counters under Iraola suited his game perfectly.

Scott's total of 431 carries was the eighth-highest by a midfielder in the Premier League last season and around half of those carries were categorised by Opta as progressive, underlining his capacity to take his team up the pitch.

Scott's physical intensity shines through in his numbers relating to off-the-ball runs. According to Opta, Scott made the sixth-most supporting runs of all Premier League players last season.

One of the best examples came with his winning goal against Arsenal at the Emirates Stadium in April, when Scott, having scanned his surroundings and identified an opportunity, charged through the middle of the pitch to be in a position to collect Evanilson's flick from David Brooks's pass before beating David Raya.

Iraola said Scott was becoming a "very complete" player after that game and there is evidence of that completeness in the tracking data. Scott's commitment to contributing at both ends of the pitch can be seen in the fact that he made more runs tracking back into position than any other Premier League player last term.

Scott also made the third-most high-speed runs in the division, and covered an incredible 27.6km at high speed, underlining the extent of his intensity as a box-to-box midfielder.

Best yet to come?

Iraola talked up Scott's ability to play in different positions last season. "He is playing as a six, as an eight, as a 10." And although the bulk of his minutes have come as an eight, his versatility is another strength. Scott was even used as a wing-back at Bristol City.

Image: Alex Scott has been used in a variety of different positions at Bournemouth

Scott's Premier League readiness is another factor which adds to his appeal. He has played 89 games in the competition over the last three seasons. But at only 22, there is also room for growth.

The main area for improvement is in front of goal.

Scott has only contributed four goals and three assists in those 89 Premier League appearances so far. Efforts to improve his output have been ongoing since his time in the second tier with Bristol City, when his numbers were similarly modest.

Image: Alex Scott celebrates his winning goal against Arsenal last season

"For him to be an eight or a 10, and for people to talk about him as an eight or a 10, he needed better numbers," Jason Euell, Pearson's assistant at Bristol City, told Sky Sports. "He wasn't getting enough assists and he wasn't scoring enough goals.

"He was doing it all in training, but never replicating it in games. When it was approaching one of the summer tournaments, I said, 'Look, it's great you've got so many Championship games under your belt, but if your numbers don't start changing, someone else is going to sneak up behind you and take your place.'"

Scott was able to fend off that competition. He played an important role in the U19 and U21 European Championship successes in 2022 and 2025. And while there remains a need for more goals and assists, Scott has proved he has plenty to offer.

Sports.title: Masquerade Ball backed to reverse form with Calandagan in King George
Sports.content:
With the King George VI and Queen Elizabeth Stakes upon us, Kate Tracey quizzed Declan Rix and Sam Boswell on the big race on the latest episode of Weekend Winners.

Nine runners are set to line up in the Saturday feature overall, with last season's winner Calandagan back to defend his crown - won at the expense of the reopposing Kalpana last term. Masquerade Ball arrives from Japan also looking to exact revenge on the Aga Khan champion, having been denied by the finest margins on home soil in the Japan Cup.

Aidan O'Brien fields four runners, headlined by Irish Derby hero Benvenuto Cellini and 2025 Arc runner-up Minnie Hauk, whilst 2024 King George winner Goliath seeks to win back his crown under Christophe Soumillon.

Declan Rix:

"I don't think this year's race will set up like that, with Action and Lambourn going forward to turn this into a proper test for Minnie Hauk and Benvenuto Cellini. "He was getting a bit of weight that day but was the younger horse who has aged up a little bit. The track is the unknown for the Japanese horse, isn't it? How has he travelled over? There was a media day in Newmarket on Wednesday and both Japanese horses looked well, with the trainer so enthused about being here.

"When I was looking at this yesterday, we were getting a bit of 9/2 - 7/2 is as short as I'd want to go. Calandagan has made me look silly throughout the course of this show, we know the ground and track are perfect for him. However, if I can get 4/1 about Masquerade Ball I'll be taking him on."
