"It has created a much more complex landscape with all of the three-digits going at once and having to figure out: do they add, how does one fit with the other, what are the exceptions?" said Kathleen Claussen, a professor at Georgetown Law School who specializes in trade law. "It is a far more complex landscape, I think, than it was a year ago."

More to come?

And still more could be coming — there's a current Section 301 investigation into more than a dozen countries and the EU. The administration says those countries are being unfair in their manufacturing — for example, by overproducing.

While Trump rolls out the new import taxes, poll after poll shows Americans don't like the tariffs, and that their approval of the president on the economy has declined.

But regardless of the politics, the president is fond of tariffs — he regularly calls tariff his favorite word in stump speeches. Indeed, the president's criticism of free trade deals such as NAFTA and willingness to entertain protectionist policies instead was part of the populist pitch that initially got him elected in 2016.

Since then, he has shown that he likes the policy in part because it helps him strong-arm other countries into giving concessions on trade deals.

Sponsor Message

And his administration maintains that the tariffs will have long-term economic benefits – primarily, boosting manufacturing.

"The problems the president's trade policy seeks to solve are generational," Greer told senators this week. "These things were not broken in the day, and they won't be fixed overnight. But they must be fixed."

The manufacturing employment boom has not come yet — employment in the sector remains below where it was when Trump took office.

That means committing to tariffs is a gamble, as Trump asks voters to weigh a policy they may dislike against what might happen in the future.

World.title: Billions in trade, 850,000 hours saved and a $6.4B price tag: Gordie Howe bridge by the numbers
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

After 25 years of planning, Prime Minister Mark Carney has announced that the Gordie Howe International Bridge, connecting Windsor, Ont., and Detroit, will open at the end of the week. For The National, CBC’s Peter Armstrong breaks down what the bridge promises and why Canadian taxpayers had to pay for it.

After 25 years of planning, seven years of construction and months of delays, the first trucks are finally set to roll over the Gordie Howe bridge on Monday.

In tow will be some of the billions of dollars worth of goods that pass through the Windsor-Detroit corridor, which the bridge will help get to their destinations faster — saving time and money.

"There's a tremendous opportunity here in dollar terms, but also in terms of what our future looks like, just embodied in that one bridge," said Moshe Lander, an economics professor at Concordia University who studies international trade.

But just how much time and money are we talking about?

Here's what you need to know.

850,000 hours per year saved

The existing Blue Water Bridge, Ambassador Bridge and Detroit-Windsor Tunnel have supported massive amounts of trade for decades. But they're near capacity, which Canadian Trucking Alliance CEO Stephen Laskowski says has led to congestion.

He says lines at customs plazas on both sides of the Ambassador Bridge have grown longer over the years. And the route leading to that crossing on the Windsor side also takes drivers through a dozen or so stoplights.

But with three lanes of capacity going in each direction, the Gordie Howe is expected to speed things up significantly.

The new bridge is expected to take 44.5 per cent of the commercial traffic that passes through the Windsor-Detroit corridor, according to a January filing from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security establishing the route as an official port of entry.

WATCH | The new bridge's expected impact on Ambassador Bridge: Here's how much the Gordie Howe bridge is expected to cut into the Ambassador Bridge | Duration 2:21 The opening of the new Gordie Howe bridge is widely expected to change the way billions of dollars worth of goods and millions of travelers cross between Canada and the U.S. But a recent U.S. government analysis puts a number on just how significant the traffic impact could be at the busiest international trade corridor in North America. The CBC's Emma Loop reports.

The Gordie Howe route also directly connects two major American and Canadian highway networks — the 75-series highways in the U.S. with the 400-series highways in Ontario.

While the new bridge might only shave off a few minutes from each trip, that time adds up. It's estimated to save truck drivers some 850,000 hours per year in wait times.

Laskowski's organization estimates the new bridge will save trucking companies between $20,000 and $100,000 a month, depending on the size of their fleet.

Lower tolls on the Gordie Howe compared to the Ambassador Bridge will shave a few bucks off of that cost, according to Laskowski, while less time spent idling in traffic will mean savings on fuel and wages.

In recent years, the Ambassador Bridge, pictured, and other routes through the trade corridor have reached the limit of how much traffic they can take, and the Gordie Howe is supposed to help speed things up. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

$1B in daily trade

Given a third of all trade that happens between the U.S. and Canada passes through this corridor, the bridge could have some serious benefits for the economy writ large.

Canada and the U.S. already ship about $1 billion daily through the Windsor-Detroit corridor, according to an estimate from Invest WindsorEssex, making it the busiest international land border crossing in North America.

"It's mind-boggling," said Lander.

As is the case for auto manufacturing, parts often cross the border multiple times before ending up in a finished product that's sold in either country.

That compounds any time savings from a single border crossing, says Sandy Baruah, CEO of the Detroit Regional Chamber of commerce.

Any delays from a slow crossing can hold things up at factories too, says Baruah, so another bridge to keep things moving would prevent delays from having a domino effect.

"In today's hyper-competitive global market, any efficiency that can be gained is a big deal."

And if businesses aren't spending as much to truck products around that could mean they don't raise prices as quickly, which Lander says could mean "inflation kept under tabs."

Beyond that, Lander says it's an important sign to businesses of just how important the trading relationship between Canada and the U.S. is and the fact that it's not going anywhere — politics aside.

Despite U.S. President Donald Trump's continued tariff threats — including the most recent 50 per cent levies on a range of Canadian products — Lander says the geography of the two countries means not trading simply isn't an option.

"They are in our backyard. We are in their backyard. It's not going away."

A $6.4B price tag

Despite the benefits, Canada will have to begin paying back the bridge's hefty price tag.

While the bridge is owned by the governments of Canada and Michigan jointly, Canada paid the entire $6.4 billion cost to get it built. But that hasn't prevented debate about who should get the funds once the bridge is open.

Temporary bracing beams connecting the Windsor and Detroit sides of the Gordie Howe International Bridge. (The Gordie Howe International Bridge/X)

In February, U.S. President Donald Trump threatened to block the bridge's opening until his country was "fully compensated for everything we have given them," in a social media post complaining about Canada.

The bridge's first crack at opening last month was later stalled at the request of the United States , in order to work out a handful of issues.

The two countries have since reached a new deal to open the bridge to travellers starting July 27 under altered terms about where toll revenue goes.

For the first 15 years under that agreement, toll revenue will be used to pay for the bridge's maintenance and operating expenses. The rest of the money will be split, with Canada getting half and the other half going to an economic development fund controlled by the U.S. government.

WATCH | What to know about the bridge deal: Gordie Howe bridge agreement released: Here’s what to know | Duration 3:18 The proposed agreement surrounding the opening of the Gordie Howe International Bridge connecting Windsor, Ont., to Detroit, was released amid escalated tariff threats by U.S. President Donald Trump.

The initial 2012 deal between the countries would have seen Canada collect all of the tolls and use the revenue in order to pay down its debt. Only once Canada's debt was dealt with would Michigan start splitting revenue.

Comments by Carney made before the text of the agreement was made public led to confusion about the money-sharing agreement and criticism from opposition parties.

The Prime Minister apologized on Thursday for the confusion but said that, either way, the terms of the deal would have "a very marginal impact on the overall economics" because revenue will be small in the first few years until traffic ramps up.

World.title: Doctors are using a regulatory gap to administer an unauthorized peptide
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Despite Health Canada's warnings against the use of unauthorized peptides as a health and fitness shortcut, a CBC News investigation uncovered doctors using a regulatory loophole to administer one of the unproven products to patients.

The popularity of peptides has surged as fitness influencers endorse them to build muscle, reverse the signs of aging and lose weight.

Peptides are short amino acid chains naturally produced by the body that act as building blocks of larger proteins that support growth, metabolism and healing.

But unlike approved peptides used in medicine, such as insulin and GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic, Health Canada tells CBC "unauthorized peptide products sold for wellness purposes have not been assessed for safety, quality, or effectiveness."

And yet, CBC News found doctors promoting and prescribing a popular unauthorized peptide called Body Protection Compound-157 (BPC-157) that is touted to help accelerate muscle growth and tissue repair.

That's because the same regulator prohibiting BPC-157’s sale as an injectable drug or a licensed natural health product says it can be compounded as a pill by pharmacies — with a doctor's prescription.

"It's maddening," said Timothy Caulfield, a professor in the faculty of law and the school of public health and research director of the Health Law Institute at the University of Alberta.

Doctors should be "warning their patients about these products, not providing them," he said.

Hidden camera claims

CBC News journalists armed with hidden cameras visited two doctors — at clinics in Ontario and B.C. — that advertised unauthorized peptides to hear the health claims offered to patients.

"I'm on some peptides myself," said Dr. Shawn Seit, speaking to an undercover CBC journalist at his Rejuuv Medi Spa in Markham, Ont. "So, that's how safe I feel they are."

In a recorded one-on-one consultation, Seit said that BPC-157 "really helps in terms of healing and inflammation."

WATCH | Getting peptides through a loophole: How Canadians are getting unauthorized peptides | Duration 10:00 A CBC News hidden-camera investigation uncovers unauthorized peptides, such as BPC-157, being promoted across Canada. For The National, CBC’s Idil Mussa breaks down what the team uncovered and how the findings sparked a series of new investigations by Health Canada.

In B.C., Dr. Charles Jiang claimed, until recently, on his Richmond Anti-Aging Clinic website that BPC-157 can be used for "musculoskeletal and gut lining repair." He also told a CBC journalist during an in-person visit that unlike peptides sold online, the ones he prescribes are safe.

"When you order online, you never know what is the truth behind it," said Jiang. "If you come to us we are professional doctors."

Caulfield says physicians that prescribe unauthorized peptides are capitalizing on a fad that could be risky.

They're "leveraging a longevity wellness trend," he said. "Despite the fact there's no evidence and real potential harm."

Jiang did not respond to CBC's repeated requests for comment.

In emailed statements, Seit said his aim is "always directed at optimizing my patients' care and treatment” and that he is permitted to compound BPC-157 as a natural health product (NHP), which Health Canada confirmed. The same is true of any doctor in the country.

Timothy Caulfield, a professor in the faculty of law and the school of public health and research director of the Health Law Institute at the University of Alberta, says doctors should be warning their patients about these products. (Curtis Trent)

Compounding BPC-157: A regulatory loophole

In a statement, Health Canada said "BPC‑157 has not been authorized, its safety, efficacy, and quality have not been assessed … and there is limited scientific evidence to support its use, including a lack of established human dosing protocols."

In addition, the regulator says BPC-157 is not approved for use in any NHPs in any form, including oral and injectable, but it can still be compounded for topical use or oral administration as an NHP.

That means doctors can prescribe BPC-157 to patients and compounding pharmacies — that mix custom medications — can formulate them.

"Nobody's minding the store," said Stuart Phillips, a professor of kinesiology at McMaster University in Hamilton.

"Health Canada won't approve it as a drug, but it slips through as a compounded natural health product, where the federal safety check basically doesn't happen."

Health Canada considers NHP compounding within a practitioner-patient relationship distinct from manufacturing and not subject to the same regulatory oversight.

"The practitioner-patient relationship is supposed to be where evidence gets turned into advice. But you can't practise evidence-based medicine on a substance that has no evidence," said Phillips.

The federal agency says compounding must not be used to circumvent the federal drug review and approval process, but Caulfield says that appears to be the case.

Stuart Phillips, a kinesiology professor at McMaster University, says when it comes to unauthorized peptides, there should be greater regulation and oversight. (Ousama Farag/CBC)

"BPC-157 is not an NHP," he said.

"Compounding is not meant to be a strategy that allows consumers to go around regulatory oversight, which seems to be what is happening here if they allow the application of NHP rules."



Seit said the prescriptions he provides "do not circumvent regulatory oversight." The regulatory bodies to which Jiang, Seit and those pharmacies belong had various responses.

In a statement to CBC News, the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario said the information physicians provide to patients or the public about treatments should be accurate and informed by evidence.

The College of Physicians and Surgeons of British Columbia said it doesn't have specific guidance on prescribing oral BPC-157, but expects "licensees to exercise professional judgment to ensure they are providing safe and appropriate patient care."

The Ontario College of Pharmacists says compounding an NHP using ingredients unauthorized by Health Canada could be investigated as a breach of professional conduct.

The College of Pharmacists of British Columbia states it "cannot be determined in general terms" whether a pharmacy has violated its standards.

Health Canada says it is illegal to promote health products that have not been authorized for sale, including compounded products tailored to individual patients.

After CBC News asked the department about the websites advertising BPC-157, it said it was investigating whether those activities complied with the Food and Drugs Act.

The mention of peptide therapy and BPC-157 was also taken down on Seit's and Jiang's websites after CBC News contacted them for comment.

All hype, no research

During CBC's undercover consultation, Seit admitted there was a lack of clinical human studies on BPC-157.

"A lot of these studies are based on animal models," he said. "They're not based on human models."

In an email to CBC News, he stated he was candid with his patients about the current research regarding BPC-157.

Jiang's clinic website also stated that BPC-157 had "limited human trial data."

Phillips, at McMaster University, says the lack of human trials raises serious questions about BPC-157's potential health risks.

"There are basically no published human efficacy trials for BPC-157."

Phillips says all he can find is one small safety study from a decade ago, and a trial that only started enrolling participants this past February.

Patricia Brubaker’s work helped pave the way for approved peptide medications like Ozempic. (Ousama Farag/CBC)

"Almost everything else is rodent work."

Patricia Brubaker, a professor emeritus of physiology at the University of Toronto, has taken a hard look at the research and has come to a similar conclusion about BPC-157's alleged benefits.

"Animal models do not always translate into humans. Dosing doesn't translate into humans. Safety doesn't translate into humans necessarily," said Brubaker.

Brubaker says drugs need to be carefully tested in stages before they are approved for use in people.

"It's really important that scientific discoveries are translated from the bench cells, animals into humans through a series of clinical trials that prove at every step, with increasing numbers of subjects, that this product is effective, that it's safe, and that you know how much of it to administer."

World.title: Alberta's got a new plan for a southern pipeline to B.C.'s coast — it still won't be easy
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Shahin Dashtgard, a sedimentologist from Simon Fraser University, holds an open palmful of muddied sand from the Fraser Valley in Delta, B.C.

This material, known as sub-surface, is weak, loose and water saturated, and it's one of the main challenges of building Alberta's proposed new pipeline terminal on the shores of southern British Columbia at Roberts Bank, near the Fraser River estuary.

As Dashtgard shakes his hand, the wet sand dissolves and runs through his fingers "almost like a soup." He's demonstrating the process of liquefaction, which could occur if there's an earthquake.

"That becomes the concern of building on top of water saturated or loose sediment or sand like this," he said.

The Fraser Valley has a famously weak, loose and water soaked sand sub-surface that could become 'almost like a soup' during an earthquake, says Shahin Dashtgard, a sedimontologist from Simon Fraser University. (Georgie Smyth/CBC)

A deviation in the route

Prime Minister Mark Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith have both been bullish on a new Alberta pipeline route, now under consideration by the Major Projects Office (MPO), which would mostly replicate the path of the existing Trans Mountain pipeline corridor.

The two met in Calgary for a joint media conference on July 2, where Smith presented the pitch as "the fastest, most cost-effective path" for the pipeline just hours after B.C.'s North Coast tanker ban was upheld .

"The best route for a new pipeline is one that goes through one that already exists, south through the Trans Mountain corridor," Carney told the journalists in Calgary.

But there's a major section of the proposed route that doesn't exist yet. The deviation would begin at Hope, B.C., where the route would continue through the Fraser Valley and terminate at Roberts Bank rather than Burrard Inlet near Metro Vancouver as two previous oil pipelines have.

There are longstanding concerns with this preferred terminus.

Seismic and environmental issues, space contraints and the influential say of local First Nations will shape the speed and direction of the project, even if it's chosen as a project of national interest by the October deadline.

Alberta has acknowledged some of those longstanding concerns in their submission, which notes that Roberts Bank and the land around it is "the highest sensitivity area along the corridor" and "the region will have strong concerns about oil and marine spills, tanker traffic and cumulative effects."

Minister of Transport Steven MacKinnon speaks at a July 16 news conference in Delta, B.C., to announce that Roberts Bank Terminal 2, a long proposed expansion of the Port of Vancouver, is being referred to the Major Projects Office. But it's not clear how that expansion could co-exist with Alberta's marine pipeline terminal proposed for the same area. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)

Port expansion project

But Roberts Bank is already being scrutinized for suitability concerning another major project — Roberts Bank Terminal 2 — an expansion of the Port of Vancouver more than 10 years in the making that would increase its container handling capacity by more than 30 per cent.

The pipeline and port terminals are roughly the same size, according to submission documents.

The port project has most of its approvals in hand, except for a federal permit under the Species at Risk Act, but proponents at the Vancouver Fraser Port Authority called for it to be fast-tracked.

At an event announcing the referral of the port expansion to the MPO in mid-July, CBC News asked port CEO Peter Xotta how the container expansion and proposed pipeline terminal could co-exist.

Xotta replied that of the two projects, the port expansion "is much further along," but he said they'd work with the MPO on details.

Later, a port spokesperson emphasized in a statement to CBC News that "it's important to keep in mind that these are two separate projects."

But environmentalists say technicalities like that won't matter to how species like Pacific Salmon, Western Sandpipers and Southern Resident Killer whales experience another terminal on these shores.

Lucero González from the Wilderness Committee says Roberts Bank is critical habitat and is already too industrialized from a container and ferry terminal. "What we see here is not just a nice spot to see. This is what the Southern Resident orcas call home," she said. (Georgie Smyth/CBC)

"It's terrifying," said Lucero González, a campaigner with environmental group the Wilderness Committee, which challenged the container terminal expansion in federal court.

"If a pipeline were to be built alongside the port expansion, it would be something that no person in British Columbia has seen in terms of project development and tanker traffic in the province," said González.

Alberta's submission to the MPO details how it plans to mitigate the impacts of its pipeline infrastructure, including on federally protected aquatic animals.

If the pipeline project is listed under the Building Canada Act, federal approvals are automatically granted. But an MPO spokesperson told CBC News the pipeline could still need some permits and authorizations.

The MPO spokesperson noted that having the project listed under the Building Canada Act means the MPO would no longer look at "whether" the project should proceed, but rather "how" it should proceed.

The Roberts Bank Wildlife Management Area is next to Canada's largest container terminal. It's nationally recognised as critical wintering grounds for the highest number of shorebirds and waterfowl found anywhere in Canada. (Submitted by Kate Paton, Georgie Smyth/CBC)

Seismic issues

Then there's what lies beneath: the Fraser Valley floor, which could turn soft and squishy in an earthquake.

Trans Mountain, the Crown corporation that holds 90 per cent equity in the project, told Canada's National Energy Board (NEB) in 2015 that geological factors around building a marine terminal at Roberts Bank would result in a significantly greater footprint and higher capital cost than a terminal in the Burrard Inlet.

When the Trans Mountain pipeline was successfully duplicated in 2024 it terminated at Westridge Marine Terminal in Burrard Inlet, in Metro Vancouver. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

In public documents submitted to the NEB, Trans Mountain said "the potential for seismically-induced soil liquefaction is an important issue." It also noted that ground improvement measures under the footprint of the pipeline and terminal may be necessary before construction.

CBC News reached out to Trans Mountain to ask what had changed since then to result in Roberts Bank becoming the preferred location for its pipeline terminal.

The company referred CBC to the government of Alberta, which noted that Roberts Bank was identified because it offered an established marine shipping corridor and existing marine safety infrastructure.

It said any engineering concerns specific to that site would be assessed as the project advances.

Alberta's plan proposes two options for pipeline routes from Hope, B.C., to Roberts Bank. The final route, it says, will depend on community consultations.

There will be different engineering approaches depending which way they go, says Ribu Dhakal, as assistant professor of Civil Engineering at the University of British Columbia.

The well known high risk of liquefaction will be the biggest challenge, he said. "They're going to have a difficult time, but it's possible."

Compacting the ground underneath the project, different trenching approaches and other engineering fixes can mitigate the risks, but Dhakal says they will likely make the project more complex and expensive.

Tsawwassen First Nation Chief Laura Cassidy is one of many First Nation leaders who will need to be consulted on the proposed pipeline terminal at Roberts Bank. In a statement the Nation said it has not taken a position on the proposed route. (Georgie Smyth/CBC)

First Nations concerns

Underpinning all of this are the rights and titles of several First Nations, whose traditional territories encompass the pipeline terminal land. Many haven't yet taken a position on Alberta's proposal and are awaiting more details.

One of them, Tsawwassen First Nation, holds territory near the proposed pipeline project's marine terminal.

It consented to the proposed port expansion, but specified in a media release that "consent does not constitute support for the project."

Tsawwassen Chief Laura Cassidy declined to be interviewed, but offered a hint about her government's appetite for more development in the Fraser River delta at the July 16 news conference announcing the port expansion project's bid for an MPO listing.

"The benefits may be national, but the environment, cultural and harvesting impacts fall most directly on Tsawwassen people," she said.

"To say we are concerned about what happens here is an understatement."

World.title: N.S. nurses to reunite with Ont. referee they saved at hockey tournament
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

When Terri Arnold first saw George Harrison, she feared he was dead.

It was February, and Harrison had collapsed after having a heart attack at a hockey tournament in North York, Ont.

"He was very pale," said Arnold. "I don't know if he was answering me or not, but I was trying to talk to him: 'George, you need to stay with us.'"

Arnold was at the tournament with her friend and colleague, Melissa Hines, to watch Hines's daughter play.

Arnold is a registered nurse in the women and children's unit at Valley Regional Hospital in Kentville, N.S., while Hines is the clinical nurse lead.

They were in line for coffee at the rink when they heard calls for help.

Harrison, a referee at the tournament from Stoney Creek, Ont., was on the ground.

Two other referees were performing CPR on the 68-year-old as his face turned blue.

Melissa Hines and Terri Arnold were vacationing in the Toronto area when they helped save George Harrison. They flew back to Nova Scotia before they had a chance to meet him. (Submitted by Melissa Hines)

The nurses took over and used an a utomated external defibrillator to shock Harrison while they waited for an ambulance to arrive.

Hines said they had no idea he survived until later that day, when his son texted the nurses.

"I think it truly sank in at that moment. This was a dad, this was a grandfather, and that he was doing OK," Hines said in an interview.

Five months later, Harrison is in Halifax for the first time, eager to meet the women who saved his life.

While he's talked to them briefly on the phone, Harrison said he didn't want to talk about the experience until they were face to face. The trio will meet for supper in Halifax on Friday night.

"I owe them a big thank you. I'm going to give them a big hug," said Harrison, who recalls nothing of the experience.

"Talking to my doctor, the doctor at the hospital, he said that those two nurses obviously knew what they were doing, otherwise you wouldn't be here."

Harrison ended up needing a double bypass after his heart attack, but has now recovered fully and is back on the ice.

While he was able to thank the referees who helped him months ago, he's been eager to get to Nova Scotia and finally meet Hines and Arnold.

"I'm just grateful they were in the spot they were in. I got lucky I guess in those regards," he said.

Terri Arnold and Melissa Hines say this is the first time they've had to use their nursing skills outside of the hospital. They're encouraging more people to get CPR training. (Submitted by Melissa Hines)

The experience is equally emotional for the women. They say they've never needed their skills out of the hospital, and they usually help newborns, not adults.

"With our career here, we go through some quite traumatic events often enough and you don't really get that followup, so it's just nice that he reached out to us and wants to meet us. It's exciting," said Hines.

Arnold and Hines hope the story inspires more people to brush up on their CPR skills.

"Anyone taking first aid and CPR courses are so important because you never know — it can happen anywhere," said Hines.

MORE TOP STORIES

World.title: Public funding for fossil fuel industry breaks another Liberal climate promise, advocates say
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Carney government's financial support for the oil and gas industry amounts to breaking a federal commitment to phase out fossil fuel subsidies, according to environmental advocates.

They say the measures represent further federal backsliding on climate policy at a time when oil industry earnings are on the rise.

After the Trudeau Liberals promised to phase out "inefficient" fossil fuel subsidies, Prime Minister Mark Carney's government introduced a new tax benefit for oil extraction and brought back an old one for natural gas.

This comes as the federal government is preparing to invest billions of dollars into a new West Coast pipeline and at least one Crown corporation is disclosing more public dollars might be directed toward fossil fuels.

The Liberals recently committed to bringing back a tax break for liquefied natural gas (LNG). The measure, which allows companies to claim accelerated depreciation on their assets for a lower tax bill, expired in 2024 but was reinstated in last year's budget.

The tax break for LNG companies will cost the government $362 million over five years, according to the Parliamentary Budget Office.

"We're seeing quite worrying steps backwards," said Nichole Dusyk, the Canada energy transition lead at the Institute for Sustainable Development.

The Carney government is also expanding its carbon capture investment tax credit to a technique used to recover more oil and gas, what's known as enhanced oil recovery or EOR. The technique injects carbon dioxide underground to squeeze more oil out of reservoirs.

It's been hailed as a "game changer" for those involved in the conventional oil business. The original carbon capture tax credit excluded oil recovery, which environmental groups argued would count as fossil fuel subsidy.

Before the tax credit was expanded to include oil recovery it was estimated to cost Ottawa $12.3 billion, according to the Parliamentary Budget Office.

"We're seeing a very worrying pattern with this government of [not only] increasing fossil fuel subsidies across a number of fronts, but the creation of new subsidies, new measures, new vehicles to transfer public dollars to the fossil fuels sector," said Dusyk.

In 2023, the federal government rolled out guidelines to end what it called "inefficient" federal subsidies for fossil fuels. Critics said the plan contained loopholes, including exemptions for subsidies that enabled significant greenhouse gas emission reductions, adoption of clean energy or technology or supported Indigenous economic participation in fossil fuel projects.

Oil benchmark again passes $100 US

Dusyk said the Carney government is offering billions in incentives for oil and gas companies at a time when the war in Iran is bringing higher revenues for the companies that can get their product to market.

On Thursday, oil prices topped $100 US per barrel as Houthi militants attacked tankers in the Red Sea, where Saudi Arabia has rerouted much of its oil exports after Iran blocked the Strait of Hormuz.

In a recent social media video, Carney said that the Iran war's impact "will be with us for a long time." He said the world needs Canada, with its massive conventional energy reserves, to step up.

Carney says his government remains committed to creating a low-carbon economy but Ottawa cannot "afford to restrain the growth of an important part of our energy mix, oil and gas" to meet short-term climate goals.

CBC News asked the office of Canada's finance minister if Ottawa was still committed to phasing out fossil fuel subsidies.

A statement from a spokesperson for the minister suggests the government hasn't abandoned the Trudeau-era framework.

"It's worth reiterating that Canada is the lone country in the world to release a rigorous analytical guide to phase out inefficient fossil fuel subsidies," said John Fragos, the press secretary for the minister of finance and national revenue.

$29B spent on sector in 2024

One group has been keeping receipts on how many federal dollars are going to boost fossil fuel expansion.

Environmental Defence Canada recently released a report that found the government of Canada provided "tremendous" public dollars to fossil fuel projects across the country.

In 2025, the group's analysis found , the federal government spent more than $10 billion on fossil fuel subsidies, financing and other incentives.

That's down from the more than $29 billion in 2024.

"The government continues to put a huge amount of our money into projects that are fuelling the climate crisis," said Julia Levin, an associate director at Environmental Defence Canada.

Most of the financing was delivered through Ottawa's export financing agency, Export Development Canada (EDC).

The agency's total support for the oil and gas sector totalled $9.3 billion, up 22 per cent compared to the previous year, according to its annual climate-related disclosure report.

"EDC expects increased demand to support Canada's domestic oil and gas sector, as it is being called upon to help strengthen Canada's resilience, competitiveness and economic security," the report notes.

"As a result, we anticipate providing increased support for certain carbon-intensive and nation-building projects."

Export Development Canada provides most of the funding for federal support available to fossil fuel projects. (David Thurton/CBC)

The report also notes that EDC is committed to supporting solar, wind, geothermal and battery energy and in 2025 EDC disbursed $1.4 billion in financing in this area.

In a statement the agency pushed back on the characterization that it's subsidizing the oil and gas industry.

"EDC's business support is not considered a subsidy as we provide Canadian companies with financing solutions on commercial terms," said spokesperson Zoé de Bellefeuille.

"EDC is a self-financing Crown corporation that equips Canadian companies with financing, equity and insurance on commercial terms — and does not provide grants or subsidies."

But Export Development Canada does provide loans, which environmental groups point out are considered subsidies by the World Trade Organization when administered by a public body.

More public dollars could be going to carbon-intensive infrastructure projects as the federal government revealed in July that the Alberta government's proposal for a pipeline to the West Coast will be built in partnership with the federal government.

The government-owned Trans Mountain Corporation and the province, through the Alberta Petroleum Marketing Commission, will build the pipeline. A private sector proponent, Pembina Pipeline, will hold a minority stake once construction begins.

Ottawa hasn't said how much the federal government will pay.

"I am quite comfortable that this is a good investment for Canadian taxpayers," Energy Minister Hodgson said in an interview with CBC's Power and Politics after the proposal was released.

World.title: Here's what I learned while shopping for a used EV
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Welcome to our weekly newsletter where we highlight environmental trends and solutions that are moving us to a more sustainable world.

I'm Nicole Mortillaro, and a few weeks ago, I wrote a piece about what those aiming to buy a used EV should look out for. Well, I bought a used EV, and I wanted to share my experience.

This week:

Here's what I learned while shopping for a used EV

The Big Picture: Stephen Guilbeault at a glacier

Can problem bears be moved instead of killed?

Here's what I learned while shopping for a used EV

Nicole Mortillaro with her recently purchased 2018 Nissan Leaf. (Nicole Mortillaro/CBC)

I did it. I made the leap. I am now the proud owner of an electric vehicle.

(I’m not only going to share what I learned about buying a used EV, but also what it’s like being an EV owner, because it really is different from a gas vehicle.)

I researched many vehicles before settling on the Nissan Leaf.

One of the things that I found most interesting when I wrote my original story was how all the experts stressed the importance of getting a battery state of health (SOH), a report that provides you with the battery's remaining capacity. Each and every expert I spoke with said that it was unwise to purchase a used EV without this report. They also said buying a used EV with a percentage below 70 was unwise.

Well, I learned that it isn't easy getting a battery SOH from used car dealerships — not one of the four I went to even knew what it was.

Then I remembered that reader Rob Bilodeau suggested buying an OBD2 sensor. These sensors can be plugged into your car and provide you with a wealth of information.

I bought one that could be used on an EV, but I couldn’t get it to work on the 2018 Leaf I was considering. So, I bought the car without an SOH.

Since I don’t have the ability to charge at home, I use Flo street charging just 200 metres from my apartment in Toronto. (Nicole Mortillaro/CBC)

Eventually, I ordered a second OBD2 sensor, plugged it in and used the app LeafSpy Pro. I held my breath and waited. Did I get a dud? Would I regret the purchase?

The reading: 87.96 per cent. Phew.

Was I lucky?

Cara Clairman, president and CEO of Plug'n Drive, a non-profit that advocates and supports the adoption of electric vehicles, said that it wasn’t really luck: EV batteries are lasting longer than originally expected.

"If you just happen to get a lemon, that could happen with any car," she said.

Clairman was surprised that the used car dealers didn't know about the battery SOH and said that perhaps this is an indication her organization needs to spread the word better. But she noted dealerships that specialize in EVs would know what that is.

One other battery-related thing I noticed was on the Carfax report, which provides a detailed history of a used car. Mine said the battery was replaced, but it wasn't clear if it was the 12-volt (which runs low-voltage electronics, for example) or the lithium ion that powers the car.

When I first told people I was shopping for an EV but wouldn't be able to charge it at home (I rent), I kept hearing the same thing: You can't buy an EV — there's not enough charging infrastructure.

I had to explain that I didn't drive a lot, and that I live in Toronto, which has plenty of public places to charge an EV.

This screenshot from PlugShare shows many of the charging stations in and around Toronto. The closer you zoom in, more are visible. (PlugShare)

I use a street charging station that is just 200 metres from my home — one of 14 charging stations within 500 metres of my home. I simply go and plug it in when there is no fee for parking.

"The infrastructure in urban-suburban parts of Canada is quite good. When the news was about, 'Well, we need more infrastructure,' it was more about doing long road trips and like cross-Canada type tours, not, you know, commuting, which is what most of us do," Clairman said.

My colleague Emily Chung suggests that perhaps that perception comes from chargers being small and not like the giant gas stations we're used to seeing. I think there might be some truth to that.

Finally, range anxiety is real. Even if I had 100 kilometres left for range, I’d be nervous, which is ridiculous. But as the days and weeks go on, I've become less concerned about this, something that Clairman says most users experience.

— Nicole Mortillaro

Old issues of What on Earth? are here . The CBC News climate page is here .

Check out our podcast and radio show. In our latest episode : Sixteen-year-old Evon Murphy loves thrift shopping. Partly because she enjoys fashion and likes to save money. But also because buying second-hand is one way to reduce the fashion industry's impact on the climate. We meet up with Evon at a Vancouver thrift store to talk about the stories she's written for CBC Kids News about emissions from clothing production, and how young people can push for solutions. And we sneak in a little browsing among the leather jackets and band tees while we're at it.

LISTEN | Doc Martens? Nice. Why this teen thrifts for the climate: What On Earth 24:11 Doc Martens? Nice. Why this teen thrifts for climate

What On Earth drops new podcast episodes every Wednesday and Saturday. You can find them on your favourite podcast app or on demand at CBC Listen . The radio show airs Sundays at 11 a.m., 11:30 a.m. in Newfoundland and Labrador.

Check the CBC News Climate Dashboard for live updates on record-breaking weather and current conditions across the country. Set your location to find out how today's temperatures compare to historical trends.

(CBC)

Reader feedback

A number of you pointed out an incorrect caption in the second photo of last week's article about photojournalist Jesse Winter's lessons learned from Canada's big wildfires . The correct caption should be "Two firefighters watch over a planned ignition at the Tsah Creek wildfire near Vanderhoof, B.C., on July 12, 2023. (Jesse Winter)" You can see it with the photo in the web version of the story .

We also featured Adam Walsh's photo of a solar parking lot in South Korea.

Julie Leach of The Atmospheric Fund wrote: "Thanks for bringing up solar canopies in parking lots. We may not have mandatory canopies in Toronto, but at least now we're allowed to build them. They weren't permitted due to zoning restrictions until last month . Thanks for the great newsletter! And go Korea!"

Anne Miller said she found the article about tourist rides on an electric plane in Ontario "very interesting," but she was "disappointed — in fact, appalled — that you didn't include this initiative out of B.C. Harbour Air has been developing the world's first all-electric commercial aircraft, the e-Beaver. It deserves attention!"

If you want to know more or see that electric seaplane in action, here are CBC News stories and videos about its first flight in 2019 and its first flight between the Lower Mainland and Vancouver Island in 2022 . The company says the e-plane is currently undergoing certification and approval with the FAA and Transport Canada .

Write us at whatonearth@cbc.ca (and send photos there too!)

The Big Picture: Guilbeault witnesses Arctic ice cap that's in trouble

(Submitted by Steven Guilbeault)

Instead of spending July under a cloud of toxic wildfire smoke, former federal environment minister and soon-to-be former Liberal MP Steven Guilbeault witnessed another stark reality of climate change.

Guilbeault visited the Greenland ice cap — a glacier that has retreated more than a kilometre over the past 20 years.

"We are ignoring climate change at our own peril," Guilbeault told What on Earth after a visit to Tasermiut Fiord .

Guibeault resigned first as a minister under Prime Minister Mark Carney , unable to stand behind the Carney government's backsliding on Canada's climate plan. As the government backs another West Coast pipeline , by the end of August he will no longer be an MP .

"What Canada is doing will not make things better," he said. "It will make things worse."

The politician was part of the 2026 Students on Ice expedition that travelled from Nuuk, Greenland, to Iqaluit. Nearly 60 young people from Canada, the U.S., Greenland, Iceland, Norway, Denmark and Finland were on the annual voyage.

"I've definitely always been passionate about climate change," said 16-year-old student Jazmin Holwell, who is from Labrador. "[This trip] made me more passionate to spread the word … and try to make a change in climate change."

— David Thurton

Hot and bothered: Provocative ideas from around the web

How much money can you save by cycling (or e-biking) instead of driving for some or all of your trips in 2026? Momentum Mag breaks it down .

In 2019, a non-profit called The Ocean Cleanup conducted a major test of a machine designed to remove plastic pollution from the sea. But it turns out that even though it can remove some plastic, most is too small to pick up. Meanwhile, there's a huge downside for animals such as sea turtles and sharks .

"Black swan" and "grey rhino" are some of the words being used by financial managers and actuaries to describe different kinds of climate risks. Here's what they mean .

Syntropically farmed chocolate, sawdust-aided mushrooms and rain catchers were among climate innovations featured at a showcase in the Philippines last month. The chocolate comes from cacao planted in pattern with trees, promoting forest growth alongside chemical-free farming.

As wildfire smoke lingers, a Greenpeace co-founder is helping lead DIY air purifier workshops near Victoria. The Narwhal reported on how to build these B.C. Lung Association-backed filters with $60 worth of supplies.

Can problem bears be moved instead of killed?

A black bear climbs on top of a picnic table in an image captured by Divyanshu Chaubisa on Aug. 31 at Burnaby Mountain in B.C. (Divyanshu Chaubisa)

On a sunny morning earlier in July, Lucy Pecile was putting children's lunch boxes out on a picnic table at North Burnaby's Forest Grove Park in Burnaby, B.C.

A man she didn't know came purposefully toward her and asked if she'd noticed the large black bear lying in a sunny patch of grass behind a bus stop bench, just metres from where the children she was looking after were playing.

"As the bear heard us calling the kids … the bear got up and started walking up towards us," she recalled.

Pecile and another caregiver gathered up the eight children and walked out of the park away from the bear, which promptly helped itself to the lunches left behind on the picnic table.

Video of the incident soon made its way onto the community Facebook page, where the inevitable debate unfolded: some expressing concern at the bear's behaviour and the safety of children, others noting the community is in bear territory and people should behave in ways that keep bears safe, says Nicole Gladish, whose four-year-old was present when the bear approached.

WATCH | Black bear spotted metres from children in North Burnaby park: Black bear spotted metres from children at North Burnaby park | Duration 0:09 This video, uploaded to a community Facebook page earlier this month, shows a black bear lying in the grass near a picnic table at Forest Grove Park in Burnaby, B.C., while children played nearby. The encounter sparked debate over public safety and how people should behave in bear territory.

It's a common debate in communities next to bear habitat — should you call the B.C. Conservation Officer Service to report a bear looking for sources of human food like garbage or kids’ lunch boxes?

Some encourage others not to report such incidents because of a belief that it amounts to a death sentence for the bear, Gladish says.

"It just always devolves into this blame game where nothing ever really gets solved."

Gladish did call conservation and questioned whether relocating "nuisance bears" — those who have lost their fear of humans and become accustomed to human food sources — was an option.

She says she was told research has proven relocation to be ineffective.

Gladish, a genetic epidemiology researcher at Stanford University, decided to dig deeper.

Research suggests age matters when moving bears

The articles she found said relocation of adult bears aged four and over is generally not successful — they tend to find their way back and resume the problem behaviour.

But it was a different story for juvenile bears between the ages of one and three who had yet to establish a home range. This was especially true of males, though one study found age to be a bigger factor than sex.

A 2009 Ontario study found male bears aged two or three, which make up the majority of nuisance bears, were unlikely to return to the area where they were captured if relocated 30 to 64 kilometres away.

Gladish discovered widespread consensus about this, even in textbooks.

She proposed a pilot project focused on the highest-conflict areas that would see juvenile black bears moved rather than killed. If successful, this would save bears' lives and perhaps encourage more consistent reporting.

But in an emailed statement, the Ministry of Water, Land and Resource Stewardship said, "Moving all young male bears that are reported in conflict with humans would not be a sustainable strategy…. Survival rates of bears after translocation are often much lower than resident bears, and the risk of the bear getting into conflict in another area is also higher."

The province did not respond to a request for peer-reviewed research to support its policy.

What happens when you report a bear

What happens after someone reports a black bear in a residential neighbourhood depends on the bear's behaviour, the Ministry of Environment and Climate Solutions said in an emailed statement.

In some situations, advice on how to better secure attractants such as garbage or bird feeders may be sufficient.

The province's guidelines say relocation will be considered "only in a few, limited circumstances."

"Bears that have lost their fear of people or are conditioned to non-natural food sources are not candidates for relocation or rehabilitation — the risk to public safety is simply far too great," the Ministry of Environment and Climate Solutions said.

Another document says moving problem wildlife "should not require the province to incur financial costs for the translocation or relocation.” However, the province confirmed that when black bears are moved, the province pays.

Meanwhile, Gladish's children continue to go to the park most days. She worries about what would happen if a bear were to startle her kids, or vice versa.

"Unfortunately bears are large and children are small. And if a conflict really were to … happen, that's not going to end well for my kids."

— Tara Carman

World.title: Powwows, dancing help wildfire evacuees ‘come together,’ easing pain of seeing First Nations burn
World.content:
Dilico Anishinabek Family Care held its eighth annual powwow on Thursday in Fort William First Nation. Amid a challenging wildfire season in northwestern Ontario that has displaced more than 2,800 people from several First Nations, here’s what it means for dancers and drummers to come together to share their culture.

Dilico Anishinabek Family Care held its eighth annual powwow on Thursday in Fort William First Nation, which neighbours Thunder Bay. The event helped bring people together as hundreds are displaced during Ontario's wildfire season.

Zander Lapensee says powwows have changed his life — and amid a difficult wildfire season in northwestern Ontario, he hopes his dancing helps raise people’s spirits.

“I'm dancing as hard as I can for them. That's my spirit out there,” said Lapensee, a grass dancer originally from Pukatawagan First Nation ( also known as Mathias Colomb Cree Nation) in northern Manitoba who moved to northwestern Ontario four years ago.

“Praying for the Creator to help them out as much as they can.”

When you're together as one, it's a lot more powerful than just being all over. - Jermaine Beaver, dancer from Nibinamik First Nation

About 180 wildfires continue to burn across the region, displacing more than 2,800 people from over a dozen communities, including several First Nations.

Dilico Anishinabek Family Care held its eighth annual powwow on Thursday in Fort William First Nation, which neighbours Thunder Bay. The organization provided a shuttle service between the event and hotels where wildfire evacuees are staying.

PHOTOS | Dilico Anishinabek Family Care hosts 8th annual powwow in Fort William First Nation:

Aungelle Wabigwan is cultural services manager with Dilico and a member of Namaygoosisagagun First Nation (also known as Collins First Nation), which was destroyed by a wildfire earlier this month. The community’s chief, Helen Paavola, is her aunt.

“We wanted to make sure that the evacuees had a fun event to come attend, look forward to,” Wabigwan said. “It's really overwhelming; my heart is just overflowing with joy to see people come together as community.”

The theme of Dilico’s annual powwow has been “coming together” each year, leading up to this one, “so I think that continues to be fitting this year during this time.”

“I hope they take away that feeling after today,” Wabigwan said of wildfire evacuees in attendance.

Hardships bring people together

Cedar Meeseetawageesic, a 16-year-old jingle dress dancer from Naotkamegwanning First Nation (also known as Whitefish Bay), was too shy to participate in powwows as a child, “but now I got the courage to dance."

Meeseetawageesic said her thoughts are with those who have lost their homes to wildfires, and she hopes Thursday’s event gave them “something to feel good about.”

Cedar Meeseetawageesic, a 16-year-old jingle dress dancer from Naotkamegwanning First Nation, says she's happy to see people take interest in powwows and want to learn more about them. (Sarah Law/CBC)

Jermaine Beaver shared a similar message.

The 19-year-old from Nibinamik First Nation (also known as the community of Summer Beaver) is a chicken dancer — a style that originates from the Prairies. Though some know it as a mating dance, he knows it as a warrior’s dance.

“It's pretty hot outside, but I'm proud to represent my community and my family,” Beaver said.

Jermaine Beaver is a chicken dancer from Nibinamik First Nation, also known as Summer Beaver. The 19-year-old says chicken dancing is a warrior's dance and he was inspired by older family members to give it a try. (Sarah Law/CBC)

As those affected by wildfires come to terms with their losses, he said, it’s important to remember the resilience of First Nations.

“When hardships like that come in our communities, a lot of the times people tend to come together, and when you're together as one, it's a lot more powerful than just being all over.”

At Dilico, Wabigwan said there are various health and wellness services available to support those affected by wildfires.

As well, the Hope for Wellness Helpline provides immediate, toll-free telephone and online chat-based emotional support and crisis intervention to all Indigenous people in Canada. It’s available 24/7 in English and French, and upon request in Cree, Ojibway and Inuktitut.

Lapensee’s words of encouragement? “Dance deadly,” he said before rejoining Thursday’s powwow circle.

World.title: Canadian men's 3x3 wheelchair basketball team gets off to strong start in Glasgow
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Canadian men's 3x3 wheelchair basketball team got off to a hot start at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow on Friday, beating Kenya 16-3.

Reed De'Aeth, of Sherwood Park, Alta., led the way for Canada with eight points and 11 rebounds. Regina's Garrett Ostepchuk added four points. The Canadians next face England on Sunday.

The Canadian women's 3x3 team, led by flag bearer Kady Dandeneau, begin their tournament today at 11:10 a.m. ET when they face South Africa.

Earlier on Friday, Canadian swimmers were in the pool for the first heats of the Commonwealth Games.

Ella Jansen, of Burlington, Ont., qualified for the women’s 400-metre freestyle final. The 20-year-old swam to a time of four minutes 10.55 seconds. Madison Kryger, 17, of Niagara Falls, Ont., will also swim in a final, qualifying in the women's 200m backstroke with a time of 2:12.36.

Canadian Para swimmers Katie Cosgriffe and Mary Jibb both qualified for the women’s 200m individual medley SM10. Cosgriffe, 20, of Burlington, Ont., won her heat in a time of 2:33.05, while the 19-year-old Jibb, of Muskoka, Ont., finished in 2:36.20.

The Canadian men's 4x100m freestyle relay team of Josh Liendo, Antoine Sauve, Benjamin Winterborn, and Lorne Wigginton won their heat in 3:17.11 and qualified for the final. Canada's women's team did not start in their qualifying heat.

Friday’s swimming finals stream live on CBCSports.ca and CBC Gem beginning at 2 p.m. ET.

World.title: Cook This: 3 recipes from Medesque, including a twist on mint chocolate chip
World.content:
Article content

When you are ready to make the triangles, get the phyllo dough out of the fridge. Lay a sheet out in front of you, short side closest to you, and brush with olive oil, then lay a second sheet on top. Spoon one-quarter of the cheese mixture over the bottom corner of the phyllo, leaving a gap around the edge, then fold that corner over into a triangle shape. Repeat, folding the triangle away from you up the phyllo sheet, tucking in the edges as you go, until you have a sealed folded parcel. Repeat with the remaining phyllo dough and cheese filling. When you have made all the triangles, set a large frying pan over a medium heat and pour in enough olive oil to just cover the base. Fry the parcels for 2-3 minutes on each side, in batches if need be so as not to crowd the pan, until golden all over. Remove from the pan onto a plate lined with paper towels to blot off excess oil, then transfer to a serving plate.

World.title: Colombia’s “Shield of the Americas” to operate from Medellin: De la Espriella
World.content:
Medellin will be the home of the US-led “Shield of the Americas” security program, according to Colombia’s President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella and Mayor Federico Gutierrez.

At a meeting with authorities from the Antioquia province, De la Espriella and Gutierrez agreed that Colombia’s second largest city is the “head of the snake of drug trafficking and organized crime.”

From Medellin, the metropolitan area, most orders are sent out to the rest of the country. So we’re going to focus our efforts on Medellin to fight crime. Abelardo de la Espriella

The announcement followed alleged calls between De la Espriella, US President Donald Trump and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and meetings between incoming Defense Minister Jorge Mora and the US’ Deputy Assistant Secretary of War for the Americas, Joseph Humire.

Following the meeting, Mora and Humire announced “Plan Patriota 2.0” and the creation of a “Regional Training Center against Drug Trafficking and Transnational Threats,” which would be “aimed at improving interoperability, operational readiness, and cooperation with allied countries” from the Americas.

During these meetings, the parties explored the joint development of a new bilateral program for cooperation and strategic assistance with a regional scope, known as Plan Patriota 2.0. This initiative is conceived as part of Colombia’s accession to the American Coalition Against the Cartels and is based on the design of the new Policy on Defense, Security, and Civic Coexistence, as well as on the strategy for military and police campaigns in priority areas for the restoration and stabilization of security. Jorge Mora

Plan Patriota was a US-backed military strategy that was implemented by former President Alvaro Uribe between 2003 and 2006.

The plan sought to dismantle the military organization of the now-defunct FARC guerrilla group, which it largely did while also killing thousands and forcibly displacing hundreds of thousands civilians.

De la Espriella has said that he seeks to restart Plan Colombia and seek to militarily destroy groups that were formed during and after peace processes with the FARC and the now-defunct paramilitary organization AUC.

World.title: “Water will run out:” Colombia declares emergency over upcoming El Niño
World.content:
Colombia’s government agreed to declare a national emergency over the consequences of El Niño, a climate phenomenon that is expected to bring extreme drought in December.

According to the government’s environmental institute, IDEAM, this year’s Niño could become the worst since the 1950’s and will peak between November 2026 an March 2027.

During a minister’s council, President Gustavo Petro said that excessive heat and water shortages could lead to energy shortages in regions that rely on hydroelectric dams for their electricity.

Petro asked Finance Minister German Avila to transfer COP4 trillion ($1.2 billion) to disaster management agency UNGRD to double the purchase of solar panels to lessen the demand on these hydroelectric dams.

In December last year, the UNGRD already signed a COP4.2 trillion deal with electricity firm Gecelca to buy solar panels.

In order to maintain food production, the president ordered the purchase of desalination plants for the Caribbean region.

Water is what’s going to run out—we don’t know to what extent, but hopefully Bogotá won’t have to suffer through this again. So, any drinking water supply project that’s already been designed but lacks funding must be funded. Drinking water—all the desalination plants we can bring in, because we don’t build them in Colombia — in all the towns in the northern Caribbean. President Gustavo Petro

Last but not least, Petro urged the Justice Ministry to secure “the accelerated surrender of lands, 500 thousand hectares, that have not been awarded” to landless farmers.

“Provide more land and more water to grow food, grow more food in Colombia, because the sun is going to scorch a lot of food and burn crops. And so it’s likely that we’ll be able to make up for the loss in food supply over these six months with new food supplies,” said the president.

Petro urged his ministers to be careful of corruption, which sank the UNGRD in a crisis in early 2024 and resulted in the detentions of multiple government officials.

World.title: De la Espriella denied aspired control over Colombia’s Congress
World.content:
Colombia’s Congress denied control over the legislative agenda to President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella and voted for a president loyal to former President Alvaro Uribe.

De la Espriella proposed his friend, Senator Alfredo Deluque of the U Party, to assume the leadership of the Senate, which would have given the government control over the congressional agenda.

Ahead of the vote, eight parties expressed their support for Deluque’s candidacy, which would have given him a 55-vote majority in the anonymous vote.

Former President Alvaro Uribe, whose Democratic Center party would be granted the presidency, accused “Abelardo’s circle” of trying to “get rid of this party” and vowed to “defend ourselves.”

Uribe had put up Democratic Center Senator Honorio Henriquez for the job and ordered his 17 senators to stick to their original vote.

If the Tiger roars to destroy the Democratic Center, we’ll have to become hardworking bees and defend ourselves, just like bees do when they’re attacked… I’m frightened by the idea circulating among De La Espriella’s inner circle of destroying that party. Former President Alvaro Uribe

The former president got the support of President Gustavo Petro, arguably Abelardo’s biggest political enemy.

At a rally that was held ahead of the vote, Petro warned senators of his leftist Historic Pact party “not to vote for fascism.”

Under the leadership of Senate bench leader Ivan Cepeda, who lost the presidential election to De la Espriella last month, all 26 of the pact’s senators voted for Henriquez.

Enjoying the secrecy of their vote, dissidents from the parties who were ordered to vote Deluque also turned on the president-elect and delivered Henrique 56 votes. Deluque ended up with only 45.

Less than three weeks before taking office, De la Espriella lost the loyalty of its largest coalition partner in Congress and will have to negotiate his agenda with them.

World.title: Petro calls for “peaceful resistance” against Colombia’s incoming “viceroyalty”
World.content:
President Gustavo Petro called on the people to “prepare peaceful resistance” to the “viceroyalty” that “has been imposed as the president of Colombia.”

During an Independence Day speech in the poor south of Bogota, Petro told thousands of supporters that “the next president of Colombia will be a servant to the rulers of the United States who helped him ‘get elected’.”

“We move from the status of a republic to the status of a viceroyalty again, just like 216 years ago,” said Petro, who on Sunday accepted to become the political leader of the leftist opposition.

It is time to give the second cry of independence… Shout freedom and resistance! Gustavo Petro

Rather than a repetition of the 1810 revolution, the outgoing president proposed to “prepare for peaceful resistance” in defense of communities who benefited from the government’s reforms.

How do you repeal the decree on hourly work that ends the labor reform that created stability, a vital wage, and better working conditions? How? Well, with a permanent general strike of millions of working men and women in Colombia! It is not just by shouting, it is not just by raising flags, they are already used to that… No, it is with a production strike, which is permitted by the National Constitution of Colombia, it is a universal right! And that indeed is civil disobedience! If they are going to strike down the stabilities, the working conditions achieved in this government, a general and indefinite strike in Colombia! Gustavo Petro

Petro threatened to “surround the centers of illegitimate power in Colombia until legitimacy exists once again, which can only be achieved through free popular decision without algorithms, and without foreign money.”

To protect the people, the president suggested the creation of unarmed “liberatory guards” that work in a network, “because they want to kill.”

Wherever they touch a neighborhood, wherever they touch a peasant estate, the network must summon solidarity, it must become a demonstration of all adjacent neighborhoods, of all adjacent villages, of the whole country if necessary. Gustavo Petro

“The only way to stop fascism,” said Petro, “is in peace. It is with joy, but it is with millions and millions of Colombian men and women.”

World.title: Petro to assume political leadership of Colombia’s leading leftist party
World.content:
President Gustavo Petro said Sunday that he would become the leader of Colombia’s largest political party on the left, the Historic Pact.

In a tweet, Petro responded to Senator Ivan Cepeda, who proposed him as party president at a political rally in the city of Tunja on Saturday.

Petro said he would “accept the proposal of my party after surrendering power to the far-right President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella.

The president said he would first go “on a vacation I deserve and didn’t have during four years of governance.”

We will work toward peace and social justice and for a national agreement that prevents violent confrontation among Colombians, and we will seek to contribute to the democratic stability of the countries that Simon Bolívar liberated. President Gustavo Petro

The Historic Pact party was formed in March from a coalition of multiple parties that have long supported the political careers of Petro and Cepeda.

Following a significant electoral victory, the party became the largest of Colombia and will assume 25 of 103 seats in the Senate.

Petro’s former party, Colombia Humana, contributed 12 senators to the collective.

The president started his political career while being a member of the M-19 guerrilla group, which demobilized in 1990.

Petro was elected to the House of Representatives in 1998 an became a senator in 2006.

Between 2012 and 2015, the president was mayor of the capital Bogota.

Petro has been the most popular and powerful leftist politician since the violent death of Liberal Party leader Jorge Eliecer Gaitan in 1948, and was sanctioned by the US Government amid his opposition to the genocide in Gaza.

The president has insisted that his successor won the June elections through fraud and has refused to recognize De la Espriella as his successor.

World.title: Colombia’s peace and human rights offices to close: De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella announced on Monday that he will close the Peace Commissioner’s Office, which was in charge of negotiating peace and implementing peace deals with illegal armed groups.

“The Office of the Peace Commissioner is coming to an end, because there will be no more sham peace processes during my administration,” said De la Espriella in his weekly address to the nation that was broadcast on his social media platforms.

According to the far-right president-elect, who will take office on August 7, other presidential commissioners that will disappear are those of National Reconciliation. and the Office of Human Rights and International Humanitarian Law.

The functions of these offices will be taken over by the Interior, Foreign and Defense ministries that, according to De la Espriella, have been doubling the work of the presidential commissioners.

“These are functions that, by law, are already carried out by other ministries,” so the government can “avoid duplication and extra costs,” said the president-elect.

De la Espriella seems keen to abruptly end the peace policy of his predecessor, President Gustavo Petro, for being too lenient to illegal armed groups.

The president-elect also promised to close war crimes tribunal JEP, which has been trying thousands of former guerrillas and former members of the military.

De la Espriella could only do this through legislation that would change the constitution and the international treaties that protect the victims of an armed conflict between the State and the now-defunct guerrilla organization FARC.

World.title: Petro to seek court order to annul election of De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Gustavo Petro said Tuesday that he will seek a court order to annul the election of President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella.

In a post on social media platform X, Petro said he had gather enough evidence to prove that his successor “was elected from abroad, with nonexistent votes.”

“Today we are presenting the body of evidence we have gathered to the representatives elected by the people, and we will file a lawsuit with the courts to annul the elections, as is our duty,” said the outgoing president.

We are not making things up when we say that Abelardo’s government was elected from abroad, with nonexistent votes included in the percentage automatically adjusted by algorithms created by private Israeli companies with the endorsement of their genocidal government. President Gustavo Petro

“We are facing not only the imminent rise of fascism in Colombia but also what may be the greatest threat to global democracy since Hitler’s time,” said Petro.

In a response that was broadcast on his social media channels, De la Espriella reiterated that Petro was a “tyrant” who was trying to perpetuate power through a coup d’etat with the help of the leftist runner-up in the election, Senator Ivan Cepeda.

Even before becoming a candidate, I warned you: Petro is a tyrant in the making who seeks to perpetuate himself in power by any means necessary. And today, as the president-elect of all of you, I ratify what I have said for so many years. This is no longer an analysis or an opinion; it is a palpable reality. From the moment nearly 13 million Colombians stood by me to defeat him and his political frontman, Petro and Cepeda began their Plan B to stay in power, no matter what it takes. And they want to do so through a coup d’état. President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella

The president-elect asked the armed forces “to protect the Constitution and democracy, and to disobey any order that Petro may be giving to the contrary.”

Resistance, dear compatriots. We cannot allow them to snatch away what we achieved at the ballot box in an epic democratic battle this past June 21. Let us resist, for August 7 is near. God, the vote, and democracy have spoken; we are going to defend the Constitution and the rule of law as we must. President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella has long claimed that he will extradite his predecessor to the United States.

World.title: De la Espriella suspends Colombia’s transfer of power
World.content:
President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella on Tuesday suspended the transfer of power after President Gustavo Petro accused him of fraud.

In a post on social media platform X, De la Espriella said he had “given instructions to the vice president-elect of the Republic to immediately suspend the handover process with the corrupt government that is ending its term.”

I have just given instructions to the president-elect of the Republic to immediately suspend the handover process with the corrupt government that is ending its term, a government that, with its decisions and its conduct, seeks to destroy Colombia. Abelardo de la Espriella

“My duty is to protect the interests of the Nation and guarantee a serious, transparent transition at the service of Colombians, never to legitimize the disaster or the disregard for the constitutional order,” said the president-elect.

In a press conference, Finance Minister German Avila said that he had also suspended cooperation with the transition process in response to comments made by a member of De la Espriella’s team, convicted fraudster Carlos ALonso Lucio, that “undermine the respect, dignity, and decency” of the transition process.

Recent statements by members of the incoming transition committee undermine the respect, dignity, and decency of a process such as the one we are carrying out. These statements were surely made intentionally to hinder the transition process. Accusations and insults have been leveled against the president and his administration, alleging that they are criminals, that they are manipulating the justice system, and that they are seeking to extradite us, among other blunders that have been made. German Avila

“All we have received are insults and disrespect, slander and offenses, and we will not tolerate a single further act of aggression or threat,” said the finance minister.

Avila asked Inspector General Gregorio Eljach to oversee the continuation of the process.

In a post on social media platform X, incoming vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo stressed that his team would continue going through the books to make sure that “those who have betrayed the trust of the Colombian people must answer to the institutions and to history.”
