The Colombia water emergency: what triggered the crisis

Since late 2023, Colombia has been locked under El Niño conditions that bring less rainfall, higher temperatures, and prolonged drought, particularly to the Caribbean, Andean, and Pacific regions.

IDEAM, the national meteorological institute, formally declared the start of El Niño on 3–4 November 2023 and activated early-warning systems across the country.

By January 2024, President Gustavo Petro signed Decree 0037, declaring a national disaster situation for 12 months that unlocked exceptional budget shifts and emergency powers.

For readers unfamiliar with the term, El Niño is a natural climate pattern marked by unusually warm ocean temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific. It disrupts normal weather worldwide, and in northern South America it typically means suppressed rainfall and extended dry spells. A national disaster declaration, meanwhile, is a legal tool that lets the executive branch fast-track spending, reallocate funds without standard congressional approval, and coordinate military and civilian agencies under a single emergency command.

The significance of this early phase goes beyond weather charts. By activating the decree when it did, the government signalled that it expected the drought to deepen and wanted to front-load resources before reservoirs hit truly critical levels. That kind of pre-emptive move is relatively rare in the region and reflects lessons from past El Niño cycles that caught administrations off guard.

Bogotá’s reservoirs and the race to avoid running dry

Bogotá became the most visible face of the Colombia water emergency when the Chingaza, Chuza, and San Rafael reservoir system fell to roughly 16–17% of capacity, the lowest level in decades.

That system supplies about 70% of the capital’s water, and officials warned that only 50 to 60 days of supply remained if conditions did not improve.

The city was divided into nine zones, each facing 24-hour water shutoffs on a rotating basis to slash consumption and give reservoirs time to recover.

Rotating rationing of this kind is a managed scarcity tool. Rather than waiting for a system-wide failure, the utility deliberately cycles outages neighbourhood by neighbourhood. This keeps pressure in the pipes high enough to prevent contamination and gives households predictable windows to store water. For a city of roughly eight million people, the logistical challenge is enormous, and compliance depends heavily on clear public communication.

What makes Bogotá’s situation especially delicate is its altitude and geography. The Chingaza system sits high in the eastern Andes, fed by páramo ecosystems—sponge-like high-altitude wetlands that slowly release water. When rainfall fails, those sponges dry out, and recovery can take months even after rains return.

Beyond the capital: a national drought unfolds

The Colombia water emergency extends far beyond Bogotá, with humanitarian reports documenting shortages in 565 municipalities and rationing in 91 of them.

Multiple departments, including La Guajira, Magdalena, Huila, Sucre, Boyacá, Santander, Atlántico, and Valle del Cauca, declared public calamity over water scarcity.

By April 2024, Colombia’s main reservoirs sat at less than 31% of capacity, just a few points above levels that would trigger national power-grid alerts.

A departmental public calamity declaration functions like a local version of the national disaster decree. It lets governors and mayors redirect budgets, request national support, and impose temporary restrictions on water use without the usual bureaucratic delays. The geographic spread of these declarations—from the Caribbean coast to the Andean interior—shows that this is not a single-region problem but a structural stress test for Colombia’s water infrastructure.

Hydropower and the economic read-through

Roughly 60% of Colombia’s electricity comes from hydropower, making the Colombia water emergency a direct threat to energy supply and business continuity.

The government redirected over US$1.2 billion toward El Niño readiness, prioritising water security, energy grid stability, and agricultural support to cushion the economic blow.

For investors and expats, the crisis signals heightened operational risk in water-intensive sectors and potential electricity cost volatility if reservoir levels do not recover.

This heavy reliance on hydropower is both a strategic advantage and a vulnerability. In normal years, it gives Colombia some of the cleanest and cheapest electricity in Latin America. During severe drought, however, the grid operator must fall back on thermal plants—usually gas or coal—which are costlier to run and can push up wholesale power prices. The US$1.2 billion redirected by the government is meant in part to subsidise those thermal backups and to fund emergency water deliveries for agriculture, a sector that employs a large share of the rural workforce.

What comes next: a “super” El Niño on the horizon

IDEAM and other agencies have warned that the probability of a very strong El Niño affecting Colombia in the coming months exceeds 80%.

Projections point to prolonged drought, record heat, further drops in reservoir levels, and increased forest fires and crop failures.

On a more encouraging note, Bogotá’s reservoirs are currently in a more stable condition than during the 2023–2024 peak, and the capital’s utility does not expect near-term rationing, though this depends on rainfall and continued conservation.

What to watch next is whether the early conservation efforts in Bogotá can hold if the predicted super El Niño materialises. Another open question is how the national grid operator will manage the balance between hydropower and thermal generation if reservoir levels dip below the alert threshold. Finally, readers with business interests in Colombia will want to monitor whether the government extends or modifies the disaster decree as the 12-month window approaches its end, since that decision will shape emergency spending and regulatory flexibility well into the following year.

Sources

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Colombia actually going to run out of water?

Not entirely, but parts of the country have come dangerously close to critically low reservoir levels where urban systems and hydropower plants could fail without drastic rationing. The national disaster declaration and emergency measures are specifically designed to prevent that outcome, though the risk remains serious if dry conditions persist.

How does the Colombia water emergency affect electricity supply?

Since hydropower generates roughly 60% of Colombia’s electricity, low reservoir levels directly threaten energy supply. When national reservoirs dropped below 31% capacity, they approached levels that trigger power-grid alerts, raising the prospect of electricity rationing or price increases for businesses and households.

What is the government doing to manage the water crisis?

President Petro declared a 12-month national disaster via Decree 0037, unlocking exceptional budget powers and emergency coordination. The government redirected over US$1.2 billion toward water security, energy grid stability, and agriculture, while local authorities imposed rotating water rationing in Bogotá and activated conservation campaigns nationwide.

World.title: Mexico Draws More Tourists but Spending per Visitor Falls
World.content:
Tourism Economics

Key Facts —Arrivals up, revenue flat. International tourist arrivals rose 5.3% in January–May 2026, but foreign-currency income fell 0.4%. —Average spend drops sharply. Spending per international tourist fell 4.9% year-on-year, to roughly US $596 per trip. —Excursionists now the majority. Same-day visitors without an overnight stay made up 53.1% of all international arrivals in May 2026. —Air arrivals weaken. The highest-spending segment—air travellers—saw an 8.2% drop in arrivals in April 2026. —Revenue quality erodes. Total tourism income hit records in 2025 at US $31.7 billion, but per-visitor yield has been slipping for over a year.

Mexico is welcoming more international visitors than ever, yet Mexico tourist spending is declining per capita, squeezing the revenue quality of one of Latin America’s largest tourism economies.

Mexico Draws More Tourists But Spending Per Visitor Falls (Photo internet reproduction)

The volume-value disconnect in early 2026

Mexico’s international tourist arrivals climbed 5.3% in the first five months of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier, according to INEGI’s International Travelers Survey. Yet total foreign-currency income from those visitors actually fell 0.4% over the same stretch.

The result is a clear erosion of per-visitor yield. Average spending per international tourist dropped 4.9% year-on-year, while the average outlay per traveller of any category fell 5.3%, from roughly US $330 to US $312.

May 2026 crystallised the trend. Total international travellers reached 8.35 million, up 5.3%, but foreign-currency income slipped 0.3% to US $2.61 billion. More people came; collectively they left slightly less money behind.

Who is arriving—and who is spending

The composition of Mexico’s visitor base has shifted decisively toward lower-spending segments. In May 2026, excursionists—same-day visitors who do not stay overnight—accounted for 53.1% of all international arrivals, overtaking traditional tourists for the first time in recent records.

These excursionists spend very little. Their average outlay was just US $61.80 per person in May. Border tourists, another fast-growing category, spent roughly US $111 on average, while air travellers—the highest-value segment—spent about US $1,269 per trip but represented a shrinking share of total flows.

Gemes Consultores, the firm that first flagged the pattern, summarised it bluntly: Mexico is receiving a relatively larger number of low-spending tourists and, in relative terms, fewer high-spending tourists. The shift is compositional, not cyclical.

The air-travel segment softens

Air arrivals are the backbone of Mexico’s high-yield tourism economy, feeding resorts, urban hotels, and business travel. In April 2026, that segment weakened notably: air-tourist arrivals fell 8.2% year-on-year, and their total spending dropped 7.2%.

The Mexican Federation of Tourism Associations (Fematur) highlighted the air-segment softness as a warning signal. Even among overnight tourists who did arrive by air, average spending fell 5.7%, suggesting broader price sensitivity or shorter stays.

This matters for investors and operators. Hotels, restaurant chains, and transport services built around international air travellers face a thinner revenue base even as headline arrival numbers set records.

The 2025 precedent: growth with slipping yield

The 2026 data extend a pattern already visible in 2025. That year, Mexico welcomed 47.8 million international tourists, up 6.1% from 2024, and tourism revenue reached a record US $31.7 billion, a 4.9% increase.

But average expenditure per international tourist fell 1.2% to US $664. In May 2025 alone, average spending per tourist dropped nearly 10% year-on-year, even as total income hit a monthly record. The headline numbers looked strong; the per-unit economics were already softening.

By early 2026, the revenue line stopped growing altogether. January set an all-time monthly record of 8.84 million international visitors, yet February’s spending rose just 0.3% on an 8.5% jump in arrivals. The decoupling had become impossible to ignore.

What this means for Mexico’s tourism economy

Tourism is one of Mexico’s largest foreign-currency earners, and the shift toward lower-yield visitors carries macroeconomic weight. When arrivals grow faster than income, the sector’s contribution to GDP, employment quality, and investment capacity can come under pressure.

Resorts and urban destinations dependent on air travellers feel the pinch most directly. Border regions see more traffic, but the economic spillover per visitor is modest—a US $111 average spend does not fill hotel rooms or high-end restaurants.

For investors and expats watching Latin America’s largest tourism market, the key metric to track is no longer just arrival volumes. Average tourist expenditure and the mix between air, land, and excursionist arrivals now determine whether record flows translate into healthy returns.

Policy and strategy implications

Mexican tourism authorities have celebrated historic visitor figures, but industry analysts are increasingly vocal about the quality of those arrivals. Gemes Consultores and Fematur both argue that average spend and segment composition deserve as much attention as total visitor counts.

The risk is an over-reliance on high-volume, low-spend tourism that strains infrastructure without delivering proportional economic benefits. Reversing the trend would require attracting and retaining more high-spending, longer-stay visitors—particularly from air markets in North America and Europe.

For now, the data tell a clear story: Mexico’s tourism boom is real, but its revenue engine is running leaner. The country is getting more tourists; it is just earning less from each one.

Sources

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is tourist spending falling in Mexico even as arrivals rise?

The main driver is a compositional shift toward lower-spending visitor segments. Same-day excursionists, who spend about US $62 per person on average, now make up more than half of all international arrivals. At the same time, higher-spending air travellers represent a shrinking share of total flows, and their own average spending has softened.

How much did Mexico earn from tourism in 2025?

Mexico’s tourism revenue reached a record US $31.7 billion in 2025, a 4.9% increase from 2024. International tourist arrivals totalled 47.8 million, up 6.1%. However, average spending per tourist already slipped 1.2% that year, foreshadowing the sharper declines seen in early 2026.

Which types of travellers spend the most and least in Mexico?

Air travellers are the highest-spending segment, averaging about US $1,269 per trip in May 2026. Border tourists spend far less, around US $111 on average. Excursionists—same-day visitors—spend the least, roughly US $62 per person. The growing weight of the latter two groups is pulling down overall average spending.

World.title: Argentina Minimum Wage Hits Historic Low Under Milei
World.content:
Argentina · Labour & Prices

Key Facts —Real decline. Argentina’s real minimum wage has fallen approximately 40% since Javier Milei took office in December 2023. —Historic low. Current purchasing power is worse than during the 2001 crisis and 66.5% below its September 2011 peak. —Bread and beef. A kilo of bread now costs 2.5 hours of minimum-wage work, up from one hour in 2016; ground beef requires nearly six hours. —Nominal vs. real. Decree-driven nominal increases have pushed the minimum wage above ARS 340,000, but inflation above 250% annually has erased real gains. —Poverty link. The wage collapse contributed to poverty rates spiking above 50% in the first half of Milei’s term.

Argentina’s minimum wage has lost roughly 40% of its purchasing power since President Javier Milei took office, leaving registered workers able to buy only six of every ten goods they could afford in late 2023.

Argentina’s minimum wage purchasing power plunges 40% under Milei (Photo internet reproduction)

What the Buenos Aires Herald and university data show

A study by the Instituto Interdisciplinario de Economía Política (IIEP) of the University of Buenos Aires, analysed by the Buenos Aires Herald’s sister outlet the Buenos Aires Times, found the real minimum wage fell 39.7% between November 2023 and May 2026.

The Centro de Investigación y Formación de la República Argentina (CIFRA) reached a similar conclusion, reporting a loss of more than 40% of purchasing power for the Salario Mínimo, Vital y Móvil since Milei assumed the presidency.

The current real minimum wage sits below levels recorded during the 2001 crisis that preceded Argentina’s convertibility collapse, and is roughly 60% lower than in 2015.

The gap between nominal hikes and real erosion

The Milei administration has raised the nominal minimum wage multiple times by decree, pushing it from ARS 156,000 (roughly US$190 at the parallel exchange rate of the time) in early 2024 to above ARS 340,000 by 2026.

Yet annual inflation exceeding 250% during the early adjustment period meant these increases never caught up with the cost of living, leaving real wages deeply negative.

The dynamic reflects a deliberate policy choice: rapid price liberalisation and the removal of subsidies were designed to correct fiscal imbalances, but the immediate cost fell heavily on wage earners.

What a collapsed Argentina minimum wage means in everyday terms

In June 2016, one hour of minimum-wage work bought one kilogramme of bread; today it takes 2.5 hours to purchase that same kilo.

For a kilogramme of ground beef, a staple of the Argentine diet, a minimum-wage worker now needs nearly six hours of labour, compared with two hours a decade ago.

These figures translate into a sharp compression of household budgets, particularly for the roughly 6.3 million registered private-sector workers whose wages are benchmarked to the minimum.

The broader social and poverty picture

The minimum-wage collapse is part of a wider erosion of household purchasing power that pushed poverty above 50% in the first half of Milei‘s term, according to official data.

Real wages across private, public, and informal sectors contracted heavily in 2023 and early 2024, even before the full impact of subsidy cuts and price liberalisation was felt.

Average household capacity to buy the basic basket had already fallen roughly 24% between 2016 and 2024, meaning Milei’s adjustment deepened a pre-existing trend rather than creating it from scratch.

The investor and expat read-through

For foreign investors and expats holding hard currency, the collapse in local purchasing power has made Argentina extraordinarily cheap in dollar terms, fuelling a boom in tourism and real estate interest in Buenos Aires.

But the same dynamic raises medium-term risks: a population squeezed to 2001-era consumption levels creates political pressure that could force policy reversals, particularly ahead of midterm elections.

The government’s bet is that stabilisation will eventually lift real wages as inflation cools, but the data so far shows the recovery in purchasing power has been slow and uneven.

What to watch next

The Milei administration faces a delicate balancing act: maintaining fiscal discipline while responding to growing social pressure over wages that have fallen to historic lows.

Any further decree-driven minimum-wage increases will be closely watched against monthly inflation prints to gauge whether real wages are finally stabilising or continuing their decline.

For markets, the key signal will be whether poverty and wage data begin to improve before the electoral cycle intensifies, or whether the social cost of adjustment becomes the dominant political narrative.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much has Argentina’s minimum wage fallen under Milei?

The real minimum wage has dropped roughly 40% since Javier Milei took office in December 2023, according to studies by the University of Buenos Aires and the CIFRA research centre. This means a minimum-wage worker can now buy only about 60% of what they could in late 2023.

Why has Argentina’s minimum wage lost value despite nominal increases?

The government has raised the nominal minimum wage multiple times by decree, but annual inflation exceeding 250% during the early adjustment period meant these hikes never kept pace with the cost of living. Rapid price liberalisation and subsidy cuts further eroded real purchasing power.

How does Argentina’s current minimum wage compare to past crises?

Today’s real minimum wage is worse than during the 2001 crisis that preceded Argentina’s convertibility collapse, and sits 66.5% below its September 2011 peak. It is also roughly 60% lower than in 2015 and about 20% below 1990s levels.

World.title: Argentina’s Economy Contracts Again in May, Exposing Uneven Recovery
World.content:
Argentina’s Fragile Rebound

Key Facts —Monthly contraction. Economic activity fell 0.5% in May from April, the second consecutive monthly decline. —Year-on-year growth missed forecasts. The economy grew just 0.2% from May 2025, far below the 2.5% analysts had expected. —Sector split. Agriculture and mining led growth, while manufacturing and retail contracted, showing a two-speed economy. —Inflation eased. Monthly inflation slowed to 2.1% in May from 2.6% in April, though annual rates remain high. —Domestic demand weak. Weak imports and tax revenues point to fragile consumer spending under President Javier Milei’s austerity programme.

Argentina’s economy shrank again in May, contracting 0.5% from April and delivering year-on-year growth of just 0.2%, well below market expectations and exposing the uneven nature of the country’s recovery under President Javier Milei.

Argentina’s Economy Contracts Again in May, Exposing Uneven Recovery (Photo internet reproduction)

The Numbers Behind the Headline

The national statistics agency INDEC reported that its monthly economic activity estimator, known as EMAE, fell 0.5% in May on a seasonally adjusted basis. It was the second straight month of contraction, confirming that the rebound seen earlier in the year is losing momentum.

Compared with May a year earlier, activity edged up only 0.2%. Economists surveyed by Bloomberg had forecast a 2.5% annual gain, making the miss one of the largest in recent months and signalling that the recovery is far softer than anticipated.

A Two-Speed Economy Splits the Recovery

The headline figures mask a sharp divide between outward-facing sectors and those tied to domestic consumption. Agriculture and mining continued to expand, buoyed by improved harvests and strong global demand for lithium and other extractive products.

Manufacturing and retail trade, by contrast, contracted. These labour-intensive sectors depend on household spending, which remains under pressure from high inflation and stagnant real wages. The result is an export-led expansion that is not yet translating into broad-based domestic growth.

What the Argentina Economy Shrank Again Means for Milei’s Programme

President Milei’s administration has staked its credibility on a harsh fiscal adjustment designed to crush inflation and restore macroeconomic order. Monthly inflation did ease to 2.1% in May from 2.6% in April, a sign that the disinflation process is continuing, albeit gradually.

Yet the back-to-back monthly contractions raise questions about the social and political sustainability of the austerity path. Unemployment has risen compared with a year earlier, and real wages remain under strain, feeding discontent even as price pressures moderate.

The Investor Read-Through Across Latin America

For international investors and expats watching Argentina, the data presents a mixed picture. The country is not in free-fall, and the disinflation trend is genuine, but the recovery is fragile and highly uneven.

Export-oriented sectors such as energy, mining, and agribusiness continue to offer opportunities, particularly as the government works to improve the business climate. However, consumer-facing industries and any investment tied to domestic demand face a tougher road until real incomes recover.

What to Watch in the Months Ahead

The key indicator to monitor is whether the export-led growth can begin to lift manufacturing and retail in the second half of the year. A sustained recovery in real wages would be the clearest signal that the benefits of stabilisation are reaching ordinary Argentines.

Political risk also looms. Midterm elections later in 2026 will test public tolerance for Milei’s austerity. A further string of weak monthly prints could erode the government’s political capital, even if inflation continues to fall.

Sources

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did Argentina’s economy shrink again in May?

The 0.5% monthly contraction was driven by weakness in manufacturing and retail trade, which offset gains in agriculture and mining. High inflation and strained real wages continue to weigh on consumer spending and domestic demand, even as export sectors perform well.

Is Argentina still in a recession?

Argentina is not in a technical recession at present, but the recovery is fragile. The economy grew 0.2% year-on-year in May, far below expectations, and has now posted two consecutive monthly declines. The picture is one of stagnation rather than outright contraction across all sectors.

How does this affect investors looking at Argentina?

Investors should differentiate between export-oriented sectors like energy, mining, and agriculture, which continue to show strength, and consumer-facing industries that remain under pressure. The disinflation trend is positive, but weak domestic demand means a broad-based recovery is still some way off.

World.title: Oaxaca Journalist Shot Dead After Criticizing State Governor
World.content:
Press Freedom Under Fire

Key Facts —The Victim. Alejandro Leyva, 60, was an independent journalist known for exposing corruption and harshly criticising Oaxaca Governor Salomón Jara. —The Attack. Gunmen on a motorcycle shot Leyva dead while he ate at a roadside food stand in San Pablo Etla, outside Oaxaca City. —Federal Takeover. The federal Attorney General’s Office (FGR) and its special prosecutor for crimes against free expression (FEADLE) have formally joined the investigation. —Prior Warnings. Leyva had reported death threats to state and federal authorities roughly a year before his murder, but no protective measures were implemented. —National Toll. Leyva is at least the seventh journalist murdered in Mexico this year and the fourth since June.

A veteran Oaxaca journalist shot dead while eating at a street stall has triggered a federal investigation, intensifying scrutiny on Mexico’s deadly environment for critical reporters and the government’s failure to protect them.

Oaxaca Journalist Who Criticised Governor Shot Dead; Federal Probe Launched (Photo internet reproduction)

A Voice Against Power Silenced in San Pablo Etla

Francisco Alejandro Leyva Aguilar, a 60-year-old independent journalist and columnist, was murdered on a recent evening in San Pablo Etla, a municipality just outside Oaxaca City. He was eating at a roadside food stand when attackers on a motorcycle pulled up, shot him, and fled.

Leyva died at the scene. For years, his reporting had focused squarely on government corruption and criminal violence in Oaxaca, often directing scathing criticism at the state’s Morena-party Governor, Salomón Jara.

Why Federal Authorities Stepped Into the Oaxaca Journalist Case

Mexico’s legal framework allows federal authorities to “attract” cases when a crime appears linked to journalism. The federal Attorney General’s Office (FGR) operates a Special Prosecutor’s Office for Crimes Against Freedom of Expression, known by its Spanish acronym FEADLE, precisely for this purpose.

In Leyva’s case, the Oaxaca state prosecutor’s office opened the initial investigation and quickly requested assistance from FEADLE. Governor Jara publicly ordered a thorough probe and instructed state officials to coordinate fully with federal prosecutors, effectively bringing the FGR into a leadership role.

This pattern mirrors other high-profile journalist murders, such as the recent kidnapping and killing of Veracruz reporter Roxana Guzmán. In that case, the FGR explicitly took over and transferred the file to FEADLE in Mexico City, treating the murder as a federal crime against free expression.

A Pattern of Threats and Inaction

Leyva’s murder did not occur in a vacuum. He had reported receiving death threats to both state and federal authorities approximately one year before he was killed. He filed complaints with the State Human Rights Commission and the federal Attorney General’s Office.

According to Reporters Without Borders (RSF), no protective measures were ever implemented despite authorities knowing the risks he faced. RSF is now demanding a public explanation for this inaction, a demand that underscores the systemic failure of Mexico’s protection mechanism for journalists and human rights defenders.

The Investment and Stability Read-Through

For investors and expats monitoring Latin America, the killing of a journalist in Oaxaca is not an isolated security incident. It is a data point in a deteriorating rule-of-law environment that directly affects operational risk assessments, insurance costs, and talent retention.

Mexico’s entrenched impunity for crimes against the press—FEADLE has been widely criticised for low conviction rates and slow progress even in emblematic cases like those of Miroslava Breach and Javier Valdez—signals a state unable to enforce its own protective mandates. This institutional weakness is a material factor for any entity with long-term exposure to the Mexican market.

What Comes Next in the Federal Investigation

Authorities have not yet publicly identified any suspects and maintain that all possible motives are under investigation. However, Leyva’s decades-long focus on corruption and his direct criticism of the sitting governor make his journalistic work a central line of inquiry for press-freedom advocates.

The practical reality of federal involvement varies. In some cases, the FGR sends a team but leaves formal control with the state. In others, it assumes full jurisdiction. The key metric to watch is whether FEADLE formally attracts the case entirely, a move that would signal federal recognition that Leyva was killed for his reporting.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who was Alejandro Leyva and why was he targeted?

Alejandro Leyva was a 60-year-old independent journalist and columnist in Oaxaca. He was known for exposing government corruption and directly criticising Governor Salomón Jara. While authorities have not confirmed a motive, he had reported death threats linked to his work a year before his murder, and no protective measures were taken.

What does it mean when the “Feds take over” a journalist murder case in Mexico?

It means the federal Attorney General’s Office (FGR) and its Special Prosecutor for Crimes Against Freedom of Expression (FEADLE) assume leadership or formal co-jurisdiction over the investigation. This happens when an attack is suspected to be linked to the victim’s journalistic work, elevating it from a state-level crime to a federal freedom-of-expression case.

How dangerous is Mexico for journalists right now?

Mexico remains one of the world’s most dangerous countries for journalists. Leyva’s killing is at least the seventh murder of a journalist in Mexico this year and the fourth since June. Impunity is the norm; the federal special prosecutor has been criticised for low conviction rates, even in high-profile cases.

World.title: The Truth About Flying Your Pet Abroad: Busting Common Relocation Myths
World.content:
EXPAT FOCUS — PET RELOCATION

Key Facts —Cargo holds are pressurised. Airlines that carry live animals use temperature-controlled, pressurised cargo compartments. —Sedation is widely discouraged. Veterinary experts warn it can cause breathing and blood-pressure problems at altitude. —Airline policies differ sharply. Cabin access, breed restrictions, and seasonal embargoes vary by carrier and route. —Some countries mandate cargo travel. Even small pets must enter certain nations as manifest cargo, not in the cabin. —Preparation takes months, not weeks. Microchipping, rabies vaccines, titre tests, and import permits can require a 4–7 month runway.

Flying your pet abroad is a heavily regulated, months-long process where preparation trumps luck — and the most persistent myths about cargo danger, sedation, and one-size-fits-all airline rules consistently lead expats into costly mistakes.

The Truth About Flying Your Pet Abroad: Busting Common Relocation Myths (Photo internet reproduction)

The cargo hold is not a dark, freezing dungeon

The single most stubborn myth about flying your pet abroad is that the cargo hold is unpressurised, unheated, and inherently dangerous. Airlines that accept live animals use dedicated compartments that are both pressurised and temperature-controlled, matching the conditions in the passenger cabin.

U.S. Department of Transportation data shows incidents involving pets are extremely rare relative to the hundreds of thousands transported annually. The real risk is not the hold itself but poor preparation: an ill-fitting crate, a pet left unattended on a hot tarmac, or a last-minute booking that skips veterinary checks.

Why vets say no to sedation during pet relocation

Many owners assume a sedated pet will sleep peacefully through a long-haul flight. Veterinary and airline sources are nearly unanimous in rejecting this logic.

At cruising altitude, the lower air pressure already reduces oxygen saturation. Sedatives compound the effect by depressing respiration and heart rate, and they impair a pet’s ability to regulate body temperature and balance.

Most airlines prohibit visibly sedated animals, and many require a signed declaration that no drugs were administered.

No two airlines handle flying your pet abroad the same way

A small dog that flies in the cabin on one carrier may be refused entirely by another — even on the same route. Policies vary by aircraft type, destination country, season, and breed.

Snub-nosed breeds face blanket bans or heightened restrictions on many airlines because of their elevated respiratory risk. Some carriers impose summer and winter embargoes when ground temperatures exceed safe thresholds, meaning a perfectly planned move can be blocked by a heatwave.

Small pets do not automatically get a cabin seat

The assumption that any pet under 8 kg can ride in the cabin is one of the costliest errors expats make. Several countries — including Australia, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom — require all incoming pets, regardless of size, to enter as manifest cargo through designated animal-reception centres.

Even when the destination permits cabin travel, the airline may not. Low-cost carriers often refuse pets outright, and full-service airlines cap the number of animals per flight.

Booking a human ticket without first reserving a pet slot can leave a family stranded at check-in.

The timeline for international pet relocation is measured in months

A common expat misstep is treating pet relocation like an add-on to a house move — something to sort out in the final fortnight. In reality, the paperwork chain alone can stretch to seven months.

The typical sequence starts with ISO-compliant microchipping, followed by a rabies vaccination administered after the chip is implanted. Certain countries then require a rabies antibody titre test drawn at least 30 days after vaccination and sent to an approved laboratory.

Only after a satisfactory result does a waiting period — often 90 days — begin before entry is permitted. Layering on import permits, parasite treatments, and a final health certificate issued within days of departure leaves zero margin for delay.

What the crate contains matters as much as the crate itself

Owners often pack a favourite blanket, toy, or chew treat to comfort their pet. Airlines and pet-relocation specialists increasingly warn against this instinct.

Loose bedding can become a choking or entanglement hazard during turbulence. Collars have been known to catch on crate doors.

Most carriers now require a hard-sided, IATA-compliant crate with a secure water source and nothing else inside — a rule born from incident data, not bureaucracy.

The Latin America read-through for expats and investors

For professionals relocating to São Paulo, Mexico City, Bogotá, or Santiago, pet logistics are a material line item. A full-service international pet move handled by a specialist firm typically runs from $2,500 to $6,000 depending on distance, animal size, and destination complexity.

Latin American import rules are generally less restrictive than those of the EU, UK, or Australia, but they are not uniform. Brazil requires a microchip, a valid rabies certificate, and a health certificate endorsed by the country of origin’s veterinary authority.

Mexico adds a preventive treatment certificate for internal and external parasites. Argentina mandates the same core documents but processes them through SENASA, its national agri-food health agency.

Getting the destination-country requirements wrong can mean quarantine, re-export, or worse.

The market for pet-relocation services has grown alongside the post-pandemic mobility wave. Specialist firms now offer door-to-door logistics, customs brokerage, and even charter-flight shares for multiple-pet households.

For expats, the cost is increasingly treated as a relocation benefit negotiated into an employment package — and for good reason.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the cargo hold safe for flying my pet abroad?

Yes. Airlines that transport live animals use cargo compartments that are pressurised and temperature-controlled, similar to the passenger cabin.

US. DOT data shows incidents are very rare relative to the total number of animals flown each year. The greater risks are poor crate fit, extreme ground temperatures during loading, and skipping veterinary pre-clearance.

Should I sedate my pet for a long-haul flight?

Veterinary and airline guidance strongly advises against sedation. At altitude, sedatives can depress breathing, lower blood pressure, and impair a pet’s ability to regulate body temperature.

Most airlines prohibit visibly sedated animals and may require a signed declaration that no drugs were given.

How far in advance should I start planning an international pet move?

Plan for a four- to seven-month runway. The process typically requires microchipping, a rabies vaccination, a waiting period, possibly a titre test sent to an approved lab, import permits, parasite treatments, and a final health certificate issued within days of travel.

Starting late is the single most common reason pets are denied boarding or entry.

World.title: Costa Rica’s San Jose Airport Is Getting Its First Hotel
World.content:
Tourism Infrastructure

Airport operator AERIS confirmed the plan, as reported by The Tico Times on 22 July 2026. —Current gap. Existing “airport hotels” like the Holiday Inn Express and Hampton by Hilton sit off-site, requiring a shuttle ride across the highway. —Strategic shift. The move aligns SJO with global hub airports that offer direct terminal or airside accommodation for transit passengers. —Brand pending. Specific details on the hotel brand, room count, and opening timeline have not yet been disclosed by AERIS.

Costa Rica’s Juan Santamaría International Airport will get its first on-site San José Airport hotel, operator AERIS has confirmed, closing a long-standing gap in the country’s primary air-travel gateway.

A First for SJO: Moving from Near to On-Site

For years, travellers passing through Costa Rica’s busiest airport have faced a small but persistent inconvenience. Every hotel marketed as a “San José Airport hotel” has actually been located off airport property.

The Holiday Inn Express and Hampton by Hilton sit roughly one kilometre away across the Pan-American Highway. The Courtyard by Marriott and Fairfield by Marriott are slightly farther, in Alajuela.

All require a shuttle or taxi ride, however short. The new project changes that equation entirely by placing accommodation directly at the terminal complex.

The Business Case: Why an Integrated San José Airport Hotel Matters

SJO handled over five million passengers annually before the pandemic and has seen traffic rebound strongly. A significant share are business travellers and connecting passengers who value time over cost.

An on-site hotel captures that high-yield segment directly. It allows a traveller arriving late to walk from gate to room without leaving the secure perimeter or waiting for a shuttle.

For early-morning departures, the value proposition is equally clear. Global hubs from Amsterdam Schiphol to Panama’s Tocumen have long understood this logic.

AERIS and the Modernisation of Juan Santamaría

AERIS, a private consortium, has managed SJO since 2009 under a concession model. The group has steadily upgraded the airport’s physical plant and commercial offerings.

Adding a hotel fits a broader pattern of extracting more non-aeronautical revenue from the asset. Retail, parking, and now hospitality diversify income streams beyond landing fees.

For AERIS’s investors, the hotel represents a long-term bet on Costa Rica’s continued appeal as a nearshore business destination and tourism magnet.

What It Means for Investors and the Hospitality Sector

The announcement signals confidence in sustained demand. Costa Rica’s tourism board reported record visitor numbers in 2025, and the country remains a top choice for digital nomads and retirees.

For existing off-site hotels, the new competitor on airport grounds may pressure rates. However, the market is segmented: budget-conscious travellers will still look to nearby Alajuela inns.

The on-site hotel will likely target a premium tier, capturing business expense accounts and time-sensitive leisure travellers. The move also opens a potential opportunity for international hotel chains to bid on the management contract.

The Latin America Read-Through: Airports as Destinations

Across Latin America, major airports are evolving from simple transit points into commercial ecosystems. Tocumen International in Panama already operates a terminal-adjacent hotel. Mexico City’s Benito Juárez and Bogotá’s El Dorado have similar offerings.

Costa Rica’s move keeps SJO competitive in a region where airport infrastructure is a factor in airline route decisions. A modern hub with seamless connections and on-site accommodation is more attractive to carriers considering new frequencies. For the expat and investor community, improved airport services reduce one more friction point in a country that already ranks high for ease of living.

What to Watch Next

The key unknowns are the brand, the timeline, and the financing structure. AERIS has not yet released a request for proposals or named a development partner.

Investors should monitor whether the project is built under a management contract with a global chain or as a fully AERIS-owned asset. The construction timeline will also be telling: a fast-tracked project signals strong confidence in near-term traffic growth.

A slower, phased approach may indicate a more cautious read on the global economy.

Sources

Frequently Asked Questions

Is there currently a hotel inside San José Airport?

No. All existing hotels marketed as airport hotels, including the Holiday Inn Express and Hampton by Hilton, are located off airport property and require a shuttle or taxi ride. The new project will be the first physically integrated at the terminal.

When will the new San José Airport hotel open?

AERIS has not yet announced an opening date or construction timeline. The project was confirmed in July 2026, and further details on the brand, room count, and schedule are expected in subsequent announcements.

What are the best current hotel options near SJO?

The closest reliable options are the Holiday Inn Express San Jose Costa Rica Airport and the Hampton by Hilton San Jose Airport, both roughly one kilometre away with frequent, free shuttle service. The Courtyard by Marriott and Fairfield by Marriott in Alajuela are slightly farther but also cater specifically to airport travellers.

World.title: Iberojet Adds Third Weekly Flight Between Madrid and Costa Rica
World.content:
Spanish carrier Iberojet will add a third weekly flight between Madrid and San José beginning in late November, expanding one of Costa Rica’s few direct links to continental Europe ahead of the Christmas travel season. The new service will depart Madrid on Thursdays, joining the airline’s existing Tuesday and Saturday departures to San Jose’s Juan Santamaría International Airport.

The addition comes under an agreement between Iberojet and the Instituto Costarricense de Turismo (ICT). According to the airline, the Thursday frequency will not be a seasonal add-on. It will remain part of Iberojet’s regular published schedule through 2027 and 2028, giving travelers a durable third option on a route that has until now clustered around the start and end of the week.

Mario Domínguez, spokesman for the tour operations division at Ávoris, the Spanish travel group that owns Iberojet, said the additional frequency reflected the route’s performance and the company’s confidence in Costa Rica as a strategic destination. He said rising demand confirmed growing traveler interest in the market and that the company intended to keep expanding the connection.

Marcos Borges, executive president of the ICT, described the expansion as strong news for the country, saying it improves air capacity with one of Costa Rica’s principal source markets in Europe and signals the airline’s confidence in the destination’s competitiveness. He added that more frequencies would bring more visitors, generate employment and increase economic activity in communities that depend on tourism.

Ricardo Hernández, executive director of AERIS, the concession holder that manages Juan Santamaría, said the third frequency demonstrated airline confidence in the airport and in Costa Rica’s potential as a destination, and that AERIS and the ICT would continue investing in improvements to support carrier growth.

The numbers behind the decision favor Spain in particular. ICT figures show that arrivals from Spain by air rose 16.8% in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period last year, reaching 24,910 visitors, up from 21,330. That was the sharpest percentage gain of any major European market apart from the Netherlands, which grew 18.6%. Europe as a whole sent 236,462 travelers to Costa Rica by air between January and June, a 9.7% increase.

June alone told a more complicated story. Total air arrivals to Costa Rica fell 1.2% that month against June 2025, the first monthly decline of the year after eight consecutive months of growth. The ICT attributed the dip to a combination of international factors including geopolitical tensions, higher jet fuel costs and travel patterns around the 2026 World Cup rather than to any loss of competitiveness by the destination. European traffic ran against that trend, rising 12.9% in June, with Spanish arrivals up 23.4% year over year that month.

For travelers on this side of the Atlantic, the practical effect is more seats and more flexibility on a corridor that carries a fair amount of connecting traffic. Madrid functions as a hub for onward travel across Europe, North Africa and the Middle East, and a midweek departure opens up itinerary combinations that were awkward under a Tuesday and Saturday schedule. Anyone planning trips to Europe, or arranging visits from family members abroad, will have a third departure day to work with from late November onward.

Fares and exact departure times for the Thursday service had not been published at the time of the announcement. Travelers planning holiday-season trips should check the airline’s schedule directly, since inaugural-period timings on new frequencies frequently shift before the first departure.

World.title: Costa Rica Lawmaker Revives Cable Car Idea for Chirripó Summit
World.content:
Costa Rica’s highest point is hard to reach, and for the past half-century that difficulty has been the policy. A proposal now circulating in the Legislative Assembly would change it. Álvaro Ramírez Bogantes, head of the National Liberation Party caucus and the deputy elected first on the party’s San José slate, said this week that he is evaluating a project to build a cable car to Cerro Chirripó, the 3,820-meter (12,533-foot) summit that crowns the Cordillera de Talamanca.

Ramírez said the idea is to widen access to the peak for more people, including those with different physical conditions, and that he has presented it to the Grupo de Acción Territorial de Pérez Zeledón, a civic organization headed by Antonio Mora. He described a group of business owners and community leaders with whom he has been discussing the concept, and said he has begun conversations with other legislative caucuses about it.

Beyond that, almost nothing about the proposal exists yet. There is no route, no engineering study, no cost estimate, no environmental impact assessment, no financing plan and no bill filed in the Assembly. Ramírez has not said whether the line would terminate at the summit itself, at the Base Crestones shelter, or somewhere below the park boundary — a distinction that would determine much of the project’s legal footing. What he has described is a conversation, and he has framed it as one.

The lawmaker said the concept borrows from a cooperation model developed for a proposed cable car to Turrialba Volcano, and that he wants to test whether the same approach could be replicated in Pérez Zeledón. That Turrialba initiative, promoted by former deputy Rosaura Méndez with support from then-legislators Alejandro Pacheco and Pilar Cisneros, is the furthest along of Costa Rica’s several cable car proposals.

Cisneros told reporters in February that the plan would stimulate tourism and improve park infrastructure. The initiative is budgeted at ₡2,053 million — roughly $4.5 million at current exchange rates — including ₡1,600 million from the Rural Development Institute for land purchase and ₡650 million from the Environment and Energy Ministry.

The Chirripó idea is not new either, and its earlier version collapsed on the same ground it would have to cross now. In February 2017 the Pérez Zeledón Municipal Council voted unanimously to declare a summit cable car a project of cantonal and public interest, and then-mayor Jeffrey Montoya asked President Luis Guillermo Solís to declare it of national interest. Montoya put the likely cost at around $20 million and said the municipality would seek a private partner.

Within weeks the plan drew organized opposition. Environmental attorney Álvaro Sagot argued that the National Parks Service Law expressly barred the kind of stations and infrastructure the municipality envisioned. Luis Diego Marín of Preserve Planet said the only route forward would be a bill amending that law, which he called very unlikely, and warned that the park supplies the water Pérez Zeledón residents drink. Osvaldo Durán of the Federación Conservacionista noted that no technical study had been produced before the council voted. The project went no further.

The legal question is genuinely contested rather than settled. The Parks Service Law restricts construction inside national parks, while Article 18 of the Forestry Law allows the state forestry administration to authorize recreation and ecotourism infrastructure within the State’s Natural Heritage under defined conditions.

Any Chirripó project would also have to reckon with the park’s international standing. Chirripó National Park sits within the Talamanca Range-La Amistad Reserves, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1983 and extended in 1990, and a major built structure inside a World Heritage property would attract scrutiny well beyond San José.

The practical arithmetic is equally unforgiving. Access to the summit today runs through a reservation system that caps overnight capacity at 60 people per night at the Base Crestones shelter, distributed across the San Gerardo, Herradura and San Jerónimo approaches, with bookings made through SINAC’s online platform.

Slots between December and April fill fastest. Critics of the 2017 plan argued that a cable car needs high throughput to pay for itself while Chirripó’s carrying capacity is deliberately low, and that the families around San Gerardo de Rivas who provide lodging, meals and porter services to hikers would lose the business that the overnight trek generates.

Neither SINAC nor the Environment and Energy Ministry, headed since May by Mónica Navarro Del Valle, has commented publicly on the Ramírez proposal. Both would be central to any serious evaluation, along with the National Environmental Technical Secretariat, which reviews environmental viability, and the park’s own management plan, which governs what activities are permitted where.

Two other cable car proposals have surfaced in recent years without producing anything built. The French group Poma pitched routes to the Cartago municipality in 2021, including Cristo Rey to Tierra Blanca and Tierra Blanca to Irazú Volcano. In 2022 then-deputy Carlos Andrés Robles, now Minister of Seas, promoted a line linking Quepos to Manuel Antonio National Park and proposed that the Rural Development Institute and the Costa Rican Electricity Institute fund a feasibility study.

For anyone planning a Chirripó climb anytime soon, nothing changes. The trek remains a reserved, multi-day hike, and any cable car — if it ever advances past conversation — would be years and several legal thresholds away.

World.title: Costa Rica Betting Operation Lands California Man in Federal Prison
World.content:
A California man who survived an assassination attempt outside an Escazú café more than a decade ago has been sentenced to federal prison for running an illegal gambling and money laundering operation out of Costa Rica. Jason Noah Feinman, 52, of Calabasas, received 27 months on June 9 in federal court in Los Angeles after pleading guilty in January to one count each of tax evasion, operating an illegal gambling business, and money laundering. A federal judge also ordered him to pay more than $1.3 million (about ₡589 million) in restitution and a $150,000 (₡68 million) fine, plus interest.

According to the Justice Department, Feinman operated a Costa Rica–based business that ran a website unlicensed bookmakers used to take wagers, including from bettors living in California, in violation of both state and federal law. The platform was a service layer for other operators rather than a consumer-facing sportsbook, and court filings do not name the business. Prosecutors say Feinman then laundered the cash the operation generated by converting it into checks made out to himself or his companies.

The mechanics were straightforward and repetitive. Between May 18, 2018 and January 2, 2024, the Justice Department says, Feinman handed a single customer more than $1.5 million (₡680 million) in cash and received 18 checks payable to him or his businesses for the equivalent amount, one of them for $200,000. Court filings identify that customer only by the initials C.K. and describe checks whose memo lines frequently referenced loans. Across the life of the operation, prosecutors say Feinman exchanged between $1.5 million and $3.5 million (₡680 million to ₡1.59 billion) in cash for checks.

The tax case ran alongside it. Feinman reported no taxable income to the Internal Revenue Service on his 2020 return and paid nothing that year, despite earning roughly $1.8 million (₡815 million), according to the Justice Department. Between 2018 and 2022 he evaded taxes on approximately $4.2 million (₡1.9 billion) in income, a loss to the United States that prosecutors put at about $1.52 million (₡689 million).

Assistant Attorney General Colin McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division and First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bilal A. Essayli for the Central District of California announced the sentence. IRS Criminal Investigation and Homeland Security Investigations conducted the investigation, and Trial Attorneys John C. Gerardi and Charles A. O’Reilly of the Criminal Division’s Tax Section prosecuted the case. The Fraud Division was created on April 7 and counts the case among its early results.

Feinman’s history in Costa Rica predates the gambling charges and includes a considerably more violent episode. In 2015 he was ambushed by gunmen on a motorcycle as he left a parking lot in Escazú, struck by nine rounds, and survived. Two men, Ricardo Francisco Solís Méndez and Steven Javier Calvo Sánchez, were tried at the Pavas courts for attempted homicide in a case that rested heavily on Feinman’s own identification of his attackers, which his attorney Miguel Jiménez Cerros said the American made on three separate occasions.

During the trial, two parking attendants who witnessed the shooting testified they had heard gunfire but could offer nothing further, with one telling the court he had a family. Jiménez Cerros said at the time that his client’s next objective was helping investigators identify whoever ordered the attack, a question the proceedings never resolved.

The case is not an outlier. In October 2025, Christopher Scott King, 51, of Santa Monica was sentenced to 21 months after admitting he ran an unlicensed bookmaking operation from Los Angeles County using a Costa Rica–based sports betting website to take wagers from California bettors. Prosecutors said King concealed $13.6 million (₡6.16 billion) in income from the IRS between 2019 and 2022 and laundered proceeds through real estate development and gold purchases.

He was ordered to forfeit $10 million (₡4.53 billion) and pay $3.8 million (₡1.72 billion) in restitution. A year earlier, Matthew Bowyer of Orange County pleaded guilty to running a betting ring that moved wagers through Costa Rican websites and casino agents, an operation whose clients included Ippei Mizuhara, the former interpreter for Los Angeles Dodgers star Shohei Ohtani, who placed roughly 19,000 bets through it.

The pattern that emerges from these prosecutions is consistent enough to be a template. American operators establish the technical and administrative side of a bookmaking business in Costa Rica, where offering online betting services to customers abroad occupies a permissive regulatory space and has supported a substantial data-processing sector for years, then use that infrastructure to reach bettors in states where the activity is plainly illegal.

What repeatedly ends these operations is not the betting itself but what happens to the cash afterward. In Feinman’s case it was checks. In King’s it was property and gold. In each, the proceeds eventually had to enter a banking system, and that is where IRS Criminal Investigation found them.

For the thousands of foreign residents working in or around Costa Rica’s online gaming and call center industry, the distinction that matters is jurisdictional rather than technical. Costa Rica does not license offshore sportsbooks in the way Curaçao or Malta do, and companies here have historically operated under ordinary commercial registration on the understanding that no bets are accepted from within the country.

That arrangement offers no protection whatsoever from United States law when American customers are on the other end of the transaction, and the last three years of federal sentencings suggest prosecutors have become considerably more systematic about following the money back to its source.

World.title: Stoney Ferguson charged with aggravated assault and insulting words
World.content:
Stoney Ferguson charged with aggravated assault and insulting words

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Stoney Ferguson, the son of Agriculture Minister Rodwell Ferguson, has been formally arrested and charged with aggravated assault and insulting words. He was subsequently granted bail.

The charges follow a July 18 incident near a police checkpoint on the Placencia Main Road. Police allege that Ferguson became confrontational with officers and later threw a large stone that missed a police corporal but damaged a police patrol vehicle.

BBN previously reported that Interim Minister of Home Affairs Julius Espat directed police to arrest Ferguson and instructed that the case be handled according to law and without political considerations.

World.title: From loss to legacy: Belizean graduates as first doctor in her family
World.content:
From loss to legacy: Belizean graduates as first doctor in her family

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Ivy Giselle Duncan has made history, not just as a medical graduate, but as the first doctor in her family, and she did it while carrying a grief that would have broken many.

The young Belizean woman recently graduated in Cuba with the Título de Oro, the gold title reserved for graduates of the highest academic distinction, capping years of study abroad with the honour every medical student dreams of.

Behind the achievement lies a journey marked by profound trial. While studying far from home, Duncan lost her father, a blow that arrived in the middle of the most demanding years of her life. With the unwavering support of her mother and her faith in God, she never lost her strength, pressing forward through the grief to the finish line he did not live to see her cross.

Resilience, discipline, and a heart full of purpose carried her through, and now they are coming home. Duncan is poised to bring her skills, knowledge, and compassion back to Belize, where she hopes to make healthcare more accessible and to be a source of hope for her community.

Her story adds to the proud tradition of Belizeans who have pursued medical training in Cuba and returned to strengthen the country’s health system, young professionals who leave home with a dream and come back with the tools to serve.

For every family that has never seen one of its own in a white coat, for every student studying through hardship, and for every child watching from a village classroom, Ivy Duncan’s journey carries a simple message: it can be done.

Congratulations, Dr. Duncan. Belize awaits your healing hands, and your father’s legacy lives on in every patient you will serve.

World.title: National Institute of Culture and History and Corozal Organization of East Indian Cultural Heritage discuss preservation of East Indian heritage
World.content:
National Institute of Culture and History and Corozal Organization of East Indian Cultural Heritage discuss preservation of East Indian heritage

By Zoila Palma: The National Institute of Culture and History (NICH) met with the Corozal Organization of East Indian Cultural Heritage (COEICH) on July 21, 2026, for a courtesy visit focused on strengthening collaboration to promote and preserve East Indian heritage in Belize.

Since its establishment in 2009, COEICH has worked to safeguard and celebrate East Indian culture through festivals, storytelling, cooking workshops, cultural literature, dance performances, summer camps and other initiatives. The organization has also contributed to the rehabilitation of Masala Park and regularly delivers cultural presentations at schools and national events.

During the meeting, COEICH shared its vision and goals, including its efforts to teach East Indian history and cuisine in schools. The organization is also working on producing a traditional cookbook as part of its efforts to document and promote cultural heritage.

NICH President Albert Vaughan thanked the Corozal Organization of East Indian Cultural Heritage for its continued commitment to preserving Belize’s cultural heritage and expressed the institute’s willingness to collaborate and support its initiatives.
