World.title: Domestic violence cases on the rise in Estonia this year
World.content:
Police in Estonia say domestic violence cases have increased in this year, though the rise could also reflect more victims reporting abuse and seeking help.

Police say incidents are more common during holidays and weekends, when people spend more time at home and alcohol use often increases.

Last year, seven domestic violence cases in Estonia ended in deaths.

"Domestic violence cases are unfortunately an everyday part of police work," said Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) development expert Martin Kreitsman.

He said DV cases had declined slightly in recent years but have risen somewhat in the first half of 2026.

"This in itself may not be a bad thing, and could mean we are being notified more and people have better access to help," Kreitsman added.

Victims may seek help 'for a friend'

Despite the uptick in police responses, the number of people contacting Ohvriabi, Estonia's victim support service, has remained steady.

Regional victim support staffer Siim Schvede said people often reach out to share their experiences, ask how to help their partner or loved one and discuss their concerns.

"Most reports we receive involve mental and physical violence," he said.

Schvede added that many people find it difficult to ask for help directly and instead seek support by describing the situation as a friend's problem.

Estonia's Victim Support (Ohvriabi) offers help in Estonian, English and Russian. Source: ERR

According to police statistics, 76 percent of perpetrators of domestic violence are men, while victims are most often women.

Most reports of DV come directly from victims, though police also receive calls from neighbors, witnesses and even children.

Kreitsman stressed that kids are especially vulnerable in DV situations because even if they are not direct victims of the violence, they are still impacted when someone in their family experiences it.

Exposure to domestic violence, he added, can shape children's future, potentially increasing the risk that they themselves may later become either victims or perpetrators of DV.

According to police figures, the highest number of DV cases is recorded in Harju County.

Resources and support available

If you are experiencing or think you may be experiencing domestic abuse or violence, help is available.

In case of emergency, call 112. The Women's Support and Information Center hotline is available 24/7 at +372 5594 9496. The Ohvriabi victim support hotline is available 24/7 in Estonian, Russian and English at 116 006. The child helpline is also open 24/7 in Estonian, Russian and English at 116 111.

World.title: Raul Eamets: Only those who learn to lead can compete for good jobs
World.content:
The labor market wants increasingly mature people, and education prepares increasingly childish ones. What are the solutions? The honest answer is that we do not yet know, writes Raul Eamets.

The impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on everyday life, our ability to think, and children's mental development has received great attention for a couple of years already. Our brain researchers' claims that the widespread use of AI already in basic school or even earlier inhibits brain development are worrying. Connections in the brain that normally form during learning remain incomplete if we start asking AI about everything very early on. It is quite frightening to think that in 20 years the parliament will be filled with representatives who think like fifth‑ or sixth‑grade teenagers.

Another major field that has been studied since ChatGPT became public is AI's impact on jobs. The media has published articles claiming that artificial intelligence takes away jobs from beginning white‑collar workers. I mean young people with higher education who enter the labor market through simpler assistant, intern and similar positions. Sorting letters, answering them, preparing memos and organizing documents is increasingly done by artificial intelligence, and for these positions there is no need to hire newly graduated bachelor's degree holders or applied higher education graduates.

This concerns all kinds of officials and office workers. Considering the rampant bureaucracy around us, which is needed to enforce all kinds of regulations, one must admit that we cannot do without this army of officials. Someone has to deal with these matters, not only in the public sector but also in the private sector. If we did not have payroll accountants, quality controllers or HR people, even an ordinary bell ringer or electrician would not get their salary, although we would prefer to think otherwise. We cannot escape white‑collar workers.

Entry‑level jobs now demand senior‑level skills

Less has been said about how job requirements are changing — that is, what employers expect from those entering the labor market. Some time ago, the Financial Times published a small but interesting overview of how requirements for entry‑level jobs have changed. It was based on PwC's 2026 global AI jobs barometer, which relied on the analysis of nearly one billion job s published online. Most likely AI was used to analyze such a massive database.

"Non technical skills and knowledge — those that distinguish humans from machines — are becoming increasingly important."

In summary, the report describes that our jobs are becoming increasingly professional (more complex), meaning simpler and more routine tasks are given to AI. The term "aging of jobs" is also used. In the context of the report, this means that jobs that used to be simple now require more experience, decisiveness and a broader outlook than before. In other words, jobs meant for juniors now require seniors' knowledge and skills.

Another trend is the democratization of jobs — we give a wider group of people AI tools that previously required a professional or specialist level. From an education perspective, this means that people with lower education and skill levels can solve more complex tasks thanks to artificial intelligence.

Against this background, I imagine a picture of people with relatively poor basic knowledge using powerful tools, and no one can check the results because they simply lack the prior knowledge. A rather chilling future.

Externally simple and clear trends, but they raise very large and complex tasks for the education system. How to reach a point where an executive assistant (secretary) must essentially be able to do the same work as a manager — that is, be able and willing to make decisions, have a broader picture, communicate freely with people. It seems like an impossible mission? Non‑technical skills and knowledge — those that distinguish humans from machines — are becoming increasingly important. Such skills include communication ability, creativity, empathy, strategic thinking, creating vision, ethics, decisiveness.

Education and labor market moving in opposite directions

Essentially, we must reach a point where a fresh school graduate or university graduate thinks and decides like an experienced leader. I exaggerate a bit, but we clearly see that a young person with a bachelor's degree is required to have prior work experience when applying somewhere. At the same time, universities want them to study as much as possible, not work.

The situation is made worse by what is happening in the education system: the advance of artificial intelligence reduces the role and importance of all these "human" qualities in our lives. When people sit down for a moment to pass time, or around a table waiting for a menu in a restaurant, they do not talk to each other — they are nose‑deep in their phones.

For my generation, when problems arise, it is customary to call the other party or meet — which would be even better — but younger people prefer text messages, not face‑to‑face meetings or conversations. They are rather feared.

I have seen how helpless people are in job interviews or oral exams, and that was when AI had not yet reached the masses. When they struggle with problem‑solving, they ask AI for advice. I have myself successfully repaired a Chinese robot vacuum cleaner with AI's help — it was not complicated. When they need to decide what to do in the evening, they ask AI. When relationships go wrong, they ask AI for help. Teamwork is preferred online, preferably with cameras off. This list could go on.

Human qualities losing ground to digital habits

The conclusion is rather ominous. The labor market wants increasingly mature people, and education prepares increasingly childish ones. This applies not only to general education but to the entire education system.

What are the solutions? The honest answer is that we do not yet know. Right now, the ship of education and the labor market are sailing in completely different directions. How to develop these so‑called human qualities when AI is forcefully advancing and rather inhibits the development of these skills? Do we ban computers (smartwatches, smart rings, smart glasses, etc.) in school until a certain age to force children to think with their own heads? This is more of a theoretical possibility, practically impossible to implement.

"If we do nothing, high paying jobs will be taken by specialists brought or attracted from abroad, who already have life and leadership experience."

Do we give higher education only once a person has reached a certain age and maturity? What do they do in the meantime? Serve two years in the defense forces and only then continue their education. The defense forces are a cross‑section of society, and every young man would see what group he belongs to and where he could belong. Or elite‑school bubble gymnasium students would have their eyes opened that, oh, such people also live in Estonia. There are likely more out‑of‑the‑box solutions.

Above all, the process of providing education must change — the approach to each student must become individual. In reality, more teachers are needed in classrooms, at least in the coming years. At some point, when student numbers begin to fall drastically (in about five to six years), teachers will begin to be in surplus because schools will start closing. Until then, it is necessary to attract people with practical experience who want to teach, to alleviate the shortage of mentors. This is not easy.

If we do nothing, high‑paying jobs will be taken by specialists brought or attracted from abroad, who already have life and leadership experience. There would certainly be willing candidates. Ways will be found to bring them here. AI offers more and more solutions for language problems, especially when communication is written.

About ten years ago, in an introductory course lecture, I asked first‑year economics students what they wanted to become after three years of study. Many thought they wanted to become managers immediately. I quickly dismissed this idea and explained at length that it takes 10–15 years before they can truly become managers. Adding that not everyone becomes a manager anyway, because you also need a separate gene for that.

It turns out that in today's context the students were right and I am completely outdated in my understanding. One must indeed become a manager immediately after receiving a diploma and behave, communicate and decide as if one had already done it for ten years. Tough stuff.

World.title: Ukraine hits ‘Russia’s Amazon’ warehouses outside St Petersburg
World.content:
Saint Petersburg – Ukrainian drones Friday hit warehouses for Russian e-commerce giant Wildberries for a third time in six days, this time near Saint Petersburg, triggering a fire that sent smoke pouring over the historic city.

Kyiv has accused Wildberries — Russia’s largest online retailer often known as the Russian equivalent of Amazon — of storing drone parts and helping the Russian army.

Ukraine has targeted Saint Petersburg as it steps up long-range drone strikes on Russian energy, military and logistics sites in recent weeks, calling the attacks justified retribution for Moscow’s nightly drone and missile barrage of its cities.

Russia’s defence ministry said its forces shot down some 571 drones overnight over more than a dozen regions and Crimea, the Black Sea peninsula that Russia annexed in 2014 — one of the largest one-night barrages of the war.

In Saint Petersburg, an AFP reporter saw grey smoke rising into the morning sky over high-rise residential buildings in the city, President Vladimir Putin’s hometown that is more than 800 kilometres (500 miles) from the Ukrainian border.

Wildberries said two of its logistics facilities in Saint Petersburg and one in Simferopol, in Moscow-annexed Crimea, were hit.

“Rapid evacuation was carried out at all the warehouses … according to preliminary data, there are no casualties,” Wildberries CEO Tatyana Kim said on social media.

Alexander Drozdenko, governor of the surrounding Leningrad region said three people were wounded in the attack, which saw at least 59 drones fired towards Saint Petersburg.

It was the third overnight attack by Ukraine on Wildberries’ sites in the past week.

Last weekend, eight night-shift workers were killed in attacks on Wildberries sites that saw one of the company’s main warehouses outside Moscow burn to the ground.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky alleged after the first attack that the facilities were used to “supply sanctioned components for drone production and navigation equipment.”

Hundreds of small businesses saw their inventories wiped out in the strike, triggering angry comments on social media.

Kyiv calls its strikes “long-range sanctions”, saying the attacks are justified retribution for Russia’s more than four-year offensive and nightly attacks on its cities.

The campaign has triggered nationwide fuel shortages and, Kyiv says, dented Russia’s financial war chest.

– ‘Escalation’ –

Columns of thick black smoke were still billowing into the sky from one of the factories hours after the hit, an AFP reporter saw.

Russian President Vladimir Putin spent the first years of the war trying to shield the population from the fall-out of his decision to launch the offensive on Ukraine.

But the strikes on oil refineries have triggered fuel shortages and big attacks near major cities have brought the dramatic visible consequences of the war into the homes of many Russians.

Firefighters and investigators had been deployed to the sites in Saint Petersburg as the blaze raged through the morning, Russian officials said.

Saint Petersburg’s Pulkovo airport suspended flights during the attack, resuming operations around 06:00 (0300 GMT), with around 50 departures disrupted.

Both Russia and Ukraine have escalated their long-range strikes in recent months.

Moscow’s forces have fired increasing numbers of ballistic missiles at Kyiv — killing dozens and ripping open apartment blocks.

US President Donald Trump has appeared to give his backing to Ukraine’s counter-attacks on Russia — calling the strikes “an escalation that can lead to an end”.

Washington’s attempts to mediate a peace deal between the warring sides have largely stalled with its own war on Iran raging.

The United Nations has reported a surge in civilian deaths in 2026, saying June was the deadliest month since mid-2022.

Hundreds of thousands of soldiers and tens of thousands of civilians have been killed since Russia launched its full-scale offensive in February 2022 — though there is no precise toll with neither side routinely revealing the number of their losses.

World.title: South Korean tycoon ordered to pay $644m in divorce
World.content:
Seoul – A South Korean court ordered an AI chip-manufacturing tycoon on Friday to make a trimmed-down $644 million divorce payment to his former wife.

Chey Tae-won, 65, is the chairman of the SK Group, which owns world-leading memory chipmaker SK hynix — a pillar of South Korea’s tech-led economy.

Seoul High Court in 2024 had told him to pay 1.38 trillion won ($940 million) to his ex-wife Roh Soh-yeong, daughter of a former South Korea president.

The sum — equal to more than $1 billion at the exchange rate at the time of the ruling — led local media to dub it the “divorce of the century”.

Chey appealed to the Supreme Court, which told the high court to reconsider its 2024 decision and led to the tycoon’s reduced divorce bill of 944 billion won ($644 million).

The settlement is not yet final, however, as either side may refer it back to the Supreme Court.

The acrimonious case centres on the definition and valuation of the couple’s shared assets, including Chey’s lucrative stake in the SK Group.

Seoul High Court ruled Friday that Roh was entitled to a cash payout worth one-third of the couple’s marital assets.

“The defendant’s shareholdings increased substantially during the marriage through his management activities,” the court said.

“The plaintiff contributed to that increase through homemaking, childcare and public-facing activities related to SK Group.”

Chey and Roh married in 1988, but the couple are believed to have lived apart for more than 15 years. In 2015 he admitted to fathering a child with his lover.

With SK hynix selling vital memory chips to AI computing company Nvidia, Chey’s stake is now worth roughly $5.5 billion, according to regulatory filings and public data.

Roh, 65, has three children with Chey and has built a career in the cultural space, running a digital art museum.

– Bribes –

The pair were wed in Seoul’s presidential Blue House when her father Roh Tae-woo led the country from 1988 to 1993.

They have battled over the split in the courts since 2022, after Chey filed for divorce in 2017 and mediation broke down.

The court’s original 2024 ruling ordering the payout to Roh cited a 30 billion won slush fund her ex-president father used to propel SK Group’s growth.

The court said at the time that could be counted as her contribution towards the couple’s shared assets.

But in October last year the Supreme Court quashed that argument, saying that any such cash likely stemmed from illegal bribes and therefore should not be counted.

Another question was whether the dramatic increase in SK Group’s value since the couple’s separation, on the cusp of the AI boom, should be reflected in the asset division.

“The court took into account the sharp rise in the value of the defendant’s shareholdings when determining the property division ratio,” Friday’s court statement said.

SK Group shares have more than tripled in value since December 2015, when Chey publicly disclosed his extramarital affair.

The Supreme Court had already separately ordered Chey to make an alimony payment to Roh of 2 billion won.

World.title: PepsiCo deepens Iraq partnership with manufacturing, agriculture deals
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – PepsiCo has inked agreements with two Iraqi partners to increase food and beverage production, boost agricultural supply chains, and create employment, adding to a string of US investments announced during Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s visit to Washington.

The agreements, inked during the U.S.-Iraq High-Level Business Summit organized by the US Chamber of Commerce, strengthen PepsiCo’s collaborations with Baghdad Soft Drinks Company (BSDC), its long-standing bottling partner in Iraq, and Green Iraq Company (GICO).

According to the deal with BSDC, PepsiCo will aim to increase yearly production capacity to more than 250 million beverage cases, maintaining Iraq’s position as one of the company’s major manufacturing and bottling centers in the Middle East.

The expansion is planned to create new employment in manufacturing, engineering, logistics, and distribution, as well as teach and provide technical skills to Iraqi engineers and technicians.

A separate deal with GICO seeks to increase food production capacity and agricultural productivity by bringing advanced irrigation methods and farming practices to local farmers, therefore boosting Iraq’s goal to become a regional food and beverage export center.

According to PepsiCo, the program aims to boost domestic supply chains by encouraging more local procurement and assisting Iraqi farmers in improving yields and sustainability.

The deals were part of a series of commercial understandings struck at the summit, in which US and Iraqi firms announced commitments in energy, banking, aviation, infrastructure, and manufacturing as Baghdad strives to diversify its economy away from oil and attract foreign investment.

Baghdad Soft Drinks Company has been working with PepsiCo for over four decades, and both agreements were signed on behalf of BSDC and GICO by majority stakeholder Tarek Al Hassan.

The investment demonstrates global firms’ rising interest in Iraq’s consumer products industry, as improved economic circumstances and government reforms stimulate more private sector investment and industrial growth.

World.title: Socceroos star Volpato allegedly tests positive for cocaine
World.content:
Sydney – Australian World Cup star Cristian Volpato allegedly tested positive for cocaine after he was pulled over for speeding in Sydney on Friday, police and reports said.

A New South Wales police statement said a 22-year-old man — widely identified as Italy-based Volpato by local media — was allegedly caught speeding twice overnight.

He passed a roadside breath test on the first occasion and was issued an infringement notice before being pulled over again two hours later.

This time he was drug tested and returned a positive result for cocaine, police claimed, with a second sample sent for further analysis.

“His international driver’s licence was suspended for a period of six months, withdrawing his driving privileges in NSW,” police said.

Volpato, who plays for Serie A side Sassuolo, made three appearances for the Socceroos at the World Cup after switching his international allegiance from Italy to Australia shortly before the tournament.

He was born and raised in Sydney before moving overseas and represented Italy at various youth levels.

Tony Basha, a Sydney-based coach who trained Volpato before he moved to Italy and remains a mentor, told the Sydney Morning Herald the attacking midfielder denied taking cocaine or any other illicit substance.

“He was adamant he didn’t touch it,” Basha said. “He was shocked. I’m shocked because it’s a big allegation.”

World.title: Volkswagen profit plunges as carmaker weighs mass job cuts
World.content:
Frankfurt – Volkswagen said Friday that its net profit plunged in the second quarter as the crisis-hit carmaker, weighing up to 100,000 job cuts worldwide, grapples with increasing competition in and from China.

Net profit for the three months to the end of June came in at 1.54 billion euros ($1.75 billion), the 10-brand group said, a fall of 32.9 percent on the same period last year. Last year’s figure was itself a decline of almost 37 percent on 2024.

The result was hit by a 500-million-euro charge the carmaker booked for stopping US production of its electric ID.4, Volkswagen said, as well as “negative mix effects”, meaning the automotive giant sold more lower-margin products.

The firm, which in addition to its own brand also includes the likes of Lamborghini, Audi, Skoda and Porsche, also cut its guidance for the year and said it now saw sales flat or falling up to three percent. It previously expected growth of up to three percent.

The results pile pressure on the beleaguered group, which has been suffering from slimmer margins from the sales of electric cars, US tariffs and above all intense Chinese competition.

“We must accelerate efforts to structurally lower our cost base and sustainably improve our earnings quality,” Volkswagen finance chief Arno Antlitz said. “What matters now is swift and consistent implementation.”

World.title: Iraq border in focus as Kuwait reports drone attack
World.content:
Dubai – Here are the main events related to the war in the Middle East:

– Iran blasts Trump assets threat –

Tehran said Friday that US President Donald Trump’s threat to pay for shipping damage with Iranian assets was an “incendiary precedent”.

Trump had said that Washington would start using frozen Iranian assets “that the United States has in its possession, and controls” to pay for “any and all damages done to Ships, Cargo or anything related” in the region.

– New US strikes –

The United States military said Thursday it was attacking Iran for the 13th night in a row, adding that strikes were aimed at military targets with the goal of diminishing Iranian ability to attack shipping.

Iranian state media reported that US missiles had hit the city of Ahvaz, near the border with Iraq, and explosions were heard in the port city of Bandar Abbas on the Strait of Hormuz and in Omidiyeh.

– Kuwait under attack –

Kuwaiti air defences have opened fire on incoming Iranian missiles and drones, hours after reporting a new drone attack at the border crossing with Iraq.

“Kuwaiti air defences are currently intercepting hostile missile and drone attacks following the wrongful Iranian aggression,” the general staff said in a message posted on social media.

– Trump rebuked –

The US House of Representatives passed a largely symbolic resolution calling for President Donald Trump to halt military action against Iran, delivering another congressional rebuke as the Middle East war escalates.

The measure directs Trump to remove US forces from hostilities against Iran unless Congress explicitly authorises the war.

– Houthi attacks ‘illegal’ –

Attacks on oil tankers in the Red Sea by Yemen’s Houthi militants have drawn condemnation from around Europe.

Germany said the attacks risked escalating conflicts, Britain condemned the group’s “reckless actions” and EU’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas said the attacks were “unacceptable” and “illegal”.

– UN chief warning –

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said the Middle East conflict was “getting out of control”.

“It is teetering on the edge of the unimaginable,” he said.

– Oil passes $100 –

The price of the benchmark international oil contract, Brent North Sea soared more than eight percent to reach $101.93 a barrel after Yemen’s Houthi rebels struck oil tankers in the Red Sea.

The main US oil contract, West Texas Intermediate, rose 7.6 percent to $93.44 a barrel.

– Island strike –

Iranian news outlet Tasnim reported that a US missile had hit a site near the town of Suza on Qeshm Island, in the disputed Strait of Hormuz.

– Trump threatens Houthis –

Trump threatened Yemen’s Houthi rebels with “major military punishment” after they launched missile and drone strikes at oil tankers in the Red Sea.

“The US will hold Iran responsible, in that the Houthis are a Surrogate and/or Proxy of Iran, and major military punishment will be inflicted upon Iran and, of course, the Houthis themselves” should the rebels launch further attacks, Trump said on his Truth Social network.

– Britain withdraws Iran staff –

Britain said it had withdrawn remaining diplomatic staff from Iran.

“Due to the security situation, UK staff have been temporarily withdrawn from Iran. Our embassy continues to operate remotely,” the foreign ministry said on its website.

World.title: Kuwait blames Iran afters drones hit border with Iraq
World.content:
Kuwait City — Kuwait on Thursday said drones hit its side of the border with Iraq, with one Kuwaiti official telling AFP Iran was to blame.

“The Al-Abdali border crossing was attacked this afternoon by hostile drones, resulting in material damage, but thankfully no casualties,” defense ministry spokesman Col. Saud Abdulaziz Al-Atwan said in a statement.

An Iraqi security source also confirmed the incident prior to the ministry’s statement.

World.title: Iraq, Iran sign transport, rail deals after Tehran talks
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Iraq and Iran inked an agreement and three memorandums of understanding on transportation, rail connection, and government collaboration as Prime Minister Ali al-Falih al-Zaidi wrapped up an official visit to Tehran aimed at improving bilateral relations.

According to the Iraqi Prime Minister’s office, Al-Zaidi met with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and conducted extensive conversations with key Iranian officials such as Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf and Judiciary Chief Gholam-Hossein Mohseni Eje’i.

The two sides signed an agreement on international road freight transport and shipping, as well as memorandums of understanding to extend a railway connecting Kermanshah, Khosravi, Khanqin, and Baghdad, establish a twinning agreement between Baghdad and Tehran municipalities, and collaborate on government administration and human resource training.

Iraqi ministers in charge of foreign affairs, electricity, and finance, as well as the head of the Planning Commission, signed the agreements in the presence of Al-Zaidi and Pezeshkian.

The proposed railway extension would improve overland transportation links between Iraq and Iran, as part of Baghdad’s larger plans to expand regional trade corridors and improve cross-border connectivity through investments in rail, road, and logistics infrastructure.

The visit takes place as Iraq aims to retain tight economic and political connections with neighboring Iran while simultaneously developing partnerships with the United States and Gulf nations as part of a larger drive to diversify investment and boost regional cooperation.

According to the New York Times, Iran rejected a US cease-fire proposal delivered by Al-Zaidi during the visit, while Iraqi authorities made no public comment on the claim.

World.title: 'There are Chinese projects on territories in J&K that belong to India': MEA objects to illegal occupation
World.content: NEW DELHI: Ministry of external affairs on Friday accused China of violating India's sovereignty and said that it is "illegally occupying" Indian territories in Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh.During a weekly press briefing, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said that the government objects to the Chinese projects in Jammu and Kashmir."EAM said that when it comes to sovereignty issues, it is actually India that should be and is raising them. India does not violate Chinaâs sovereignty in any manner and has been consistent," Jaiswal said."But China has been in illegal occupation of Indian territories in Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh since 1963, where Indiaâs right is officially acknowledged even by China. There are Chinese projects on territories in Jammu and Kashmir that belong to India, and we object to that," he added.

World.title: Evening news wrap: Cabinet clears tougher anti-paper leak Bill; 13 feared dead in Himachal landslide
World.content:
The Union cabinet has approved a tougher anti-paper leak Bill proposing up to 10 years in jail and a Rs 10 crore fine, signalling a major crackdown on exam fraud.

The Centre has sought more time to decide on Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation as talks with NEET protest leaders ended without a breakthrough.

Here are your top stories of the day.



Cabinet clears tougher anti-paper leak Bill with stricter penalties



The Union Cabinet has approved amendments to the anti-paper leak law, proposing a maximum jail term of 10 years and fines of up to Rs 10 crore for offenders. The Bill also seeks to raise the minimum prison sentence from three years to five years and comes amid nationwide protests over alleged NEET irregularities.

The government is expected to introduce the legislation in Parliament soon.

13 feared dead after taxi crushed by landslide in Himachal Pradesh



At least 13 people, including a six-month-old infant, are feared dead after a taxi was struck by falling boulders on the Sansari-Killar-Tandi road in Himachal Pradesh's Lahaul-Spiti district. The road had reopened earlier in the day after a landslide, but another collapse buried the vehicle, prompting a large-scale rescue operation.

The incident comes as heavy rains continue to trigger landslides across the hill state.

Govt seeks more time on Pradhan demand after second round of CJP talks



The second round of talks between the Centre and the Cockroach Janata Party ended with the government seeking time until Saturday to respond to the demand for Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation. The CJP said the government had given in-principle approval to demands for compensation for affected families and withdrawal of legal cases against protesting students, but maintained that Pradhan's resignation remains its key demand.





Sensex extends losing streak as oil prices and global concerns weigh on markets



Indian equity benchmarks ended lower for a fifth consecutive session, with the Sensex closing in the red and the Nifty50 slipping below 23,800. Investor sentiment remained under pressure due to elevated crude oil prices, Middle East tensions, foreign institutional investor selling and renewed concerns over US trade tariffs. Weakness in heavyweight stocks such as Infosys and HDFC Bank added to the decline.

Bangladesh President Shahabuddin resigns ahead of Hasina's planned return



Bangladesh President Mohammad Shahabuddin has resigned nearly two years before the end of his term, according to local media reports cited by Reuters. His resignation follows reports of differences with the government and comes days after former prime minister Sheikh Hasina announced plans to return to Bangladesh later this year. Parliament Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmad will serve as interim president until a successor is elected.

World.title: Instagram vs WhatsApp: How CJP protests are different and why that matters
World.content:
has ended his 26-day hunger strike after government assurances on paper-leak cases, examination reforms and protections for peaceful protesters, prompting PM

to wish him a quick recovery and promise fast-track courts and tougher punishment for offenders.

The story so far

Wangchuk said his decision followed lengthy negotiations and concerns about possible violence. He also urged supporters to remain peaceful.

Activist Sonam Wangchuk ended his fast after 26 days

A reshuffle of the education bureaucracy was also under way: New secretaries were appointed for higher and school education, while the incumbent handling both departments was moved to the panchayati raj ministry.

Union minister JP Nadda laid out what the government is actually offering: No cases against those who protested peacefully at Jantar Mantar or marched to Parliament on July 20, a parliamentary discussion on paper leaks and exam reforms, and "positive consideration" of compensation for NEET paper-leak suicide victims.

For a government that has publicly ruled out education minister Dharamendra Pradhanâs resignation, these shifts are a way of signalling change.

But for now, Cockroach Janta Party has vowed to continue protesting until education minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigns.

representatives and ministers have met today to arrive at some kind of settlement.

That, in brief, is the story so far. A satirical social-media page created barely two months ago has developed into a youth movement powerful enough to force a direct intervention from the PM himself.





Although its immediate cause is the NEET paper leak, the anger on the street is about something much larger.

Why CJP protest is different

Earlier protests against the Modi government could usually be placed inside identifiable social or geographical categories. The anti-CAA mobilisation came to be portrayed largely as a Muslim protest. The farm agitation remained largely concentrated among agricultural communities and in north India.

CJP protest is harder to categorise. Examination anxiety cuts across caste, religion and region.

More importantly, the movement has found resonance among aspirational middle-class families, including those that have traditionally been receptive to the BJPâs message of merit, mobility and a better future.

It is a protest that does not look political in the traditional sense. One does not need to attend party meetings or be bused to a rally to participate. Posting a reel, designing a meme, sharing a police-action video or changing a profile picture can make you a part of the protest.

You can join it from anywhere. Not necessarily be present at Jantar Mantar. That informality makes the movement easier to join and harder for established institutions to understand.

Instagram takes on WhatsApp

The CJP has unsettled the BJP by challenging it on terrain the party has dominated for over a decade: The digital public square of X and WhatsApp. The BJPâs communication model relies on organised networks, centrally crafted talking points and mass WhatsApp forwards.

Similarly, older protest movements largely lived on WhatsApp forwards and TV debates.

But CJP speaks the native language of Instagram: Reels, memes, remixes and short videos that are decentralised, irreverent and difficult to control. Students, comedians, rappers and amateur creators can produce content faster than an official communication team can rebut it.

Police action, in this case, does not necessarily suppress the movement.

It produces content for it. Every baton charge and crying student becomes distributable evidence for an online audience. Wangchukâs forcible hospitalisation similarly transformed a weakening hunger strike into a fresh source of mobilisation.

PM Modi goes selfie-style

Interestingly, the governmentâs response eventually borrowed from this new media language. PM Modi did not depend on an official statement or formal televised address.

In a selfie-style, self-recorded video released around midnight, he spoke directly to young people about paper leaks, fast-track courts and stringent punishment.

The format mattered almost as much as the announcement. It showed that the protest had forced the government to change not only its message but also its medium. To respond to the Instagram generation, Indiaâs most formidable political communicator picked up a phone, looked into the camera and spoke in the informal style of a social-media creator.

The oppositionâs awkward embrace

The protestersâ appeal comes partly from their distance from conventional politics.

But Congress, AAP and other opposition parties naturally see an opportunity. CJP, however, presents them with a dilemma. If they stay away, they surrender a rare wave of anti-government mobilisation. If they embrace it too tightly, they risk making an organic youth movement look like another opposition-sponsored campaign.

That tension was visible when Wangchukâs wife, Gitanjali Angmo, described Rahul Gandhiâs protest near the PM residence as âinsincereâ, arguing that opposition leaders should have joined the students at Jantar Mantar instead.

She also took a swing at the BJP directly, saying there was "nothing Hindu or nationalistic" about how the government had handled young protesters.

Why it matters

It would be premature to liken the cockroach protests as Indiaâs version of the Gen Z rebellions seen elsewhere in South Asia. India has always followed its unique path; democracy flourished in India when no one gave a chance after Independent.

CJP is not likely to become another JP Movement or even another Anna Hazare agitation.

Its internal contradictions could eventually weaken it. Social-media enthusiasm can disappear as quickly as it arrives, while public attention can move on to the next crisis.

But CJP has delivered a message no government can comfortably ignore: Indiaâs aspirational youth will no longer accept repeated institutional failure as an unavoidable part of growing up.

Something has already changed. A generation routinely described as distracted, politically disengaged and mainly glued to its phone has used that very phone to create a national protest.

For a generation raised on the promise of âNew Indiaâ, the last few months have been a crash course in the limits of that story.

The government, that built its brand on youth aspiration, now finds itself being judged, liveâstreamed and factâchecked by those very aspirants.

The opposition, meanwhile, is playing the catch-up game.

World.title: CJP students protest: RAF probes excessive force, pellet gun charges in July 20 crackdown
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The Rapid Action Force (RAF) has begun an internal verification of the conduct of its personnel during the July 20 student protests in Delhi, amid allegations of excessive use of force and the use of pellet guns to disperse demonstrators, officials told news agency PTI on Friday.

The Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF), under which the RAF functions, has directed the inspector general of the anti-riot unit to verify the sequence of events involving its teams during the protest, including the actions taken to control demonstrators and instances where RAF personnel themselves came under attack, officials said.

A formal Court of Inquiry has not yet been ordered. According to CRPF officials, such a probe will be initiated only if the ongoing verification establishes grounds for further investigation.

The violence erupted during the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)-led 'Chalo Sansad' march on July 20. Students had marched from Jantar Mantar towards Parliament, demanding Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation over the alleged NEET question paper leak. The protest ended in clashes with security personnel, who used batons and tear gas to disperse the crowd.

Officials told PTI that the RAF has taken cognisance of multiple videos and photographs circulating on social media showing personnel in the force's distinctive blue camouflage uniforms using lathis and firearms during the operation.





The footage also includes visuals of RAF personnel allegedly being surrounded and attacked by protesters.

"All legal procedures stipulated to examine the conduct of personnel during such operational duties will be followed," a senior officer told PTI.

Officials said the RAF is equipped with 12-bore pump-action guns, commonly referred to as pellet guns, as part of its standard riot-control equipment. Under the force's standard operating procedure (SOP), these weapons may be used only in extreme situations where personnel face a serious threat to their lives.

The SOP also requires the weapons to be fitted with a deflector so that the metal or rubber pellets cause limited injuries and are aimed only below the waist, officials said.

The verification assumes significance amid allegations that at least two students sustained pellet injuries during the July 20 clashes and were admitted to hospitals.

While the Delhi Police has denied possessing pellet guns and termed reports suggesting their use as misleading, neither the CRPF nor the RAF has publicly confirmed or denied whether RAF personnel fired pellet ammunition during the protest.

Apart from the allegations of excessive force, the verification will also examine videos showing RAF personnel allegedly being attacked by protesters, footage of an RAF uniformed man appearing to trip a running protester, and another clip that purportedly shows a stun gun being used during the clashes, officials said.

The CRPF has also instructed commanders of RAF and other units deployed during the protests not to speak to the media after comments made earlier this week by a woman RAF officer were considered "undesirable", officials said.

Separately, the force is examining social media posts allegedly made by RAF assistant commandant Sonia Sehrawat through her Instagram account to determine whether they violated the CRPF's social media policy, according to officials. The paramilitary force's 2023 guidelines prohibit personnel from commenting on controversial or politically sensitive issues online.

World.title: 'Anna part two': Congress MP accuses Wangchuk of striking a deal with govt; BJP hits back
World.content:
NEW DELHI:

MP Imran Masood on Friday targeted activist

for ending his 26-day hunger strike and accused him of "striking a deal" with the government.

Terming the climate activist "Anna part two", Masood said that just as

remained silent for 12 years, Sonam Wangchuk would also remain silent from now on.

"He is Anna (social activist Anna Hazare) part two. For 12 years, Anna has remained silent, and now Sonam Wangchuk will remain silent," the Congress MP said.

"You were striking a deal with the government yesterday; at the time, was any student present there? What else is there except your personal deal with the government?" he added.

Meanwhile, the Bharatiya Janata Party (

BJP

) latched on to Masood's remarks to target the opposition, accusing it of "stooping low."

BJP spokesperson Shehzad Poonawalla claimed that while the government successfully engaged with the protesters, Congress had resorted to insulting the climate activist through its leaders.

"How low can Congress stoop in the fight for credit? The 'Yuvraj' of Congress (Rahul Gandhi) stayed abroad for 21 days; he never visited Sonam Wangchuk, nor did he go to the Jantar Mantar protest. In fact, today, when the government spoke with the protesters and Sonam Wangchuk, and got him to break his fast, the entire country is happy about it," Poonawalla said in a video message.





"The Congress party, keeping only its ego at the forefront, along with the Aam Aadmi Party, Samajwadi Party, and CJP, is abusing Sonam Wangchuk just so he doesn't get the credit. Even Sonam Wangchuk's wife said that Congress is insincere. This is the real face of Congress; they are not with the students, they are only after the credit," he added.

This comes after Wangchuk ended his 26-day hunger strike in the presence of Union ministers JP Nadda and Jitendra Singh, saying the decision followed prolonged negotiations and was taken to avoid any possibility of violence in the country.

In a post on X, Wangchuk said he broke his fast in the presence of the two Union ministers and senior leaders of the Apex Body of Leh Ladakh. He said 65 MPs from different political parties had either visited him or signed letters urging him to end the fast.

On the other hand, the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) has called for nationwide "peaceful protests" to continue, demanding the resignation of Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan over the alleged NEET-UG 2026 paper leak.

"The Cockroach Janata Party's peaceful protest at Jantar Mantar will continue until Dharmendra Pradhan resigns," Dipke said in a statement after Wangchuk ended his hunger strike.

World.title: 'You do whatever you like?' Delhi HC pulls up EC for deploying school teachers for BLO duties during SIR
World.content:
Delhi HC pulls up EC for deploying school teachers for BLO duties during SIR

NEW DELHI: The Delhi high court on Friday questioned the Election Commission (EC) over deploying school teachers as Booth Level Officers (BLOs) for the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in the national capital, asking under what legal authority teachers were being compelled to carry out election work.Hearing a public interest litigation (PIL) challenging the deployment of government, municipal and government-aided school teachers for BLO and SIR duties, a division bench of Chief Justice Devendra Kumar Upadhyaya and Justice Tejas Karia sought an explanation from the poll body on the legal basis for its decision.During the hearing, the bench expressed reservations over the commission's reliance on Article 324 of the Constitution."Taking shade of Article 324, you do whatever you like?" ANI quoted the chief justice saying.The court also questioned the Commission's claim that teachers were serving as "volunteers", pointing out that those refusing election duties could face disciplinary action."Make a statement that this is voluntary, and we will dispose of the petition," the Bench told the Commission.Appearing for the ECI, advocate Sanjay Vashishtha argued that the Special Intensive Revision exercise in Delhi was nearing completion and that only around 10 to 14 per cent of school teachers were eventually engaged for electoral roll revision work.He submitted that the commission derives its power to requisition staff from Section 13B(2) of the Representation of the People Act and that such powers are exercised sparingly. Vashishtha also said teachers are assigned BLO duties only during holidays and non-teaching hours in line with the commission's guidelines.The bench, however, questioned why teachers should have to give up their holidays for election work."Somebody is not interested in your honorarium or compensation. Can these instructions issued by you be said to be mandatory? Can you say no, no, no, we are compensating, please come. Destroy their holidays? Don't they need rest?" the court asked.The hearing comes days after the Office of the Chief Electoral Officer (CEO), Delhi, issued a circular on July 23 directing district election authorities to ensure that teachers' academic responsibilities are not affected during the SIR exercise.

World.title: Himachal Pradesh: At least 13 feared dead after taxi crushed by boulders in Lahaul-Spiti
World.content:
Himachal Pradesh: At least 13 feared dead after taxi crushed by boulders in Lahaul-Spiti

NEW DELHI: At least 13 people, including a six-month-old infant, are feared dead after a taxi was hit by boulders on the SansariâKillarâTandi (SKTT) road near Kadu Nala in Himachal Pradesh's tribal Lahaul-Spiti district on Friday.The taxi, carrying 15 passengers from Udaipur in Lahaul Spiti to Pangi, was crushed when a large section of the hillside collapsed near Kadu Nala on the Udaipur-Killar stretch of the SKTT road.The route had been reopened earlier in the day after remaining closed due to a landslide, and the passengers, who had been stranded overnight in Tindi, had resumed their journey when the fresh slide struck.Police, local administration and rescue teams rushed to the spot and launched a rescue operation. One injured passenger was initially pulled out of the debris and shifted to hospital, while heavy machinery was deployed to clear the landslide and search for the remaining occupants.In a statement, Bharmour MLA Janak Raj said that 13 of the 15 occupants had lost their lives, including a six-month-old infant, while two people were safe. He said he was in constant touch with senior officials of the Chamba and Lahaul-Spiti district administrations to monitor the rescue and relief operations and ensure all possible assistance to the affected families.Expressing grief over the tragedy, the MLA conveyed his condolences to the bereaved families.Meanwhile, a woman from Kullu was killed and seven members of her family were injured after a boulder fell from a hillside while they were travelling to the Simsa temple in Mandi district on Friday morning.The accident occurred around 10 am near Gumma in Jogindernagar subdivision when the family, travelling in two vehicles from Sultanpur in Kullu district, stopped by the roadside to drink water. Moments later, a rock suddenly dislodged from the hillside and struck the group.The deceased was identified as Rameshwari Sharma, wife of Gopal Krishna and a resident of Sultanpur, Kullu. She died on the spot.

World.title: Delhi Police deploys facial recognition cameras at Jantar Mantar to track wanted criminals
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Delhi Police has deployed four Facial Recognition System (FRS) units around the NEET protest site at Jantar Mantar to identify wanted criminals, absconders, and habitual offenders, news agency PTI reported, citing sources.

According to the sources, the FRS units have been positioned at key entry and exit points around the protest site and are directly linked to the Delhi Police database.

"The objective is to ensure that people with criminal backgrounds do not exploit the protest to create law and order issues," sources told PTI.

"The system is connected with the Delhi Police database and can identify wanted criminals, absconders, history-sheeters, and Bad Characters (BCs) whose details already exist in police records," they added.

According to an officer, the FRS does not target ordinary protesters but is meant to identify those with criminal antecedents who may attempt to take advantage of large gatherings.

"These are high-resolution cameras capable of capturing facial images even from a distance. Once a face is captured, it is quickly matched with the police database. If a wanted or absconding accused is detected, the concerned police unit is immediately alerted, and legal action can be initiated without delay," he said.





Police said the technology will also help identify habitual offenders who have repeatedly figured in criminal cases and are listed as "Bad Characters" in Delhi Police records.

"The deployment acts as both a preventive and investigative tool. It helps us remain alert against anti-social elements who may try to infiltrate the protest, create a nuisance, or disturb law and order," another officer said.

The installation of the FRS forms part of enhanced security arrangements around Jantar Mantar.
